She has noticed herself becoming increasingly fatigued on moderate exertion. Her younger sister died suddenly the previous year and she is very worried about the risk of sudden death. Which of the following treatments is known to reduce her risk of sudden death?
answer_text: B-blocker (e.g. metoprolol) B-blockers have been shown to reduce the risk of sudden death in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 55 year old woman presents with a history of acute, severe, constricting central chest pain associated with anterior ST segment elevation on the 12-lead ECG. She immediately undergoes coronary angiography, which shows no evidence of coronary artery disease and no coronary occlusion. An echocardiogram shows left ventricular apical dilatation, with normal left ventricular basal contraction. Which of the following factors is most likely to have precipitated this illness?
answer_text: Acute emotional stress Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy is precipitated by acute emotional stress.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: The following medical treatments are all associated with improved symptoms in patients with heart failure due to left ventricular systolic dysfunction. However, which of the treatments has NOT been shown to also improve survival?
answer_text: Furosemide Furosemide improves symptoms but has not been shown to improve survival.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: An 80 year old woman presents with shortness of breath and swollen ankles. Her ECG showed some poor R-wave progression. She was referred for an echocardiogram and was found to have a high ejection fraction. Which of these conditions is the most likely cause of her presentation?
answer_text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy A high ejection fraction with symptoms suggests restrictive cardiomyopathy.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Neuroendocrine system activation is a feature of heart failure. Abnormalities of which hormone can cause heart failure rather than result from heart failure?
answer_text: Thyroxine Thyrotoxicosis can cause heart failure rather than result from it.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: An army recruit is referred for assessment because there is a family history of sudden cardiac death and an uncle was diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. In what manner is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy commonly inherited?
answer_text: Autosomal dominant Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: An 83 year old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP of 180/100 mmHg and a SaO2 of 85%. Which treatment is UNLIKELY to be helpful in this setting?
answer_text: Intravenous dobutamine Dobutamine increases cardiac work and is not beneficial in hypertensive pulmonary oedema.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 43 year old woman with a past history of breast cancer is referred with a gradual onset of breathlessness. An echocardiogram demonstrates a dilated poorly contracting left ventricle. You wish to investigate potential causes of her dilated cardiomyopathy. Which of the following would be an irreversible cause of her dilated cardiomyopathy?
answer_text: Anthracycline chemotherapy Anthracycline chemotherapy can cause irreversible dilated cardiomyopathy.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 75-year-old man presents to your emergency department appearing quite ill. His family says he has not had his normal energy for the last 6 months, and they noted he was confused and lethargic for the last day or two. As you take a history from the family, you palpate the patient’s radial pulse and notice a regular beat-to- beat variability of pulse amplitude, although his rhythm is regular. Indeed, as you later take his blood pressure, you note that only every other phase I (systolic) Korotkoff sound is audible as the cuff pressure is slowly lowered and that this is independent of the respiratory cycle. Based on this, you suspect this patient has which of the following?
answer_text: Severe left ventricular dysfunction The presence of pulsus alternans (alternating pulse amplitude) is most commonly seen in severe LV dysfunction.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 78-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with decompensated heart failure. He has longstanding ischemic cardiomyopathy. ECG shows atrial fibrillation and left bundle branch block. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and bilateral alveolar infiltrates with Kerley B lines. Which of the following is least likely to be present on physical examination?
options: Reversed splitting of the second heart sound
answer_text: Fourth heart sound A fourth heart sound is not typically found in atrial fibrillation, making it the least likely finding.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 24-year-old man is referred to a cardiologist after an episode of syncope while playing basketball. He has no recollection of the event, but he was told that he collapsed while running. He awakened lying on the ground and suffered multiple contusions as a result of the fall. He has always been an active individual but recently has developed some chest pain with exertion that has caused him to restrict his activity. His father died at age 44 while rock climbing. He believes his father’s cause of death was sudden cardiac death and recalls being told his father had an enlarged heart. On examination, the patient has a III/VI mid-systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur. His ECG shows evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy. You suspect hypertrophic cardiomyopathy as the cause of the patient’s heart disease. Which of the following maneuvers would be expected to cause an increase in the loudness of the murmur?
answer_text: Standing and Valsalva maneuver Decreasing venous return (by standing or performing Valsalva) increases the outflow gradient in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, intensifying the murmur.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 66-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for progressive dyspnea on exertion and fatigue. He has a past medical history of tobacco abuse and is widely traveled, recently returning from a multicountry trip through South America. On presentation, his heart rate is 104 bpm and irregularly irregular. Blood pressure is 96/76 mmHg. You note an elevated jugular venous pulsation and marked lower extremity edema. Echocardiogram reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%, and still images from his echocardiogram are shown in Figure V-20. To elucidate the etiology of his heart failure, which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to perform next?
options: Positron emission tomography cardiac stress test
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and light chain assay
answer_text: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and light chain assay The echocardiographic findings are suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis; evaluation for a light chain paraproteinemia is the appropriate next step.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 71-year-old woman with ischemic cardiomyopathy and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 38% has been hospitalized for the past week with acute decompensated heart failure. After diuresis and medication optimization, she is feeling immensely better. She is on the maximally tolerated doses of an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, B-blocker, and appropriate diuretic dose. You are planning for discharge today. On rounds, the nurse notes that the patient had several short (5-10 beats) runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) and multiple premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) overnight, although she remained asymptomatic. A medical student on the team asks if the NSVT carries any prognostic significance and if any intervention is needed. What is the most appropriate response?
options: “NSVT is common in patients with cardiomyopathy and carries no significance.”
“NSVT is concerning in this patient. We should suppress the PVCs and NSVT with amiodarone.”
“NSVT is associated with an increased mortal ity in patients with heart failure. We will refer her for an automated implantable defibrillator.”
“NSVT is associated with an increased mortality in patients with heart failure. We should suppress the NSVT with flecainide.”
“NSVT is associated with an increased mortality in patients with heart failure. However, suppression of PVCs and NSVT with antiarrhythmic drugs does not change this prognosis.”
answer_text: “NSVT is associated with an increased mortality in patients with heart failure. However, suppression of PVCs and NSVT with antiarrhythmic drugs does not change this prognosis.” Studies indicate that although NSVT in heart failure is a poor prognostic marker, antiarrhythmic suppression does not improve mortality.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction and congestive heart failure is comfortable at rest. However, when walking to his car, he develops dyspnea, fatigue, and sometimes palpitations. He must rest for several minutes before these symptoms resolve. Which of the following is his New York Heart Association classification?
answer_text: Class III Symptoms with exertion that resolve on rest indicate NYHA Class III.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 47-year-old postmenopausal woman is seen for onset of severe dyspnea over the last few weeks. She reports no preceding chest pain, cough, sputum, or fever, although she does report leg swelling. Physical examination is notable for a blood pressure of 145/78 mmHg and heart rate of 123 bpm. Exophthalmos is present, as well as bilateral inspiratory crackles occupying approximately one-third of the lower chest with neck vein distention. She has a third heart sound with no murmur. Bilateral lower extremity edema is also present, with warm extremities and a fine hand tremor. Which of the following is the most likely pathophysiologic explanation for her heart failure?
options: Chronic systemic hypertension with resultant left ventricular hypertrophy and nonsystolic heart failure
Myocardial infarction with depressed left ventricular systolic function
answer_text: Thyrotoxicosis with high-output state The presence of exophthalmos and tremor in conjunction with heart failure symptoms is most consistent with thyrotoxicosis.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: From a pathophysiologic perspective, all of the following are upregulated in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction EXCEPT:
options: Calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
answer_text: Calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum In heart failure, calcium reuptake is impaired rather than upregulated.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath. He is found to have an elevated serum BNP. In addition to heart failure, all of the following may also cause an elevation in BNP EXCEPT:
options: Pulmonary embolism with right heart strain
answer_text: Obesity Obesity is known to cause falsely low BNP levels.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: You are taking care of a patient with cor pulmonale in the medical intensive care unit. Unfortunately, he suffered a respiratory arrest at home and requires intubation and mechanical ventilation. Currently, with a tidal volume of 500 mL, FiO2 of 0.4, positive end-expiratory pressure of 20 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 20, his pH is 7.40, PCO2 is 40 mmHg, and oxygen saturation is 86%. You are concerned about the afterload experienced by his right ventricle. All of the following are likely to increase his right ventricular afterload EXCEPT:
options: Increasing FiO2 to increase arterial oxygen saturation to 95%
answer_text: Increasing FiO2 to increase arterial oxygen saturation to 95% Improving oxygenation reduces pulmonary vasoconstriction and RV afterload.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Mr. George is a 52-year-old man with long standing hypertension and poorly controlled diabetes. He presents complaining of several months of breathlessness with exertion, acute episodes of shortness of breath when recumbent, and lower extremity edema. On examination, he has an elevated jugular venous pulse and an S4 on auscultation. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55% with a large left atrium. You suspect this patient has the syndrome of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Drugs targeting which of the following have convincingly demonstrated mortality reduction for patients with HFpEF?
answer_text: None of the above No pharmacologic therapies have yet shown a mortality benefit in HFpEF.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: You are evaluating a 64-year-old woman with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy. She presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath. You note that she has gained 11 kg since her last cardiology appointment 2 months ago. Physical examination confirms findings associated with acute decompensated heart failure, including pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pulse, abdominal ascites, lower extremity edema, and a square wave blood pressure Valsalva response. Her extremities are warm, and blood pressure is 110/78 mmHg with a heart rate of 75 bpm. Her laboratory studies return with a sodium of 128 mEq/L and creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL (which is increased from her prior level of 1.2 mg/dL). Chest x-ray shows a diffuse alveolar filling pattern consistent with pulmonary edema. What is the next most appropriate step?
options: Insert a large-bore central IV line and prepare for ultrafiltration
Insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic monitoring
Start dobutamine at 5 pg/kg/min and titrate to a urine output of 1 mL/kg/hr
answer_text: Administer furosemide 40 mg IV Initial management should be diuresis to relieve congestion.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following statements regarding nesiritide is true in patients with acute decompensated heart failure requiring invasive hemodynamic monitoring?
options: Nesiritide has no significant effect on blood pressure.
Nesiritide improves renal perfusion in states of acute decompensated heart failure.
Nesiritide is associated with a decreased rate of rehospitalization, but not death, from acute decompensated heart failure.
Nesiritide reduces pulmonary capillary wedge more rapidly than IV nitrates.
None of the statements are true.
answer_text: Nesiritide reduces pulmonary capillary wedge more rapidly than IV nitrates. While nesiritide lowers filling pressures, its overall clinical benefits are limited.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Mr. Jones is a 21-year-old man who presents to the emergency department with several days of worsening shortness of breath and lethargy 1 week after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. His family brought him in after he lacked the energy to rise from the couch unassisted. His blood pressure is 88/72 mmHg, heart rate is 115 bpm, and room air oxygen saturation is 90%. Physical examination reveals pulmonary crackles, elevated jugular venous pressure, an audible S3 gallop, and cool extremities. He is lethargic and slow to respond to questions. Laboratory analysis reveals a creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL, elevated BNP level, and mildly elevated lactate. Bedside echocardiography reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15% with global hypokinesis. You start dobutamine at 5 µg/kg/ min and prepare to insert a pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic monitoring. Which of the following hemodynamic parameters is most likely increased?
answer_text: Systemic vascular resistance In severe decompensated heart failure, low output leads to compensatory increase in SVR.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following statements regarding the initiation of B-blockers versus ACE inhibitors in HFrEF is most correct?
options: ACE inhibitors should always be started before B-blockers.
B-blockers should always be started before ACE inhibitors.
It does not matter which is initiated first; both are essential and should be optimally titrated.
ACE inhibitors are more important than B-blockers in reducing mortality.
B-blockers have a stronger dose effect on survival than ACE inhibitors.
answer_text: It does not matter which is initiated first; both are essential and should be optimally titrated. Studies show similar outcomes regardless of which drug is started first, as long as both are titrated to optimal doses.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 22-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus is on optimal doses of the three medications forming the foundation of neurohormonal therapy for HFrEF. Which additional therapy is most appropriate at this time?
options: None – she is already on optimal therapy
answer_text: None – she is already on optimal therapy There is no additional mortality benefit from adding these agents when optimal therapy is established.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Mr. Jones is a 21-year-old man with HFrEF. Which of the following is most appropriate regarding prophylactic therapy to prevent sudden cardiac death?
options: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) placement is indicated in patients with an LVEF <35%.
ICD is indicated only in patients with NYHA class IV symptoms.
ICD placement is not recommended in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy.
ICD placement should be delayed until after 5 years of optimal therapy.
answer_text: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) placement is indicated in patients with an LVEF <35%. ICD therapy is recommended for primary prevention in patients with reduced EF despite optimal medical therapy.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 19-year-old university rower presents for the pre-Oxford–Cambridge boat race medical evaluation. He is healthy and has no significant medical history. However, his brother died suddenly during football practice at age 15. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the brother’s death?
answer_text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes in the UK. It is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the heart failure outpatient clinic with increased shortness of breath and swollen ankles. On examination his pulse was 100 beats/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg and jugular venous pressure (JVP) +10 cm water. The patient currently takes furosemide 40 mg BD, spironolactone 12.5 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg OD and ramipril 2.5 mg BD. Which of the following is true?
options: Diuretics reduce the degree of neurohormonal activation in heart failure
Diuretics alone rarely provide rapid symptomatic relief
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are unlikely to induce hypotension if an adequate diuresis has been achieved with diuretics
answer_text: Treatment with spironolactone reduces mortality Treatment with spironolactone reduces mortality along with beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors in heart failure.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 65-year-old man has NYHA class III chronic heart failure. Despite conventional therapy with appropriate dosages of a diuretic, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-adrenergic blocker, his left ventricular ejection fraction hovers around 35%, and he continues to have shortness of breath on exertion. His latest urea and electrolytes test results were normal and you consider adding digoxin to his treatment regimen. Which one of the following is true regarding digoxin therapy in this situation?
options: A reasonable dosage is 0.50 mg/day orally
Serial drug levels are generally not necessary
A loading dose will be necessary
It is not likely to improve the ejection fractions
It is the treatment of choice if the patient’s ECG shows AV block
answer_text: Serial drug levels are generally not necessary Serial digoxin levels are not generally necessary; dosing is usually in the range of 125–250 mcg daily.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and fatigue. On examination you note pitting oedema in both his lower limbs. You suspect heart failure. Which investigation is most likely to demonstrate the aetiology?
answer_text: Echocardiogram An echocardiogram is the most useful investigation to determine the cause of heart failure.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath. She comments that she feels particularly breathless when lying down and uses five pillows to sleep at night. On examination her pulse rate is regular at 122 beats/ min and her blood pressure is stable at 122/65 mmHg. You note bibasal crackles when listening to her chest. You suspect heart failure and order a CXR and echocardiogram. The following may all be features on her CXR EXCEPT?
options: Fluid in the left horizontal interlobar fissure
answer_text: Fluid in the left horizontal interlobar fissure Fluid in the left horizontal fissure is not a typical CXR feature of heart failure.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure secondary to previous MIs is on regular digoxin and furosemide without much effect. A recent echocardiogram shows global dysfunction. His renal function is normal. Which medication should be added to his management?
answer_text: ACE inhibitors ACE inhibitors are first-line in managing heart failure and can improve outcomes when added to existing therapy.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 65-year-old man presents with shortness of breath at rest. Physical examination reveals evidence of pitting oedema over the sacrum and leg oedema to the midthigh. An echocardiogram is requested which demonstrates an ejection fraction of 0.4. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
answer_text: Diuretic In a fluid overloaded patient with heart failure, diuretics are the first-line treatment.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old man with known cardiac failure comes to see his GP. He is currently on a diuretic. His GP decides to commence an ACE inhibitor. The following are all side effects of ACE inhibitors EXCEPT?
answer_text: Hypokalaemia ACE inhibitors are more commonly associated with hyperkalaemia rather than hypokalaemia.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 64-year-old man with known cardiac failure presents with acute shortness of breath and a cough productive of frothy pink sputum. He comments that he feels nauseous. On examination you note wheezes and crackles throughout his chest. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
answer_text: Furosemide Furosemide is indicated to relieve pulmonary oedema in acute heart failure.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 21-year-old fit university student with no past medical history has sudden loss of consciousness 1 hour into a gym session. CPR is administered by bystanders. On arrival of the paramedics, he has regained consciousness. What is the most effective means of preventing sudden death in high-risk patients with asymptomatic HCM?
answer_text: An implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) An ICD is the most effective modality for preventing sudden death in high-risk asymptomatic HCM patients.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: An elderly woman complains of abdominal distension, due to ascites, upper abdominal pain from an enlarged tender liver and flatulence. She is mildly jaundiced and has marked pitting of the legs. Her arterial pulse is rapid and irregular, and she is sitting propped up in bed where it is evident that her face is cyanosed, and her jugular veins are engorged and pulsating in systole. She is passing little urine and the urine contains 2+ of protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Congestive heart failure The clinical picture is consistent with congestive heart failure leading to hepatic congestion and ascites.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 31-year-old man presents with several months of shortness of breath and chest discomfort. An ECG shows evidence of T-wave flattening. You request an echocardiogram which demonstrates dilated ventricles with global hypokinesis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Dilated cardiomyopathy The echocardiogram findings are classic for dilated cardiomyopathy.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 27-year-old footballer presents with laboured breathing and chest pain. An ECG shows evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can present with LVH on ECG and symptoms in athletes.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 78-year-old woman is admitted with heart failure secondary to aortic stenosis. Which sign is most likely to be present?
answer_text: Bibasal crepitations Bibasal crepitations indicate pulmonary edema from left ventricular failure due to aortic stenosis.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 78-year-old woman with a 3-day history of shortness of breath and white frothy sputum is suspected of having congestive cardiac failure. Which chest x-ray sign is NOT typically seen in congestive cardiac failure?
answer_text: Lower lobe diversion Lower (upper lobe diversion is seen) – the other signs are typical findings in CHF.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 71-year-old man with congestive heart failure complains of nausea, anorexia, and yellow rings around lights. Which medication is most likely responsible?
answer_text: Digoxin These are classic signs of digoxin toxicity.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old man with congestive heart failure (EF 45%) desires minimal medications. What additional treatment is indicated?
options: An ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker
answer_text: An ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers improve survival in patients with heart failure.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of CHF (EF 25%), diabetes, and hypertension presents with nocturnal dyspnea and bibasilar crackles. What is the most likely etiology for his heart failure?
answer_text: Coronary artery disease Coronary artery disease is the predominant cause of heart failure in industrialized countries.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old woman with hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history presents with epigastric pain, sweating, and breathlessness for 45 minutes. ABG shows pH 7.49, pCO2 32 mm Hg, and pO2 57 mm Hg. Which abnormality best explains her condition?
answer_text: Increase pulmonary capillary pressure An MI can cause cardiogenic pulmonary edema with increased pulmonary capillary pressure.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 59-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension and diabetes is brought to the ED with worsening dyspnea. His exam reveals bibasilar crackles and hypoxemia. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
answer_text: Administer intravenous furosemide IV furosemide reduces preload and pulmonary congestion in acute decompensated heart failure.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old man with congestive heart failure (EF 25%), diabetes, and hypertension presents with nocturnal dyspnea and bibasilar crackles. What is the most likely etiology for his heart failure?
answer_text: Coronary artery disease Coronary artery disease is the predominant cause of heart failure in industrialized countries.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 71-year-old man with congestive heart failure complains of nausea, anorexia, and yellow rings around lights. Which medication is most likely responsible?
answer_text: Digoxin These are classic signs of digoxin toxicity.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old man with congestive heart failure (EF 45%) desires minimal medications. What additional treatment is indicated?
options: An ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker
answer_text: An ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers improve survival in patients with heart failure.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 66-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes presents with a 3-week history of exertional dyspnea. Cardiac exam reveals an S3 gallop. What further evaluation is most likely to show?
options: Elevated serum brain natriuretic peptide levels
Earlier onset of abnormal cardiac sound with standing
answer_text: Elevated serum brain natriuretic peptide levels An elevated BNP level is highly suggestive of congestive heart failure.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 58-year-old man with a 5-day history of worsening dyspnea and fatigue, who is a long- term smoker, has a chest x-ray showing a perihilar ‘batwing’ pattern. What is the most likely cause of his findings?
answer_text: Tricuspid regurgitation The x-ray findings are consistent with cardiogenic pulmonary edema secondary to left ventricular failure.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 15-year-old male presents to your office on the advice of his football coach. The patient started playing football this year and suffered a syncopal episode at practice yesterday. He reports that he was sprinting with the rest of the team and became lightheaded. He lost consciousness and fell to the ground, regaining consciousness within one or two minutes. He suffered no trauma during the event. He has no prior history of head injury or recent illness. He has had no prior episodes of syncope. The patient is adopted and family history unavailable. Physical examination is unremarkable. What is the best course of action regarding this patient’s syncopal episode?
options: Perform an ECG and echocardiogram. The patient may not return to competitive sports until results are available.
Perform an ECG. The patient may not return to competitive sports until results are available.
Perform an ECG. The patient may return to competitive sports pending the results.
Reassurance. The patient may return to competitive sports provided he increases his water consumption during practice times.
Reassurance. The patient may return to competitive sports with no restrictions.
answer_text: Perform an ECG and echocardiogram. The patient may not return to competitive sports until results are available. Exertional syncope → suspect HOCM with dynamic LVOT obstruction; echo diagnostic; avoid sports until workup.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old patient presents to you after a 3-day hospital stay for gradually increasing shortness of breath and leg swelling while away on a business trip. He was told that he had congestive heart failure, but is asymptomatic now, with normal vital signs and physical examination. An echocardiogram shows an estimated ejection fraction of 38%. The patient likes to keep medications to a minimum. He is currently on aspirin and simvastatin. Which would be the most appropriate additional treatment?
options: Begin an ACE inhibitor and then add a beta-blocker on a scheduled basis.
Begin digoxin plus furosemide on a scheduled basis.
Begin spironolactone on a scheduled basis.
Given his preferences, no other medication is needed unless shortness of breath and swelling recur.
answer_text: Begin an ACE inhibitor and then add a beta-blocker on a scheduled basis. Post-MI/ LV dysfunction: start ACEi/ARB early; add beta-blocker; diuretics for congestion; spironolactone for NYHA III–IV; digoxin for symptomatic systolic esp AF; nitrates symptom only.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 34-year-old woman is referred by an OB- GYN colleague for the onset of fatigue and dyspnea on exertion 1 month after her second vaginal delivery. Physical examination reveals a laterally displaced PMI, elevated jugular venous pressure and 2+ pitting lower extremity edema. Echocardiogram shows systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 30%. Which statement most accurately describes her condition?
options: This disease may occur unexpectedly years after pregnancy and delivery.
About half of similar patients will recover completely.
The condition is idiosyncratic; the risk of recurrence with a future pregnancy is no greater than average.
This condition will require a different therapeutic approach than the typical dilated cardiomyopathy.
This condition will require endomyocardial biopsy for diagnosis.
answer_text: About half of similar patients will recov er completely. Peripartum cardiomyopathy: last month pregnancy to 6 mo postpartum; multiparity, >30 y; ~50% recover, 10–20% mortality; avoid future pregnancy; ACEi contraindicated in pregnancy.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old Caucasian male presents with shortness of breath that awakens him at night. At baseline he is able to walk less than a block before stopping to catch his breath. Physical examination findings include bilateral basilar rales and neck vein distention. The patient has a known history of congestive heart failure, and his last echocardiogram revealed an ejection fraction of 25%. The patient is compliant with a medication regimen including an ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, and loop diuretic. Blood pressure is well controlled. What additional treatment should you begin next?
answer_text: Spironolactone HFrEF core: ACEi + beta-blocker; add spironolactone if NYHA III–IV, EF <35%; hydralazine–isosorbide for Black patients still symptomatic; antithrombotics/amlodipine do not improve HF.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 32-year-old male presents to your office with concern about progressive fatigue and lower extremity edema. He has experienced decreased exercise tolerance over the past few months, and occasionally awakens coughing at night. Past medical history is significant for sickle cell anemia and diabetes mellitus. He has had multiple admissions to the hospital secondary to vasoocclusive crises since the age of three. Physical examination reveals a displaced PMI, but is otherwise unremarkable. ECG shows a first degree AV block and low voltage. Chest x-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Which of the following would be the best initial diagnostic approach?
options: Order serum iron, iron-binding capacity, and ferritin level.
Order CT scan of the chest.
Arrange for placement of a 24-hour ambulatory cardiac monitor.
answer_text: Order serum iron, iron-binding capacity, and ferritin level. Sickle cell with transfusions → secondary iron overload; high ferritin/TSAT; causes diabetes and restrictive cardiomyopathy with low-voltage ECG; BNP gauges HF only.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 65-year-old female with a known history of heart failure presents for an annual check- up. She is found to have a blood pressure of 170/100 mmHg. Her current medications are furosemide and aspirin. What is the most appropriate medication to add?
answer_text: Enalapril HF with HTN: start ACE inhibitor before beta-blocker; both improve prognosis; ACEi better for BP.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 71-year-old woman is admitted with acute dyspnoea to the Emergency Department. Oxygen saturations are 94% on 28% supplementary oxygen and her respiratory rate is 30/min. A rapid B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) assay is reported as follows: BNP 62 pg/ml What is the best interpretation of this result?
options: No conclusion can be drawn from this result
Pulmonary embolism is the most likely cause of her symptoms
If a further BNP level is above 50 pg/ml after one hour then this is diagnostic of heart failure
Heart failure is unlikely to be the cause of her dyspnoea
Heart failure is highly likely to be the cause of her dyspnoea
answer_text: Heart failure is unlikely to be the cause of her dyspnoea BNP 62 pg/mL → HF unlikely; BNP <100 has high NPV for HF. Do not diagnose HF from small serial rises; consider other causes like PE with imaging if indicated.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 79-year-old man is admitted with congestive cardiac failure. Bloods on admission show: BNP 354 pg/ml Which one of the following would result from elevated BNP levels?
answer_text: Inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system BNP actions: natriuresis; vasodilation; RAAS and sympathetic inhibition. Does not reduce sodium diuresis or cause coronary vasoconstriction.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Where is B-type natriuretic peptide mainly secreted from?
answer_text: Ventricular myocardium BNP mainly from ventricular myocardium under strain; rises in HF, ischemia, valvular disease, CKD; reduced by ACEi, ARB, diuretics; causes vasodilation and natriure sis.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: You have ordered a B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) test on a patient with suspected heart failure. It has come back as being slightly elevated. Which one of the following factors may account for a falsely elevated BNP?
answer_text: COPD Chronic HF diagnosis: start with NT-proBNP for all; high → echo within 2 weeks; raised → echo within 6 weeks.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 65-year-old builder is seen by his general practitioner for worsening shortness of breath. This is not associated with any chest pain or cough. Three weeks ago he was admitted and treated for an anterior ST-elevated myocardial infarction by primary percutaneous coronary intervention. He has a background of asthma and hypercholesterolaemia. On examination his lung fields sound clear and he has a slight tachycardia of 101 beats per minute, with oxygen saturations of 96% on air and blood pressure of 145/91 mmHg. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia with anterior, concave ST-elevation in leads V1-V5 associated with deep Q waves. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Left ventricular aneurysm Persistent ST elevation >2 weeks post-STEMI without pain → LV aneurysm; Q waves persist; T waves flatten or invert. End Blocks 2025

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 32-year-old lady referred for cardiac clinic because of incidental systolic murmur at pulmonary area, with fixed splitting of second heart sound. Chest X-ray was plethoric with prominent main pulmonary artery. ECG revealed incomplete right bundle branch block. The most likely diagnosis for this presentation is:
answer_text: Atrial septal defect. The clinical findings are characteristic of an atrial septal defect. Previous CVS

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following congenital heart defects is associated with a bicuspid aortic valve
answer_text: Coarctation of the aorta Coarctation of the aorta is associated with a bicuspid aortic valve.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 18-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension is noted to have a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg in the right arm and 120/80 mmHg in the left arm. What is the most likely underlying cause of his high blood pressure?
answer_text: Coarctation of the aorta A difference in arm blood pressures in a young patient is classically seen with coarctation of the aorta, which causes elevated pressures proximal to the narrowing.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: In the same patient, what best explains the difference between the blood pressure readings in the two arms?
options: Atherosclerotic plaque in the left subclavian artery
Congenital anomaly of the brachial arteries
Coarctation of the aorta causing decreased flow to one arm
Incorrect cuff size on the left arm
answer_text: Coarctation of the aorta causing decreased flow to one arm In coarctation of the aorta, the narrowing (usually just distal to the left subclavian artery) results in lower pressures in the left arm compared to the right.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which chest X-ray finding is most typically associated with coarctation of the aorta?
answer_text: Rib notching Rib notching due to collateral circulation is a classic radiographic sign of coarctation of the aorta.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: What is the definitive treatment for coarctation of the aorta in a patient with significant symptoms?
answer_text: Surgical repair Surgical repair is the definitive treatment for coarctation when significant hemodynamic compromise or symptoms are present.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 24-year-old asymptomatic woman with a small secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) is planning pregnancy. What is the expected risk during pregnancy?
options: High risk of developing Eisenmenger’s syndrome
answer_text: Minimal risk with appropriate follow-up Small ASDs are generally well tolerated during pregnancy with minimal risk.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: In this patient, what is the risk of infective endocarditis during routine dental extraction?
options: Minimal risk, so prophylaxis is not indicated
Risk only if the defect is large
Risk only with prior endocarditis history
answer_text: Minimal risk, so prophylaxis is not indicated Current guidelines indicate that prophylaxis for infective endocarditis is not required for uncomplicated dental procedures in patients with isolated ASD.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which of the following best describes the second heart sound (S2) in patients with an ASD?
options: Wide splitting of S2 that varies with respiration
Loud S2 with a prominent P2
answer_text: Fixed splitting of S2 A fixed splitting of S2 is classically associated with an ASD due to constant left-to-right shunting.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: What is the most common electrocardiographic finding in patients with a secundum ASD?
answer_text: Incomplete right bundle branch block An incomplete right bundle branch block is frequently seen in patients with secundum ASD.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: What is the risk of developing Eisenmenger’s syndrome in a patient with a small secundum ASD?
options: Risk only if associated with ventricular septal defect
answer_text: Low risk Small ASDs rarely lead to significant pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger’s syndrome.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 17 year old male presents to the emergency department with an episode of collapse. Witnesses report he became extremely blue at the time of collapse, which occurred on walking. The patient tells you he has a history of congenital heart disease. On examination you note he is centrally cyanosed. Which of the following congenital conditions is the most likely explanation for this presentation?
answer_text: Tetralogy of Fallot Tetralogy of Fallot is characterized by right-to-left shunting leading to central cyanosis.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Which of the following is true of Eisenmenger’s syndrome?
options: Breathlessness and fatigue are uncommon symptoms
It occurs in patients with patent foramen ovale
Left to right shunting occurs because of pulmonary hypertension
Patients are peripherally but not centrally cyanosed
answer_text: Life expectancy is markedly reduced Eisenmenger’s syndrome results from long-standing shunt reversal with a marked reduction in life expectancy.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 48 year old woman registers with a new family physician. She tells the doctor she had a small hole in her heart from birth but that it did not require any treatment. On examination, pulse is 70 beats/min and regular; BP 122/76 mmHg. You detect a loud, high-pitched systolic murmur at the left sternal border, accompanied by a thrill. Which of the following conditions would explain the history and physical findings?
answer_text: Ventricular septal defect A small VSD can produce a loud murmur with a thrill despite minimal hemodynamic consequence.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: You are working in a rural health clinic in Northern India. You evaluate an 8-year-old boy who has never seen a physician. His mother tells you that he is unable to keep up with his peers in terms of physical activity. On your initial examination of his skin, you notice clubbing and cyanosis in his feet, but his hands appear normal. Without any further examination, you suspect that he has which of the following congenital abnormalities?
options: Patent ductus arteriosus with secondary pulmonary hypertension
answer_text: Patent ductus arteriosus with secondary pulmonary hypertension Differential cyanosis (clubbing limited to the lower extremities) is classic for a PDA with developed pulmonary hypertension.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Mrs. Hellwig is a 25-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) complicated by nephropathy, hemolytic anemia, and pleuritis. Her disease is well controlled on therapy. She recently discovered that she is pregnant, and presents today for prenatal counseling. She specifically is concerned about the effect her autoimmune disease may have on the infant. You tell her that the most common cardiac complication in children born to mothers with SLE is:
options: Pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular (RV) failure
answer_text: AV block Congenital AV block is the most common cardiac manifestation in infants of mothers with SLE.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: A 37-year-old woman with no significant past medical history except for a childhood murmur is evaluated for sudden-onset severe pain in her right lower extremity. Examination is notable for pallor distal to the right knee, a cold leg, and absent dorsalis pedis pulse on the right, with the left leg being normal. Which of the following studies is likely to diagnose the underlying reason for the patient’s presentation?
options: Venous ultrasound of right upper extremity
answer_text: Echocardiogram with bubble study A bub ble study can detect an intracardiac shunt (e.g., atrial septal defect) responsible for paradoxical embolism.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: You are called to see a 21-year-old man in the ER with new onset slurred speech and left hemiparesis. Auscultation reveals a systolic murmur at the pulmonic region with a diastolic rumble along the left sternal border and a fixed split second heart sound. What is the likely cause of his symptoms?
answer_text: Atrial septal defect The findings, including a fixed split S2 and mid-diastolic rumble, are characteristic of an ASD, which can allow paradoxical embolism.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 16-year-old boy is diagnosed with a small VSD on screening due to family history of HOCM. He is asymptomatic with a small left- to-right shunt. What is the most likely significant complication?
answer_text: Endocarditis Small VSDs are primarily at risk for endocarditis.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: You are helping with school sports physicals and see a 16-year-old boy who has had trouble keeping up with his peers. Which of the following auscultatory findings suggests a previously undiagnosed ventricular septal defect?
options: A systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border with radiation to the carotids; the murmur is augmented with exercise.
A systolic murmur at the pulmonic area and a diastolic rumble along the left sternal border.
A holosystolic murmur at the mid-left sternal border.
A diastolic decrescendo murmur at the mid- left sternal border.
A continuous murmur through systole and diastole at the upper left sternal border.
answer_text: A holosystolic murmur at the mid-left sternal border. VSD: holosystolic at mid-LSB; MR shares maneuvers; AS at RUSB; ASD gives pulmonic flow ± diastolic rumble; AR diastolic decrescendo LSB; PDA continuous ULSEB.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 3-day-old neonate born prematurely at 34 weeks’ gestation has been slow to wean off the ventilator since birth. On examination, she has been found to have a continuous heart murmur. An echocardiogram has detected a patent ductus arteriosus. No other structural heart abnormalities have been found. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and mildly congested lung fields. What initial treatment should be started to manage this condition?
answer_text: Indomethacin PDA closure: indomethacin or ibuprofen inhibit prostaglandins; surgery if medical fails; beta-blockers and IV fluids not helpful; prostaglandin keeps duct open when needed.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Which one of the following complications is least associated with ventricular septal defects?
answer_text: Atrial fibrillation VSD complications: right HF, pulmonary HTN, AR, Eisenmenger, IE. AF is not typical VSD complication.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: You are helping with school sports physicals and see a 16-year-old boy who has had trouble keeping up with his peers. Which of the following auscultatory findings suggests a previously undiagnosed ventricular septal defect?
options: A systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border with radiation to the carotids; the murmur is augmented with exercise.
A systolic murmur at the pulmonic area and a diastolic rumble along the left sternal border.
A holosystolic murmur at the mid-left sternal border.
A diastolic decrescendo murmur at the mid- left sternal border.
A continuous murmur through systole and diastole at the upper left sternal border.
answer_text: A holosystolic murmur at the mid-left sternal border. VSD: holosystolic at mid-LSB; MR shares maneuvers; AS at RUSB; ASD gives pulmonic flow ± diastolic rumble; AR diastolic decrescendo LSB; PDA continuous ULSEB.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 3-day-old neonate born prematurely at 34 weeks’ gestation has been slow to wean off the ventilator since birth. On examination, she has been found to have a continuous heart murmur. An echocardiogram has detected a patent ductus arteriosus. No other structural heart abnormalities have been found. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and mildly congested lung fields. What initial treatment should be started to manage this condition?
answer_text: Indomethacin PDA closure: indomethacin or ibuprofen inhibit prostaglandins; surgery if medical fails; beta-blockers and IV fluids not helpful; prostaglandin keeps duct open when needed.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Which one of the following complications is least associated with ventricular septal defects?
answer_text: Atrial fibrillation VSD complications: right HF, pulmonary HTN, AR, Eisenmenger, IE. AF is not typical VSD complication.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: One of the fallowing is true for Mobitz I second degree heart block
options: ECG shows progressive prolongation of PR intervals
answer_text: ECG shows progressive prolongation of PR intervals. Progressive prolongation of PR intervals is characteristic of Mobitz I heart block.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: The following are recognized causes of prolonged PR interval except:
answer_text: Hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia is not a recognized cause of prolonged PR interval.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: The most important complication of atrial fibrillation is
answer_text: Stroke due to thrombo-embolism Stroke due to thrombo-embolism is the most important complication of atrial fibrillation.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: 45-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department. He was found collapsed by neighbours. An ECG on arrival shows torsades de pointes. Which one of his medications is most likely to have contributed to this presentation?
answer_text: Risperidone Risperidone, an antipsychotic, can cause QT prolongation leading to torsades de pointes.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: most common cause of AF
answer_text: htn Hypertension is the most common cause of atrial fibrillation.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: The following are therapeutic options for treatment of atrial fibrillation except
options: Radiofrequency pulmonary vein isolation with ablation
answer_text: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator Implantable cardioverter defibrillator is not used as a therapeutic option for atrial fibrillation.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted with palpitations. During the cardiovascular examination you notice irregular cannon a’ waves. Which one of the following would account for this finding?
answer_text: Complete heart block Complete heart block can produce cannon a waves.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: patient with WPW and SVT which statement regarding treatment is true
answer_text: IV Adenosine IV Adenosine is used to treat SVT in patients with WPW.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 75 year old woman presents to her family physician with a 24-hour history of rapid, irregular palpitations accompanied by fatigue. In an elderly patient, what is the most likely cause of palpitations?
answer_text: Atrial fibrillation Atrial fibrillation is the most common cause of a rapid, irregular rhythm in the elderly.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 72 year old hypertensive woman presents with a history of sudden-onset, rapid, irregular palpitation. She has had several episodes over the previous 3 months, which have resolved within 1 hour. She feels tired and slightly lightheaded during episodes. From this history, which of the following most likely explains her symptoms?
answer_text: Atrial fibrillation Atrial fibrillation is the most common cause of rapid, irregular palpitations in older patients.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: An 85 year old man presents with a 6-month history of sudden episodes of lightheadedness, which last up to 15 seconds. He is admitted to hospital with an episode of syncope resulting in facial injury. Examine the rhythm strip below. Which conduction abnormality does this show?
options: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
Wenckebach (Mobitz type I) second-degree AV block
answer_text: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block Mobitz type II is characterized by sudden non-conduction of some P waves without progressive PR lengthening.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Which of the following rhythms is NOT commonly associated with sick sinus syndrome (sinoatrial disease)?
answer_text: Ventricular tachycardia Ventricular tachycardia is not typically seen in sick sinus syndrome.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 75 year old woman has a history of hypertension and diabetes. She presents with atrial fibrillation. What is her CHA2DS2-VASc score?
answer_text: 5 She scores 2 for age (≥75), plus 1 each for female, diabetes, and hypertension, totaling 5.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: The ECG below shows a regular, narrow complex tachycardia in a patient presenting with sudden-onset, rapid palpitation. Which of the following should be used first in attempting to terminate this rhythm?
answer_text: Vagal manoeuvres, e.g. Valsalva manoeuvre Vagal manoeuvres are the quickest and least invasive method to terminate supraventricular tachycardia.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: For which of the following scenarios would a permanent pacemaker be an appropriate treatment?
options: Prevention of sudden death due to ventricular fibrillation
Sick sinus syndrome associated with syncope
answer_text: Sick sinus syndrome associated with syncope Permanent pacemakers are indicated for symptomatic bradycardia due to sick sinus syndrome.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Which of the following is associated with excessive alcohol consumption?
answer_text: Atrial fibrillation Excessive alcohol consumption is associated with atrial fibrillation (and dilated cardiomyopathy).

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old African American woman with no past medical history presents precipitously to the emergency department with syncope and the electrocardiogram (ECG) noted in Figure V-3A below. You also note painful subcutaneous nodules on her legs (similar to those pictured in Figure V-3B below). You suspect that the cardiac and skin abnormalities are most likely due to:
answer_text: Sarcoidosis The combination of complete heart block on ECG and leg lesions resembling erythema nodosum is most consistent with sarcoidosis.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following is represented in the ECG shown in Figure V-13?
options: S1Q3T3 (McGinn-White pattern) indicative of right ventricular strain
answer_text: Right bundle branch block The ECG shows a classic rSR’ pattern in V1 and a broad terminal S wave in lateral leads, indicative of RBBB.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Mr. Hendricks is a 21-year-old sommelier at a well-known restaurant in the city. His primary hobby is competitive bicycle racing, and he has a 150-km race coming up next weekend for which he has been training for the last 6 months. The race coordinators require every competitor to complete a comprehensive cardiovascular assessment prior to competing, and thus he comes to visit your clinic. On your assessment, you note a resting heart rate of 45 bpm with an occasional pause of up to 2 seconds. His blood pressure is 108/72 mmHg. He feels well and reports no syncopal or presyncopal episodes at rest or during exercise. Aside from the bradycardia, you note no other abnormalities on his examination. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with a PR interval of 128 msec, QRS duration of 80 msec, and occasional pauses as long as 2.2 seconds. Which of the following would be appropriate advice for Mr. Hendricks?
options: Perform electrophysiologic evaluation for consideration of a pacemaker.
He should not compete in the upcoming race due to concern for bradycardia and will need a tilt table test.
No further follow-up is needed. Good luck with the race!
He should undergo a treadmill stress ECG to determine the presence of chronotropic competence.
answer_text: No further follow-up is needed. Good luck with the race! In highly trained athletes, mild sinus bradycardia with occasional pauses is a normal finding.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old man is undergoing an electrophysiology study for evaluation of syncope. After careful venous cannulation and placement of conductance and pacing catheters and after administration of 0.2 mg/kg of propranolol and 0.04 mg/kg of atropine, his heart rate is 65 bpm. After stopping the drugs and allowing adequate time for washout, his superior/lateral right atrium is paced 140 bpm. On cessation of this overdrive pacing, his next sinus beat occurs 1800 msec later. Based on these observations, this patient can be diagnosed with which of the following?
answer_text: SA nodal disease A prolonged sinus node recovery time indicates SA nodal dysfunction.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: All of the following are reversible causes of SA node dysfunction EXCEPT:
answer_text: Radiation therapy Radiation therapy causes permanent (intrinsic) SA node damage unlike the other reversible causes.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following is a risk factor for development of thromboembolism in patients with the tachycardia-bradycardia variant of sick sinus syndrome?
options: None of the above; there is no increased risk of thromboembolism with the tachycardia-bradycardia variant of sick sinus syndrome
answer_text: Atrial enlargement Atrial enlargement in creases the risk of thromboembolism in sick sinus syndrome.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Normal cells within the AV node exhibit a property known as decremental conduction. If you wanted to demonstrate this property during an electrophysiology study, what maneuver could you perform?
options: Pace the right atrium at serially decreasing cycle length and measure the pace-to-His conduction time.
Pace the ventricle and record right atrial potentials.
Administer atropine 0.04 mg/kg and record AV nodal conduction time by measuring the time it takes an atrial pacing beat to reach the His bundle.
Administer metoprolol 10 mg intravenously and record AV nodal conduction time by measuring the time it takes an atrial pacing beat to reach the His bundle.
Administer adenosine 12 mg intravenously and record the AV nodal recovery time.
answer_text: Pace the right atrium at serially decreasing cycle length and measure the pace-to-His conduction time. This maneuver demonstrates the slowing of AV conduction with increasingly rapid atrial rates.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: An 87-year-old man with a history of well-treated hypertension and aortic stenosis has become symptomatic from his aortic stenosis over the last 2 months. Yesterday, he underwent surgical aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic 25-mm valve with excellent intraoperative results. He was rapidly weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass and extubated within 24 hours. Per surgical protocol, he had temporary epicardial pacing wires placed on the ventricular surface and has been pacing at 90 bpm. On rounds this morning, you briefly pause his ventricular pacing to check his underlying rhythm. You note an atrial rate of 80 bpm, but a ventricular rate of 32 bpm with a wide QRS complex. There is no relationship between the P waves and QRS complexes. This patient’s ventricular bradycardia is most likely due to which of the following?
options: Development of a systemic disease such as sarcoidosis or Lyme disease causing AV node dysfunction
Endocarditis of the new aortic bioprosthesis causing AV node block
Slowed AV nodal recovery after overdrive pac ing
Surgical injury to the AV node
answer_text: Surgical injury to the AV node Postoperative AV block due to surgical injury to the conduction tissue is common after valve surgery.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Mr. Hoffman, an 82-year-old former tightrope performer, presents to your office for complaints of syncope. He states that twice in the past week, he has spontaneously passed out with no warning symptoms. Once, he struck his face, and you note that he has periorbital ecchymosis on exam. Other than this, you find nothing abnormal on examination. You request an ECG and step out of the room to begin your documentation. Shortly thereafter, your medical assistant requests your urgent presence in Mr. Hoffman’s clinic room. He had another “spell” during the ECG and lost consciousness. Serendipitously, the medical assistant captured the spell on ECG, pictured in Figure V-30. What type of AV block is present and is matched to the appropriate treatment or diagnostic test?
options: Complete SA nodal block - Permanent pacemaker implantation
Second-degree Mobitz type II SA nodal block - Exercise treadmill study
Second-degree Mobitz type I AV block - No intervention necessary
Second-degree Mobitz type II AV node block - Permanent pacemaker implantation
answer_text: Second-degree Mobitz type II AV node block - Permanent pacemaker implantation The ECG and clinical picture are indicative of a high- grade infranodal block requiring pacemaker therapy.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 19-year-old long-distance runner, who finished in the top 10 of the local marathon last year, presents for cardiac evaluation after his primary care physician ordered a Holter monitor for screening purposes. On his Holter report, several episodes of second-degree, Mobitz I (Wenckebach) AV block were noted, all occurring during sleep. The patient reports no symptoms but thinks he may have a grandfather who had a pacemaker implanted at an advanced age. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Serologic testing including thyroid-stimulating hormone levels
answer_text: Reassurance Asymptomatic Mobitz I block in young athletes is a normal variant and requires no further workup.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 47-year-old woman with a history of tobacco abuse and ulcerative colitis is evaluated for intermittent palpitations. She reports that for the last 6 months, every 2-4 days she notes a sensation of her heart “flip-flopping” in her chest for approximately 5 minutes. She has not noted any precipitating factors and has not felt light headed or had chest pains with these episodes. Her physical examination is normal. A resting ECG reveals sinus rhythm and no abnormalities. Aside from checking serum electrolytes, which of the following is the most appropriate testing?
options: Abdominal computed tomography (CT) with oral and intravenous (IV) contrast
Reassurance with no further testing needed
answer_text: Event monitor Given the intermittent nature of her symptoms, an event monitor is preferred over a Holter for capturing infrequent episodes.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: After further testing, the patient in Question V-32 is found to have several episodes of atrial premature contractions. Which of the following statements regarding the dysrhythmia in this patient is true?
options: Atrial premature contractions are less common than ventricular premature contractions on extended ECG monitoring.
Echocardiography is indicated to determine if structural heart disease is present.
Metoprolol should be initiated for symptom control.
The patient should be reassured that this is not a dangerous condition and does not require further evaluation.
The patient should undergo stress test to determine if ischemia is present.
answer_text: The patient should be reassured that this is not a dangerous condition and does not require further evaluation. Atrial premature contractions in an otherwise healthy patient are benign.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Ms. Milsap is an 18-year-old high school volleyball star with a sports scholarship to the local university. As part of her admission process, she is required to undergo a full medical assessment prior to taking part in collegiate sports. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities, although she reports the rare episode of palpitations and light-headedness. ECG reveals a PR interval of 0.06 msec, QRS duration of 140 msec, and a slurred upstroke or delta wave in the initial part of the QRS. You correctly diagnose this as Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern. Which of the following findings is reassuring that Ms. Milsap will suffer no ill effects or need catheter ablation due to this abnormality?
options: Ability to increase the heart rate to 185 bpm on an exercise treadmill test
Electrophysiology study demonstrating that the accessory pathway has both antegrade and retrograde conduction properties
Electrophysiology study demonstrating that the accessory pathway is located in the posteroseptal region.
Exercise treadmill study demonstrating disappearance of the delta wave and wide QRS at a heart rate of 120 bpm
Holter monitoring demonstrating occasional runs of atrial fibrillation
answer_text: Exercise treadmill study demonstrating disappearance of the delta wave and wide QRS at a heart rate of 120 bpm Loss of preexcitation at higher heart rates indicates a low-risk accessory pathway.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: An 85-year-old woman with no prior cardiac history presents to the emergency department with 2 hours of palpitations. Blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and heart rate are normal, although you note an irregularly irregular rhythm on examination. ECG shows an irregularly irregular, narrow QRS without discernable P waves at a rate of 75 bpm. Echocardiogram reveals no structural heart disease. Despite the nor mal heart rate, the patient is quite symptomatic with her atrial fibrillation and wants to pursue achievement of sinus rhythm. All of the following interventions may be beneficial EXCEPT:
answer_text: Adenosine intravenously Adenosine is not effective for conversion of atrial fibrillation.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 79-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, ischemic cardiomyopathy with a last left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction of 30%, and hypertension presents to your office with no new complaints. Blood pressure is 108/56 mmHg, heart rate is 88 bpm, and arterial oxygen saturation is 98%. His rhythm strip is shown in Figure V-36. Based on this ECG, the patient now has a definite (class I) indication for which of the following therapies?
options: Systemic anticoagulation with warfarin or a novel oral anticoagulant
Transesophageal echocardiography followed by direct current (DC) cardioversion
answer_text: Systemic anticoagulation with warfarin or a novel oral anticoagulant In patients with atrial fibrillation and structural heart disease, systemic anticoagulation is indicated.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 43-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department after sudden onset of palpitations 30 minutes prior to her visit. She was seated at her work computer when the symptoms began. Aside from low back pain, she is otherwise healthy. In triage, her heart rate is 178 bpm and blood pressure is 98/56 mmHg with normal oxygen saturation. On physical examination, she has a “frog sign” in her neck and tachycardia but is otherwise normal. ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia without identifiable P waves. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step to manage her tachycar dia?
answer_text: Carotid sinus massage Increasing vagal tone via carotid sinus massage is first-line for AV nodal reentrant tachycardia.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following statements regarding restoration of sinus rhythm after atrial fibrillation is true?
options: Dofetilide may be safely started as an outpatient.
In patients who are treated with pharmacotherapy and are found to be in sinus rhythm, a prolonged Holter monitor should be worn to determine if anticoagulation can be safely stopped.
Patients who have pharmacologically maintained sinus rhythm after atrial fibrillation have improved survival compared with patients who are treated with rate control and anticoagulation.
Recurrence of atrial fibrillation is uncommon when pharmacotherapy is used to maintain sinus rhythm.
answer_text: In patients who are treated with pharmacotherapy and are found to be in sinus rhythm, a prolonged Holter monitor should be worn to determine if anticoagulation can be safely stopped. Studies show asymptomatic recurrences; prolonged monitoring is needed before stopping anticoagulation.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A young woman is brought to the emergency department after witnesses observed her suddenly lose consciousness while jogging in the nearby park. She has a fractured nose and broken teeth from her fall. She does not have identification. She is nonresponsive to painful stimuli. Blood pressure is 50/palp and heart rate is close to 280 bpm. A 12-lead ECG is shown in Figure V-40. What is the next most appropriate step?
options: Emergent CT scan with contrast to evaluate for pulmonary embolism
answer_text: DC defibrillation The patient is hemodynamically unstable with a very high rate; immediate cardioversion (defibrillation) is indicated.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: What is the underlying rhythm in the patient in Question V-40?
options: Atrial fibrillation with antegrade conduction through an accessory tract
answer_text: Atrial fibrillation with antegrade conduction through an accessory tract The very high rate in an unstable patient suggests AF with preexcitation through a non-decremental accessory pathway.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented 3 hours ago to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain and dyspnea of acute onset. There, ST elevations were noted in the anterior and lateral leads on his ECG, and thrombolytics were administered. He was admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit. Now, his nurse calls you to his room because he is having unusual tracings on his monitor. A sample rhythm strip recorded from lead Vg is shown in Figure V-42. What rhythm does this represent?
options: Complete heart block with a junctional escape
Normal sinus rhythm with a left bundle branch block
answer_text: Idioventricular rhythm A slow ventricular rhythm (<100 bpm) without P waves is indicative of an idioventricular rhythm, often seen post-reperfusion.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Ms. Milsap is an 18-year-old high school volleyball star with a sports scholarship to the local university. As part of her admission process, she is required to undergo a full medical assessment prior to taking part in collegiate sports. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities, although she reports the rare episode of palpitations and light-headedness. ECG reveals a PR interval of 0.06 msec, QRS duration of 140 msec, and a slurred upstroke or delta wave in the initial part of the QRS. You correctly diagnose this as Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern. Which of the following findings is reassuring that Ms. Milsap will suffer no ill effects or need catheter ablation due to this abnormality?
options: Ability to increase the heart rate to 185 bpm on an exercise treadmill test
Electrophysiology study demonstrating that the accessory pathway has both antegrade and retrograde conduction properties
Electrophysiology study demonstrating that the accessory pathway is located in the posteroseptal region.
Exercise treadmill study demonstrating disappearance of the delta wave and wide QRS at a heart rate of 120 bpm
Holter monitoring demonstrating occasional runs of atrial fibrillation
answer_text: Exercise treadmill study demonstrating disappearance of the delta wave and wide QRS at a heart rate of 120 bpm Disappearance of preexcitation during exercise indicates a low-risk accessory pathway.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 47-year-old woman who is maintained on methadone for a prior history of narcotic abuse recently contracted an upper respiratory tract infection, and her friend offered her some leftover erythromycin pills. Today, she felt multiple episodes of palpitations and light-headedness, prompting presentation to the emergency department. There, a rhythm strip demonstrated multiple nonsustained runs of the arrhythmia featured in Figure V-47. You administer 2 mg of IV magnesium sulfate; however, the episodes of nonsustained arrhythmia do not abate. Her laboratory examination shows a normal potassium level. What is the next most appropriate step?
options: Metoprolol 5 mg IV repeatedly until her resting heart rate is 60 bpm
IV isoproterenol infusion titrated to a rate of 100-120 bpm
answer_text: IV isoproterenol infusion titrated to a rate of 100-120 bpm In drug-induced long QT syndrome with torsades de pointes, increasing the heart rate with isoproterenol can suppress arrhythmia.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: In an ECG with wide complex tachycardia, which of the following clues most strongly supports the diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia?
options: Classic right bundle branch block pattern
Irregularly irregular rhythm with changing QRS complexes
Slowing of rate with carotid sinus massage
answer_text: Atrial-ventricular dissociation AV dissociation is a hallmark of ventricular tachycardia.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: An 18-year-old man with no prior past medical history presents for his required medical assessment before beginning his freshman year at the local university. His history and examination uncover no concerning symptoms or signs. However, his ECG shows an irregular rhythm and is pictured in Figure V-49. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Electrophysiology study and planned ablation of an ectopic atrial focus
Holter monitor to define arrhythmia burden
answer_text: Reassurance The ECG demonstrates sinus arrhythmia, a normal variant in young adults.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Ms. Hardy is a 22-year-old triathlete with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus. Unfortunately, her pharmacy provided her with an expired batch of insulin due to a clerical error, and she presented to the hospital in diabetic ketoacidotic crisis 3 days ago. With aggressive hydration, electrolyte repletion, and insulin administration, her ketoacidotic crisis was reversed. She is feeling much better and is planned for discharge tomorrow. You are called by the monitor station and told that Ms. Hardy is bradycardic. Her ECG is shown in Figure V-50. You check on her and note that she is sleeping soundly. The anatomic location of her heart block is likely where?
answer_text: AV node The presence of a narrow QRS with 2:1 block in a young, asymptomatic athlete suggests an AV nodal (Wenckebach) block.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: If you were to administer atropine intravenously to Ms. Hardy, the patient in Question V-50, you would expect which of the following to occur?
options: Increase sinus rate and maintain 2:1 AV block
Increase sinus rate and improve heart block to 1:1 conduction
Increase sinus rate and worsen heart block to >2:1
No change in sinus rate and worsen heart block to >2:1
answer_text: Increase sinus rate and improve heart block to 1:1 conduction Atropine improves AV nodal conduction in cases of nodal block.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: An 87-year-old man with Parkinson disease takes levodopa. After running out of his medication and failing to obtain a refill, he presents to the emergency department with a parkinsonian exacerbation. On initial evaluation, he has the ECG shown in Figure V-52. Which of the following is the next most appropriate step?
options: Check serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and obtain targeted respiratory history
answer_text: No further testing or intervention The ECG demonstrates tremor artifact rather than true arrhythmia, requiring no intervention.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Mr. Tillman is a 68-year-old man with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy, hypertension, and a transient ischemic attack 6 months ago with no obvious cause after appropriate workup. He presents to the emergency department with 5 days of not feeling well. On examination, he appears tired. Blood pressure is 110/78 mmHg, and his heart rate is 150 bpm. His jugular veins are not distended and lungs are clear. His ECG is pictured in Figure V-53. You appropriately administer 5 mg of IV metoprolol twice, which brings his heart rate down to 75 bpm. He feels much better. You consult the cardiac electrophysiologist for consideration of ablation of the etiologic arrhythmia. What is the next most appropriate step?
answer_text: Systemic anticoagulation Patients with atrial flutter are at risk for thromboembolism and require anticoagulation before rhythm conversion.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Ms. Schoop is a 22-year-old pottery store owner who presents to you for evaluation of palpitations. Her ECG is pictured in Figure V-54. She likely has a bypass accessory tract located in the:
answer_text: Right ventricle The ECG features of WPW localize the accessory pathway to the right ventricle.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: Mr. Cooper underwent tPA administration for acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction 1 hour previously. He had an excellent response with resolution of his ST-segment elevation and chest pain. However, the nurse pages you to evaluate a change in his rhythm. You note a wide complex ventricular rhythm with a rate of 75 bpm. Mr. Cooper continues to feel well without new symptoms, and his blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. The next most appropriate therapeutic maneuver is which of the following?
options: Administer amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes
Administer metoprolol 5 mg IV every 5 minutes × 3
answer_text: Continue observation Accelerated idioventricular rhythm post-reperfusion is benign and requires no treatment.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 73-year-old woman complains of suddenonset chest pain. On examination you note her pulse is regular at 53 beats/min. You request an electrocardiogram (ECG) which demonstrates a time interval of 3 seconds between each consecutive P wave. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Sick sinus syndrome Sick sinus syndrome is characterized by a prolonged interval between P waves, indicating sinoatrial node dysfunction.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 63-year-old man complains of gradual-onset chest pain. On examination you note his pulse is regular at 60 beats/min. You request an ECG which demonstrates an increasing PR interval which eventually culminates in an absent QRS complex after the P wave. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Mobitz type 1 block Mobitz type 1 block (Wenckebach phenomenon) is characterized by progressively lengthening PR intervals until a beat is dropped.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 28-year-old man with no past medical history and not on medications presents to the emergency department with palpitations for several hours and was found to have supraventricular tachycardia. Carotid massage was attempted without success. What is the treatment of choice to stop the attack?
answer_text: IV adenosine IV adenosine is the treatment of choice for terminating supraventricular tachycardia.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
