stem: A 75-year-old cigarette smoker with known ischaemic heart disease and a history of cardiac failure presents to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of increasing dyspnoea. His ECG shows a narrow complex regular tachycardia with a rate of 160 beats/min. What is the most appropriate initial step in patient care?
options: His heart rate should be slowed using IV atenolol to aid in the diagnosis of the rhythm
He should be given a single IV dose of lignocaine (50 mg) followed by an infusion at 4 mg/ min
He should be given IV adenosine to aid in the diagnosis of the rhythm
His rhythm may represent a ventricular tachycardia and he should be immediately cardioverted
He should not be given high flow oxygen
answer_text: He should be given IV adenosine to aid in the diagnosis of the rhythm IV adenosine can help to slow the heart rate and unmask the underlying rhythm in narrow complex tachycardias.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 57-year-old man comes to his general practitioner (GP) concerned about his general health. He is particularly worried as there is a strong family history of heart disease. The GP performs an ECG which shows a prolonged PR interval of 0.3 seconds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: First-degree AV block A prolonged PR interval of 0.3 seconds is indicative of first-degree AV block.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 75-year-old man is referred by the GP to the cardiology outpatient clinic. The patient has atrial fibrillation (AF) and hypertension. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 124/80 mmHg and his pulse varies between 90 and 130 beats/min. His last echocardiogram (done 1 month ago) revealed left atrial chamber dimensions that are increased above normal. What is the most effective management?
answer_text: Digoxin, with warfarin Rate control with digoxin and anticoagulation with warfarin is appropriate given the risk of thromboembolism in AF with enlarged atria.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: You are a house officer on call when a nurse bleeps you to review an ECG. The ECG demonstrates an intermittent absence of the QRS complex but no evidence of progressive PR interval increase. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Mobitz type 2 block Mobitz type 2 block is characterized by intermittent non-conducted P waves without prior PR prolongation.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: You are a house officer on call when you are bleeped to see a patient complaining of dizziness. On further questioning the patient comments that he has blacked out on several occasions in the past. You perform an ECG which shows regular P and QRS complexes occurring independently of one another. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Complete heart block Complete heart block with dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity can cause blackouts and dizziness, often requiring pacemaker insertion.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: You are a house officer on call when you are asked to see a 48-year-old man who is found to be unresponsive by the nursing staff. You cannot obtain a palpable carotid pulse and the cardiac monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the first appropriate measure?
options: One ampoule injection of IV calcium chloride
One ampoule injection of IV adrenaline
answer_text: Defibrillation with 200 J In ventricular fibrillation, immediate defibrillation is the first step according to advanced life support guidelines.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A medical student attending a teaching session on ECG interpretation. The consultant tells you that a patient was admitted to the coronary care unit with an atrial rate of 300 beats/min and a ventricular rate of 150 beats/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Atrial flutter Atrial flutter with a 2:1 block typically presents with an atrial rate of 300 and a ventricular rate of 150.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: You are a house officer on call when you are asked to review a patient in the coronary care unit. You note that the patient has an atrial rate of 300 beats/ min and a ventricular rate of 150 beats/min. The nurse says this is of new onset. Which management plan would you instigate first?
answer_text: Electrical cardioversion Electrical cardioversion is the initial management for new onset atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A previously fit and well 36-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 2-month history of palpitations and sweats. These attacks come on suddenly and are unrelated to food intake, supine posture or exercise. She is a nonsmoker and does not drink alcohol. Which of the following investigations is the LEAST useful to evaluate this patient?
answer_text: Upper gastrointestinal study An upper gastrointestinal study is not useful in evaluating palpitations unrelated to gastrointestinal symptoms.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 57-year-old Bangladeshi patient is admitted to accident and emergency (AE) with palpitations. He speaks very little English but tells you he has a ‘heart problem’. On examination you note his pulse is irregular at 145 beats/min. An ECG is performed which demonstrates no P waves. Which management plan would you instigate first?
answer_text: Bisoprolol Beta-blockers like bisoprolol are the initial management for rate control in atrial fibrillation.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 37-year-old woman is complaining of palpitations following recent surgery. On examination her pulse rate is regular at 175 beats/min and blood pressure is stable at 125/70 mmHg. She tells you she was seen the night before by the on-call cardiologist for the same problem. Her past medical history includes asthma. You request an ECG which shows normal-shaped QRS complexes but no P waves. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
answer_text: Carotid sinus massage Carotid sinus massage is a useful non-pharmacological maneuver to manage SVT, especially when adenosine is contraindicated due to asthma.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 16-year-old boy athlete is brought to AE after he collapsed during football training. On arrival, he appears alert and orientated. His vital signs and physical examination are normal. He remembers feeling dizzy prior to collapsing but cannot recall much else. He is normally healthy and not on any regular medications. Blood tests have been sent. What is the most appropriate next step for this patient?
answer_text: Order an ECG An ECG is essential in evaluating syncope in an athlete to rule out cardiac causes.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: An otherwise healthy 50-year-old male presents to the GP with palpitations and is noted to have an irregular heartbeat. He is otherwise fit and healthy. This resolves without treatment. Total duration was less than 2 hours. Full blood count, metabolic profile, thyroid studies, ECG and echocardiogram were all normal. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate treatment?
answer_text: Do nothing In the absence of document ed arrhythmia and with normal investigations, no treatment is necessary.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted to the coronary care unit (CCU) with unstable angina. She is started on appropriate medication to reduce her cardiac risk. She is hypertensive, fasting glucose is normal and cholesterol is 5.2. She is found to be in atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate treatment?
answer_text: Warfarin Anticoagulation with warfarin is indicated in high-risk patients with atrial fibrillation to reduce stroke risk.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 21-year-old man is on his way home from a party when he experiences the sudden onset of rapid palpitations. He feels uncomfortable but not short of breath and has no chest pain. He goes to the nearest accident and emergency department, where he is found to have a supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) at a rate of 170/ minute. Carotid sinus massage produced transient reversion to sinus rhythm, after which the tachycardia resumed. What would be the next step in your management?
answer_text: IV adenosine IV adenosine is the drug of choice for terminating SVT due to its rapid onset and offset.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 29-year-old woman goes to see her GP complaining of fatigue and palpitations. She says she has also lost weight, though without dieting. On examination, her pulse rate is approximately 120/min and irregularly irregular. Her blood pressure is 142/89 mmHg and her body mass index is 19. There are no added cardiac sounds. The ECG confirms the diagnosis of atrial fibrillation. What would you suggest as the most useful next investigation?
answer_text: Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4) Thyrotoxicosis is a common cause of new-onset atrial fibrillation in young patients.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 62-year-old male presents with palpitations, which are shown on ECG to be atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of approximately 130/minute. He has mild central chest discomfort but is not acutely distressed. He first noticed these about 3 hours before coming to hospital. As far as is known this is his first episode of this kind. Which of the following would you prefer as first-line therapy?
options: Anticoagulate with heparin and start digoxin at standard daily dose
Administer bisoprolol and verapamil, and give warfarin
Wait to see if there is spontaneous reversion to sinus rhythm
answer_text: Attempt DC cardioversion Acute onset favors DC cardioversion without prior anticoagulation.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: In the ICU, a patient suddenly becomes pulseless and unresponsive, with cardiac monitor indicating ventricular tachycardia. The crash cart is immediately available. What is the best first therapy?
answer_text: Defibrillation Defibrillation is the standard first-line treatment for ventricular fibrillation or unstable VT.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 36-year-old man presents with the sensation of a racing heart. His blood pressure is 110/70, respiratory rate 14/minute, and O2 saturation 98%. His ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia with rate 180, which you correctly diagnose as paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Carotid massage and Valsalva maneuver do not improve the heart rate. Which of the following is the initial therapy of choice?
options: Verapamil 2.5 to 5 mg IV over 1 to 2 minutes
answer_text: Adenosine 6-mg rapid IV bolus Adenosine is the drug of choice for SVT due to its safety and short half-life.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old woman develops chest pain, respiratory distress, and confusion after right hip replacement surgery. She is confused and appears in respiratory distress. Blood pressure is 80/50, heart rate of 155/minute. ECG reveals atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the best management of this patient’s arrhythmia?
answer_text: Immediate electric cardioversion Immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated in hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 69-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and asthma is evaluated. Which statement regarding her management is correct?
options: Digoxin effectively prevents recurrence of the arrhythmia
Flecainide orally may be an effective as-needed treatment to abort an attack
answer_text: Flecainide orally may be an effective as-needed treatment to abort an attack Flecainide is recommended as an as-needed treatment; other agents are either ineffective or contraindicated in her context.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 67-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of shortness of breath. On exam, his pulse is irregular at 140 bpm. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. What JVP finding would you expect?
answer_text: Absent ‘a waves’ Atrial fibrillation results in absent ‘a waves’ due to loss of effective atrial contraction.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 56-year-old man presents with exertional chest tightness relieved by rest. ECG reveals first degree heart block. Which ECG finding is typical?
answer_text: PR interval > 200 ms First degree heart block is defined by a PR interval >200 ms.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: An 82-year-old white female is admitted to the hospital for observation after presenting to the emergency department with dizziness. After being placed on a cardiac monitor in the ER, the rhythm strip below was recorded. There is no past history of cardiac disease, diabetes, or hypertension. With prompting, the patient discloses several prior episodes of transient dizziness and one episode of brief syncope in the past. Physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best plan of care?
options: Reassurance. This is a benign condition, and no direct therapy is needed.
Reassurance. The patient may not drive until she is symptom free, but otherwise no direct therapy is needed.
Nuclear cardiac stress testing; treatment depending on results.
Arrange placement of a permanent pacemaker.
answer_text: Arrange placement of a permanent pacemaker. Tachy-brady syndrome with symptomatic pauses → pacemaker; may still need antiarrhythmic for tachy; consider anticoagulation; aspirin in sufficient.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 30-year-old female presents with a chief complaint of palpitations. A 24-hour Holter monitor shows occasional unifocal premature ventricular contractions and premature atrial contractions. Which of the following is the best management for this patient?
answer_text: Reassurance, no medication Isolated PVCs without structural disease are benign; no therapy; beta-blocker if symptomatic; avoid class I drugs; digoxin not useful.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: An active 78-year-old female with history of hypertension presents with the new onset of left hemiparesis. Cardiac monitoring reveals atrial fibrillation. She had been in sinus rhythm on checkup 3 months earlier. Optimal manage ment at discharge includes a review of antihypertensive therapy, a ventricular rate control agent, and which of the following?
options: Automated implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (AICD)/permanent pacemaker to avoid the need for anticoagulation
Antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin, without warfarin
Antiplatelet therapy plus warfarin with a target INR of 1.5
Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0.
answer_text: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0. AF with stroke risk → warfarin INR 2–3 (mechanical valve 2.5–3.5); anticoagulate before cardioversion or TEE-guided; AICD is for ventricular arrhythmias.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled hypertension develops a viral upper respiratory infection. On his second day of symptoms he experiences palpitations and presents to the emergency room. His blood pressure is 118/78. The following rhythm strip is obtained. What is the best next step in the management of this patient?
options: Initiation of chest compressions and preparation for semielective intubation
answer_text: Administration of intravenous metoprolol Atrial flutter with RVR: if stable, rate control via AV nodal blockade (metoprolol). Adenosine diagnostic only; amiodarone for maintenance; no CPR.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: An otherwise asymptomatic 65-year-old man with diabetes presents to the ER with a sports-related right shoulder injury. His heart rate is noted to be irregular, and this ECG is obtained. Which of the following is the best immediate therapy?
answer_text: Observation AV block types; tracing = Mobitz I (Wenckebach) with progressive PR then dropped beat; usually benign, often drug or inferior MI; rarely needs pacing.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: In the ICU, a patient suddenly becomes pulseless and unresponsive, with cardiac monitor indicating ventricular tachycardia. The crash cart is immediately available. What is the best first therapy?
answer_text: Defibrillation at 200 J VF/unstable VT → defibrillate, epinephrine as needed, then amiodarone/lidocaine/procainamide; magnesium for torsades/hypomagnesemia.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 36-year-old male presents with the sensation of a racing heart. His blood pressure is 110/70, respiratory rate 14/minute, and O2 saturation 98%. His ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia with rate 180, which you correctly diagnose as paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Carotid massage and Valsalva maneuver do not improve the heart rate. Which of the following is the initial therapy of choice?
options: Verapamil 2.5 to 5 mg IV over 1 to 2 min
answer_text: Adenosine 6-mg rapid IV bolus Stable SVT: adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg; verapamil next; diltiazem/digoxin slower; cardioversion if unstable; lidocaine for ventricular rhythms.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A patient has been in the coronary care unit for the past 24 hours with an acute anterior myocardial infarction. He develops the abnormal rhythm shown below, although blood pressure remains stable at 110/68. Which of the following is the best next step in therapy?
answer_text: Arrange for pacemaker placement. Complete heart block in MI: AV dissociation → temporary then likely permanent pacing; atropine temporizes; avoid AV-nodal blockers and lidocaine.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 62-year-old male with underlying COPD develops a viral upper respiratory infection and begins taking an over-the-counter decongestant. Shortly thereafter he experiences palpitations and presents to the emergency room, where the following rhythm strip is obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with 2:1 atrioventricular block
Complete heart block with 2:1 atrioventricular block
answer_text: Atrial flutter with 4:1 atrioventricular block Atrial flutter with 4:1 conduction: atrial ~300, ventricular 75; sawtooth waves; excludes PAT/ junctional.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: An 80-year-old woman was admitted to your service for dizziness. Cardiac monitoring initially revealed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Her ventricular rate was controlled with beta-blocker. An echocardiogram revealed an enlarged left atrium and an ejection fraction of 50%. No evidence of diastolic heart dysfunction was noted. She is now asymptomatic, with blood pressure 130/80, heart rhythm irregularly irregular, and heart rate around 80/minute. Which of the following is the best management strategy of this patient’s arrhythmia?
options: Continued rate control plus prolonged anticoagulation
answer_text: Continued rate control plus prolonged anticoagulation AF strategy: rate control first; cardiovert only if symptomatic despite control; large LA predicts relapse; continue long-term anticoagulation.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: You are performing medical screening of new military recruits when an 18-year-old male reports several episodes of palpitation and syncope over the past several years. Physical examination is unremarkable. An ECG is obtained with excerpts shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Prior myocardial infarction secondary to coronary artery disease
answer_text: Preexcitation syndrome (Wolff-Parkinson-White) WPW: short PR + delta wave + wide QRS; can mimic Q waves; not MI or MS; HOCM shows LVH changes.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 38-year-old with no past medical history is referred to the clinic after an abnormal ECG finding is identified as part of a preoperative workup. Long QT syndrome is identified on repeat ECGs. On further questioning, the patient reports his father had a heart condition identified in his 20s, although he is unsure of the specific diagnosis, and he has experienced previous episodes of syncope following exertion. The patient is started on a beta-blocker and a plan to insert an implantable cardioverter defibrillator is made. A loss of what function is associated with this patient’s condition?
answer_text: Potassium channels Long QT usually from K+ channel loss or drugs or electrolytes; affects ventricular repolarization. AV node disease changes PR not QT. Brugada and early repolarization ≠ LQTS. SA node issues affect P waves. Na+ channel loss less typical than K+ in LQTS.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of ischaemic heart disease presents to the Emergency Department with palpitations for the past 10 days. Examination of his pulse reveals a rate of 130 bpm which is irregularly irregular. He has had one previous episode of atrial fibrillation 3 months ago which was terminated by elective cardioversion following warfarinisation. What term best describes his arrhythmia?
answer_text: Persistent atrial fibrillation AF patterns: first detected; paroxysmal <7 days; persistent >7 days; permanent when accepted or non-cardiovertible. Goals: rate control and anticoagulation as indicated.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with lightheadedness. He has a past medical history of hypertension and ischaemic heart disease. His medications include bisoprolol, amlodipine, and aspirin. Observations: - Heart rate 38 beats per minute - Blood pressure 96/54 mmHg - Respiratory rate 18/minute - Oxygen saturations 97% on room air - Temperature 37.1°C An ECG demonstrates a regular P-P interval and a regular R-R interval but there is no apparent relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes. When auscultating this patient’s heart sounds, what is an expected finding?
answer_text: Variable intensity of S1 Complete heart block → variable S1 intensity. Loud S1: MS or TS. Soft S1: MR, severe HF, LBBB, 1° AV block. Loud S2: systemic HTN. Soft S2: severe AS.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 56-year-old gentleman is brought in by paramedics. The patient fainted this morning and has not regained consciousness. No injuries reported from his faint. On examination his heart rate is 37 beats/minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths/minute, blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg. You order an ECG: The ECG shows prolonged PR interval. What would be the initial management?
answer_text: IV atropine Symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features → give IV atropine first; adenosine treats SVT; escalate to pacing if no response.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 75-year-old woman was admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with pneumonia. Her only past medical history of note is transient ischaemic attack 2 months previously. On initial assessment, ECG revealed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 103. She was treated with intravenous fluids and antibiotics. She improved significantly. Two further ECGs overnight revealed normal sinus rhythm. The following day, she was deemed medically fit for discharge. What is the single most appropriate management option regarding her episode of atrial fibrillation?
answer_text: Oral anticoagulation Single paroxysmal AF episode still needs anticoagulation if CHA₂DS₂- VASc high; aspirin not used; Holter not required before starting OAC.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following the acute onset of palpitations. Blood pressure is 124/84 mmHg and her pulse is 150/min. An ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia. Intravenous access is gained and 6mg of adenosine is given with no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
answer_text: Intravenous adenosine 12 mg SVT unresponsive to first adenosine dose → give next dose per protocol.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Each one of the following may cause left bundle branch block, except:
answer_text: Atrial septal defect (ostium secundum) LBBB: WiLLiaM pattern (W in V1, M in V6). New LBBB is pathologic; causes include MI, HTN, AS, cardiomyopathy; also fibrosis, digoxin toxicity, hyperkalemia.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department following an episode of syn cope. An ECG is performed, which demonstrates sinus rhythm at rate 85 bpm. The QRS duration is 110 ms, PR interval is 180 ms and corrected QT interval is 500 ms. Of the following, what is the cause for the abnormality seen on the ECG?
answer_text: Hypokalaemia Long QT from hypokalemia; normal QTc <430 ms men, <450 ms women. Other acquired causes: hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, many drugs, CNS injury, malnutrition, hypothermia.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following a collapse. An ECG shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which one of the following is not associated with an increased risk of developing torsade de pointes?
answer_text: Hypercalcaemia Hypocalcemia prolongs QT and risks torsades; hypercalcemia shortens QT.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a 4-day history of palpitations and increased breathlessness on exertion. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a rate of 118 beats per minute. His past medical history includes brittle asthma, hypertension, and congestive cardiac failure, and his recent echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 32%. What is the most appropriate medication to control the heart rate in this man?
answer_text: Digoxin AF with HFrEF: avoid rate-limiting CCBs; beta-blockers usual but avoid if brittle asthma; digoxin reasonable for rate control in sedentary HF.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old man presents with lethargy and palpitations for the past four or five days. On examination his pulse is 123 bpm irregularly irregular, blood pressure is 118/70 mmHg and his chest is clear. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the appropriate drug to control his heart rate?
answer_text: Bisoprolol AF long-term rate control: beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB preferred to digoxin in most; choose rate control based on age and symptoms.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Which one of the following is not an indication for insertion of a temporary pacemaker?
options: Complete heart block following an inferior MI - blood pressure normal
Complete heart block following an anterior MI - blood pressure normal
Mobitz type II heart block following an anterior MI - blood pressure normal
Symptomatic bradycardia not responding to drug treatment
answer_text: Complete heart block following an inferior MI - blood pressure normal Post-inferior MI complete heart block often transient; if stable, no pacing. Temporary pacing for unstable bradycardia unresponsive to atropine and for anterior MI high-grade block.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A 71-year-old man with history of rheumatic heart disease for 20 years presents with breathlessness on exertion. On auscultation, the first heart sound is soft, the second heart sound is normal, the apex beat is displaced. Which valvular lesion is most likely?
answer_text: Mitral regurgitation A soft S1 and displaced apex beat suggest MR rather than MS.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A 42-year-old female presents with shortness of breath and chest discomfort. On physical exam, a mid-diastolic murmur was heard at the left sternal border with an opening snap after S2. Which valvular lesion is suspected?
answer_text: Mitral stenosis , Mitral stenosis is classically associated with a mid-diastolic murmur and an opening snap after S2, best heard at the apex or left sternal border. The opening snap is due to sudden tensing of the stenotic mitral valve leaflets during diastole.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: A 66-year-old man presents with shortness-of-breath on exertion. On examination his blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular. Auscultation of his chest reveals an early diastolic murmur Which one of the following conditions is most associated with this kind of murmur?
answer_text: Aortic regurgitation An early diastolic murmur is most associated with aortic regurgitation.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic mitral stenosis now presents with progressive dyspnea and signs of congestion. What is the most likely underlying cause of her new symptoms?
answer_text: Progression to pulmonary hypertension In rheumatic mitral stenosis, progression to pulmonary hypertension is a common cause of worsening symptoms.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: On physical examination of a patient with mitral stenosis, what is the typical character of the apex beat?
answer_text: Tapping only In mitral stenosis, the apex beat is typically localized and tapping in character, due to a palpable first heart sound (loud S1) caused by the stiff mitral valve snapping shut. This tapping apex beat is a classic clinical finding and more specific than simply saying “soft.”

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which auscultatory finding is most indicative of pulmonary hypertension in a patient with mitral stenosis?
answer_text: Loud P2 component of S2 A loud P2 (ac centuated pulmonary component of S2) is a key sign of pulmonary hypertension.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy is indicated in which patient with mitral stenosis?
options: Symptomatic patients with favorable valve morphology and minimal mitral regurgitation
All patients with any degree of stenosis
Only in patients with associated atrial fibrillation
answer_text: Symptomatic patients with favorable valve morphology and minimal mitral regurgitation This procedure is reserved for symptomatic patients who have pliable valves without significant regurgitation.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 34 year old woman presents with symptoms of breathlessness on exertion, a malar flush and has a past history of rheumatic fever. She is in sinus rhythm and has an echocardiogram that confirms mitral stenosis. Which physical sign is she likely to have?
answer_text: Pre-systolic accentuation Mitral stenosis is typically associated with a mid-diastolic murmur that has pre-systolic accentuation.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: An 80 year old man presents with an incidental ejection systolic murmur. His family physician notices a parasternal thrill. What is the likely underlying reason for the thrill?
answer_text: Aortic stenosis A parasternal thrill is most commonly associated with aortic stenosis.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 43 year old man undergoes a routine health check with his employers. He is found to have a murmur, isolated systolic hypertension (180/60 mmHg) and left ventricular hypertrophy on his ECG. A significant regurgitant blood flow is noticed across the aortic valve on echocardiogram. Which of the following clinical signs is likely to be observed?
options: Palpable thrill in the aortic area
Prominent pulsation in the neck (de Musset’s sign)
answer_text: Prominent pulsation in the neck (de Musset’s sign) De Musset’s sign (neck pulsations) is characteristic of severe aortic regurgitation.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: An 84-year-old woman with a history of diabetes and hyperlipidemia presented to the emergency department 3 weeks ago with an ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. She underwent emergent primary percutaneous coronary intervention to an acutely occluded left anterior descending artery. A 3.5 × 24 mm everolimus-eluting stent was placed with excellent angiographic result and complete resolution of her symptoms. She has been feeling excellent since then. Her discharge medications were metoprolol, aspirin, clopidogrel, rosuvastatin, lisinopril, and sliding scale insulin. She recently went to see her ophthalmologist who noted a right eye cataract. The ophthalmologist has contacted your office asking about your opinion on discontinuing her aspirin and/or clopidogrel to reduce bleeding risk during her cataract surgery, which has been scheduled for next week. She feels the bleeding risk on both medications is too high to perform the surgery. Which of the following should you recommend?
options: “Discontinue aspirin, continue clopidogrel, and proceed with cataract surgery.”
“Discontinue clopidogrel, continue aspirin, and proceed with cataract surgery.”
“Discontinue both aspirin and clopidogrel and proceed with cataract surgery.”
“Postpone the surgery for at least 6 months, and preferably 12 months, at which time the clopidogrel can be discontinued.”
“I advise to perform the surgery while she is on both aspirin and clopidogrel as she will never be able to stop either medication.”
answer_text: Postpone the surgery for at least 6 months, and preferably 12 months, at which time the clopidogrel can be discontinued. Postponing elective surgery minimizes the risk of stent thrombosis by allowing completion of dual antiplatelet therapy.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: Mrs. Edwards is an 87-year-old woman with a history of extensive tobacco abuse and resultant COPD with a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) of 0.76 L, poorly controlled diabetes, and stage III chronic kidney disease. She was previously your patient, but has not followed up with you for the preceding 8 years. However, she comes to your clinic today complaining of chest pressure with exertion, leg swelling, shortness of breath, and accelerating fatigue with even minimal exertion. On examination, you quickly note a harsh, late-peaking systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating the carotid arteries and with a musical quality at the apex. You cannot appreciate a second heart sound, and the carotid impulses are muted and arrive late compared to the PMI on palpation. You suspect severe aortic stenosis, and indeed, an echocardiogram later that day confirms aortic stenosis with a valve area of 0.59 cm2. You refer Mrs. Edwards to a cardiothoracic surgeon who informs you that Mrs. Edwards is much too high risk for a surgical aortic valve replacement, citing a higher than 15% risk of in-hospital mortality. You are due to see Mrs. Edwards tomorrow. Which of the following statements to her would be rea sonable?
options: “For this condition, medications have been shown to reduce the risk of mortality.”
“It is okay that you are not a surgical candidate. Your condition carries a low risk of 1- and 5-year mortality, and we can control your symptoms with medications.”
“Percutaneous aortic balloon valvotomy is a good nonsurgical treatment option and has been found to have excellent short- and long-term outcomes.”
“Since you are not a surgical candidate, no other procedure exists for aortic valve replacement for you. We should consider hospice options.”
“We should consider referring you for further testing to see if you are a candidate for transcatheter aortic valve replacement.”
answer_text: We should consider referring you for further testing to see if you are a candidate for transcatheter aortic valve replacement. TAVR is now a viable option for high-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. On examination you note a loud first heart sound (HS) and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Mitral stenosis The clinical findings are typical of mitral stenosis, often presenting with a loud first heart sound and diastolic rumble.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath on exertion and fatigue. On examination you note a soft first HS and a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to her axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Mitral regurgitation Mitral regurgitation typically presents with a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 62-year-old man presents with angina and dyspnoea. On examination you note an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal border radiating to his neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Aortic stenosis Aortic stenosis often presents with an ejection systolic murmur that radiates to the neck.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with dyspnoea and orthopnoea. On examination you note a blowing early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Aortic regurgitation A blowing early diastolic murmur is characteristic of aortic regurgitation.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 42-year-old man is reviewed in the outpatient cardiology department following a recent echocardiogram (echo). The echo demonstrates right ventricular dysfunction. On examination you note an elevated JVP in addition to a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Tricuspid regurgitation Tricuspid regurgitation presents with an elevated JVP and a pansystolic murmur along the lower left sternal border.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 62-year-old man presents with angina and dyspnoea. On examination you note a murmur at the upper right sternal border radiating to his neck. Which investigation is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?
answer_text: Echocardiogram An echocardiogram is the first-line investigation for cardiac murmurs.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 42-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. On examination you note a loud first HS and a rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. You request an echocardiogram and a CXR. The following are all features of the CXR in this condition EXCEPT?
answer_text: Narrowed carina A narrowed carina is not a typical feature of the CXR in mitral stenosis.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 20-year-old student sees his GP for blurred vision. On further questioning, he reports he had a ‘lens problem’ a year ago. On examination he also has pectus excavatum, a high arched palate and signs of hypermobility. Which of the following cardiac disorders is often associated with this patient’s condition?
answer_text: Mitral valve prolapse Mitral valve prolapse is commonly associated with connective tissue disorders, as seen in this patient.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 65-year-old man sees his GP with worsening central chest pain and breathlessness following exertion for 3 months. These symptoms usually resolve with rest. Lately he has also been feeling dizzy. On examination a systolic murmur is heard. ECG shows large R waves in leads I, aVL and V4–6, and large R waves in leads V1–3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Aortic stenosis Aortic stenosis in the elderly can present with angina, syncope, and heart failure symptoms along with LVH on ECG.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 32-year-old woman attends her GP for a routine medical examination and is noted to have a mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap. Her blood pressure is 118/71 mmHg and pulse is 66/min. She is entirely asymptomatic and her chest x-ray and ECG are normal. What would be the most appropriate investigation at this point?
answer_text: Echocardiography Echocardiography is the investigation of choice in suspected mitral stenosis.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A patient is admitted with pneumonia. A murmur is heard on examination. What finding points to mitral regurgitation?
options: Murmur louder with patient in left lateral position
Murmur louder over the right 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line
answer_text: Murmur louder with patient in left lateral position Mitral regurgitation is best heard at the apex and accentuated in the left lateral decubitus position.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 49-year-old woman presents with increasing shortness of breath on exertion over the past three months, with no chest pain, cough, or ankle swelling. On examination, BP is 158/61 mmHg, pulse 88/min, and crackles are present at both lung bases. A decrescendo diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Aortic regurgitation Aortic regurgitation typically presents with a decrescendo diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 59-year-old man presents for a routine check-up. Examination reveals a mid systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex, but he is asymptomatic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Barlow syndrome The mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is characteristic of mitral valve prolapse (Barlow syndrome).

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 57-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever and essential hypertension presents with worsening shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance. Which of the following is NOT a clinical sign associated with mitral stenosis?
options: Pan-systolic murmur which radiates to axilla
answer_text: Pan-systolic murmur which radiates to axilla Mitral stenosis is associated with malar flush, atrial fibrillation, a tapping apex beat, and right ventricular heave; a pan-systolic murmur is not typical.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: An asymptomatic 31-year-old woman is told she has mitral valve prolapse after an ECG. Which statement is correct?
options: One or both leaflets of the mitral valve are pushed back into the left atrium during systole
Significant mitral regurgitation will eventually develop
answer_text: One or both leaflets of the mitral valve are pushed back into the left atrium during systole Mitral valve prolapse is defined by the systolic displacement of one or both leaflets into the left atrium; no specific therapy is indicated in asymptomatic patients.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 76-year-old male collapses at home but recovers quickly. He also reports increasing shortness of breath on exertion and occasional central chest pain. Examination reveals BP 115/88 mmHg, a few rales at the bases, and borderline LVH on ECG. Which auscultatory finding would you expect?
options: Mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the apex
Crescendo systolic murmur best heard at the right sternal edge
Diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge
Pan-systolic murmur best heard at the apex
Pan-systolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge
answer_text: Crescendo systolic murmur best heard at the right sternal edge This presentation is classic for aortic stenosis, which produces a harsh systolic murmur best heard at the right sternal border.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 15-year-old student, newly active in football, experiences a syncopal episode during practice. Examination reveals a systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and apex, and ECG shows LVH. Which physical finding is most likely?
options: A systolic ejection murmur at the apex that diminishes with squatting/handgrip and increases with Valsalva/standing
A systolic murmur with a mid to late systolic click at the apex, with the click and murmur occurring earlier with squatting/handgrip and delayed with Valsalva/standing
A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla that increases with squatting/handgrip and diminishes with Valsalva/standing
A blowing holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border which increases with squatting/ handgrip and diminishes with Valsalva/standing
A low pitched mid systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
answer_text: A systolic murmur with a mid to late systolic click at the apex, with the click and mur mur occurring earlier with squatting/handgrip and delayed with Valsalva/standing Although the explanation provided discusses paradoxical embolism, the answer given is the murmur of mitral valve prolapse with the characteristic mid to late systolic click.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 75-year-old patient presents to the ER after a syncopal episode with occasional substernal chest pressure and exertional dyspnea. BP is 110/80 with bibasilar rales. Which auscultatory finding best explains his symptoms?
options: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border
A diastolic decrescendo murmur heard at the mid-left sternal border
A holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex
answer_text: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border This finding is classic for aortic stenosis, which is associated with syncope.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 78-year-old man is brought to the ED with a 3-week history of productive cough, leg swelling, and fatigue. He had a porcine valve replacement for severe mitral regurgitation 12 years ago. Examination reveals bilateral basilar rales, a laterally displaced apical beat, and a grade 3/6 decrescendo-crescendo diastolic murmur at the apex. Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
answer_text: Valve Degeneration Biological valves degenerate over time, leading to dysfunction and heart failure.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 75-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 50-year smoking history presents with progressive shortness of breath and fatigue. Physical exam shows weak peripheral pulses. Which diagnosis is most likely?
answer_text: Aortic stenosis Aortic stenosis causes a narrow pulse pressure and weak peripheral pulses due to LV outflow obstruction.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and dyspnea for 2 months, with nocturnal dyspnea and occasional palpitations. He has type 2 diabetes and peripheral arterial disease. Examination shows bilateral basilar rales. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: MR The auscultatory findings are indicative of mitral regurgitation, a common cause of left-sided heart failure.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: 1. A 75-year-old patient presents to the ER after a syncopal episode. He is again alert and in retrospect describes occasional substernal chest pressure and shortness of breath on exertion. His blood pressure is 110/80 and lungs have a few bibasilar rales. Which auscultatory finding would best explain his findings?
options: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border
A diastolic decrescendo murmur heard at the mid-left sternal border
A holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex
answer_text: A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border Aortic stenosis triad: dyspnea, angina, syncope; narrow pulse pressure; systolic ejection murmur. Other listed murmurs ≠ this triad.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: 2. A 72-year-old male comes to the office with intermittent symptoms of dyspnea on exertion, palpitations, and cough occasionally productive of blood. On cardiac auscultation, a low-pitched diastolic rumbling murmur is faintly heard at the apex. What is the most likely cause of the murmur?
options: A silent MI within the past year
answer_text: Rheumatic fever as a youth Mitral stenosis: dyspnea, palpitations, hemoptysis; diastolic rumble ± opening snap, loud S1; rheumatic origin; HTN gives S4, MI causes MR (systolic), anemia causes flow murmur.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: 3. A 68-year-old male was intubated in the emergency room because of pulmonary edema. Stat echocardiogram reveals an ejection fraction of 45% and severe mitral regurgitation. In spite of aggressive diuresis with furosemide, the patient continues to require mechanical ventilation secondary to pulmonary edema. What is the best next step in treating this patient?
options: Arrange for mitral valve replacement surgery.
answer_text: Begin intravenous enalapril. Acute severe MR with pulmonary edema → reduce afterload (ACEi/hydralazine/nitroprusside); plan MV surgery after stabilization; IABP/extra diuretic/BB not helpful.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: 4. You are volunteering with a dental colleague in a community indigent clinic. A nurse has prepared a list of patients who are scheduled for a dental procedure and may need antibiotic prophylaxis beforehand. Of the patients listed below, who would be most likely to benefit from antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis?
options: 17-year-old male with coarctation of the aorta
26-year-old female with a ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood
answer_text: 65-year-old male with prosthetic aortic valve IE prophylaxis only for highest risk: prior IE, prosthetic valves, unrepaired cyanotic CHD, graft <6 mo; dental prophylaxis amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 min pre-procedure; many procedures need none.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 5. A 62-year-old man who had a mechanical mitral valve replacement four years ago is reviewed. What long term antithrombotic therapy is he likely to be taking?
options: Aspirin + clopidogrel for the first 12 months
answer_text: Warfarin Prosthetic valves: mechanical → warfarin ± aspirin if other indication; bioprosthetic → aspirin; DOACs contraindicated in mechanical valves.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 6. A 34-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with fatigue and exertional shortness of breath. He has no significant past medical history and is on no medications. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. On examination, he is of tall stature (2.08 metres) and thin. A high arched palate is noted on examination. Auscultation of the precordium reveals a pansystolic murmur, heard loudest in inspiration. From the options listed below, what is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?
answer_text: Tricuspid regurgitation Tricuspid regurgitation: pansystolic; louder on inspiration; fits Marfan’s clues. MR louder on expiration; MS diastolic rumble; PR diastolic decrescendo.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 7. A 45-year-old female who has a background of intravenous drug abuse presented with difficulty in breathing and bilateral lower leg swelling. Upon examination, it was found she had a regular pulse with a pansystolic murmur heard lowest over the left lower sternal edge. There was shifting dullness when assessing her abdomen. What is the most likely finding when evaluating her jugular venous pressure (JVP)?
answer_text: Prominent V waves Prominent V waves on JVP indicate tricuspid regurgitation. Cannon A: complete heart block. Absent A: AF. X descent patterns fit tamponade or AF, not this case.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 8. Which one of the following conditions is most associated with a bisferiens pulse?
answer_text: Mixed aortic valve disease Bisferiens pulse → mixed aortic valve disease. Not typical for tamponade, severe LV failure, isolated AS, or PDA.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 9. Which one of the following is a cause of a soft second heart sound?
answer_text: Aortic stenosis S2 patterns: loud in HTN; soft in severe AS; fixed split in ASD; reversed split in LBBB.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 10. Which of the following conditions is not associated with the development of aortic regurgitation?
answer_text: Dilated cardiomyopathy Dilated cardiomyopathy causes functional MR, not AR. AR causes: valve disease like rheumatic or calcific; root disease like bicuspid or spondyloarthropathy.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 11. A 2-year-old boy is seen by the general practitioner as his parents are concerned that he is struggling to gain weight and is excessively short of breath on exertion. He was previously diagnosed with congenital pulmonary stenosis which was managed conservatively; however, the parents are now questioning whether surgical intervention may be required. What murmur is likely to be heard on examination?
answer_text: Ejection systolic, louder on inspiration Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur louder on inspiration. MR: holosystolic louder on expiration. TR: holosystolic louder on inspiration. MVP: late systolic click. Aortic stenosis: ejection systolic louder on expiration.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following is not a feature of cardiac tamponade?
answer_text: Loud heart sounds Tamponade typically features distant or muffled heart sounds, not loud heart sounds.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A patient with acute myocardial infarction came with repeated severe dyspnea. On examination PR was 112 beats/min with pulsus paradoxus, BP 90/55 mmHg, JVP was elevated, and heart sounds were muffled. The next day, what is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Cardiac tamponade Muffled heart sounds, elevated JVP, and pulsus paradoxus strongly suggest tamponade post-MI.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A middle-aged lady presents with fatigue, abdominal distension, and lightheadedness. On examination, a pericardial knock was heard, a loud P2, and a diastolic rumble. A diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis was made. Which of the following finding(s) is against this diagnosis?
answer_text: Pulsus paradoxus Pulsus paradoxus is more commonly seen in tamponade, not typically in constrictive pericarditis.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: A 55 year old man has progressive shortness of breath and ankle oedema. He has come from Africa originally and gives a history of probably tuberculosis many years ago. On examination, he has a blood pressure of 105/55 mmHg: raised J VP +5 cm with a rapid y descent and significant ankle oedema What is the likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Pericardial constriction Rapid y descent is indicative of pericardial constriction.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: Dressier’s syndrome results from:
answer_text: Autoimmune response Dressler’s syndrome is an autoimmune response following myocardial infarction.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with chest pain following a week of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Her cardiac examination reveals distant heart sounds and her chest X-ray shows an increased cardiac silhouette. What is the most likely cause of the increased cardiac silhouette?
answer_text: Pericardial effusion An enlarged cardiac silhouette in this context suggests a pericardial effusion, often seen with pericarditis.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Based on her history and exam, what is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Acute pericarditis with effusion The combination of chest pain, recent infection symptoms, distant heart sounds, and enlarged cardiac silhouette points to acute pericarditis with effusion.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which investigation is most important to confirm the diagnosis?
answer_text: Echocardiography An echocardiogram is the key investigation to visualize a pericardial effusion and assess its hemodynamic impact.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: In a patient with a life-threatening pericardial effusion causing hemodynamic compromise, what is the best mode of therapy?
answer_text: Urgent pericardiocentesis Urgent pericardiocentesis is indicated to relieve cardiac tamponade from a large pericardial effusion.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 21 year old man presents with a recent history of an influenza-like illness initially characterised by fever, myalgia and headache. He develops pleuritic-type chest discomfort and breathlessness. On examination, pulse is 105 beats/min and regular; BP 105/60 mmHg. The JVP is not elevated. Heart sounds 1 and 2 are present with a loud to-and-fro harsh sound present in systole and diastole. Which of the following conditions explains this clinical presentation?
answer_text: Acute viral pericarditis The clinical picture is most compatible with acute pericarditis following a viral illness.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: What is the appropriate initial treatment for the symptoms of acute pericarditis?
answer_text: Oral aspirin Aspirin is effective as an initial anti-inflammatory treatment for pericarditis.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Which of the following conditions may result in chronic pericardial constriction?
answer_text: Tuberculosis Tuberculosis is a recognized cause of chronic pericardial constriction.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 75 year old male smoker presents with a 6-week history of progressive exertional breathlessness and fatigue. Latterly he has noticed his ankles swelling in the afternoon. On examination, pulse is 100 beats/min and regular; BP 92/60 mmHg. The JVP is elevated and rises on inspiration. Heart sounds are quiet and there are no added sounds. There is bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. A chest X-ray is requested, which shows apparent cardiomegaly with a globular cardiac silhouette. You suspect a possible pericardial effusion. Which of the following statements is true?
options: A large effusion can be a sign of malignancy
A pericardial rub is always heard if the effusion is large
An ECG is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis
High-dose diuretic therapy will resolve the pericardial effusion
In symptomatic patients, cardiac surgery is required to remove the pericardial fluid
answer_text: A large effusion can be a sign of malignancy A large pericardial effusion may indicate an underlying malignancy.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: An 18 year old man presents with sudden onset of sharp chest pain. The pain is made worse by deep inspiration or lying down flat. It is relieved by sitting forward and taking shallow breaths. He presents to the emergency de partment and an ECG is recorded because the attending doctor suspects acute pericarditis. What is the most specific ECG change in pericarditis?
answer_text: PR segment depression PR segment depression is highly specific for acute pericarditis.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: In patients with a pericardial effusion, what is the most important clinical sign to determine whether there is cardiac tamponade?
answer_text: Pulsus paradoxus Pulsus paradoxus is a key sign indicating cardiac tamponade.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 75-year-old woman with widely metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer is admitted to the intensive care unit with a systolic blood pressure of 73/52 mmHg. She presented complaining of fatigue and worsening dyspnea over the last 3-5 days. Her physical examination shows elevated neck veins. Chest radiograph shows a massive, water bottle-shaped heart shadow and no new pulmonary infiltrates. Which of the following additional findings is most likely present on physical examination?
options: Fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration
Lack of fall of the jugular venous pressure with inspiration
Late diastolic murmur with opening snap
Rapid y-descent of jugular venous pressure tracing
answer_text: Fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration In cardiac tamponade, an exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure (pulsus paradoxus) is observed.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: You are asked to evaluate a 27-year-old internal medicine resident reporting 1 week of cough, coryza, and a low-grade fever. Today, he has developed rapidly escalating chest discomfort while in clinic. He notes that the pain becomes more intense when he takes a deep breath. You perform a standard 12-lead ECG (see Figure V-18). On examination, his blood pressure is normal, he is afebrile, and his jugular venous pulse is not elevated. However, he appears mildly uncomfortable from the chest pain. The next most appropriate step would be which of the following?
options: Administer aspirin, intravenous heparin, sublingual nitroglycerin, and clopidogrel.
Emergently obtain transthoracic echocardiogram with possible pericardiocentesis.
Emergently perform coronary angiography to evaluate for acute myocardial infarction.
answer_text: Prescribe ibuprofen and colchicine. The presentation and ECG are most consistent with pericarditis, best managed with NSAIDs and colchicine.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 23-year-old man who has recently recovered from an upper respiratory tract infection presents to the AE department with chest pain made worse on breathing. On examination he is febrile, and has a ‘scratchy’ sound heard on auscultation in systole and diastole. ECG reveals widespread saddle-shaped ST segment elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Acute pericarditis The presentation is consistent with acute pericarditis, especially following a viral infection.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A previously fit and well 30-year-old gym instructor is admitted to hospital following a stab wound to the left side of his chest. He has a blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg and heart rate of 125 beats/min. Breath sounds are present throughout but his HSs are muffled. His JVP appears raised. What additional feature is most likely to be present in this patient?
options: Diastolic murmur over the praecordium radiating towards the left axilla
An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during inspiration
An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during expiration
answer_text: An 18-mmHg blood pressure drop during inspiration An 18-mmHg drop in systolic blood pressure during inspiration (pulsus paradoxus) is indicative of cardiac tamponade.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with chest pain. She comments that the pain is worse on inspiration but is relieved by leaning forward. Her past medical history includes breast carcinoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Acute pericarditis The clinical picture is classic for acute pericarditis, with pain relieved by leaning forward.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 43-year-old obese woman with known breast cancer complains of shortness of breath. On examination you note soft HSs and obscuration of the apex beat. Which investigation is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?
answer_text: Echocardiogram An echocardiogram is the most sensitive investigation for detecting pericardial effusion.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a dry cough and severe chest pain beginning that morning. Two months ago, he was diagnosed with inferior wall myocardial infarction and was treated with stent implantation of the right coronary artery. He has a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. His medications include aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, and enalapril. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 92/ min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched scratching sound best heard while sitting upright and during expiration. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. An ECG shows diffuse ST elevations. Serum studies show a troponin I of 0.2 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
answer_text: Dressler syndrome Dressler syndrome (post-MI syndrome) is an immune-mediated pericarditis occurring weeks after infarction.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: Two weeks after hospital discharge for documented myocardial infarction, a 65-year-old returns to your office concerned about low- grade fever and pleuritic chest pain. There is no associated shortness of breath. Lungs are clear to auscultation and the heart is free of murmur, gallop, or rub. ECG is unchanged from the last one in the hospital. Which therapy is most likely to be effective?
answer_text: An anti-inflammatory agent Post–cardiac injury (Dressler): days–6 w after MI/surgery; fever + pleuritic pain; treat NSAIDs or steroids; not PE, pneumonia, or ACS.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 35-year-old male complains of substernal chest pain aggravated by inspiration and relieved by sitting up. Lung fields are clear to auscultation, and heart sounds are somewhat distant. Chest x-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Which of the following is the best next step in evaluation?
answer_text: Echocardiogram Pericarditis with effusion: pleuritic pain better sitting up; echo confirms fluid; CXR may show enlarged silhouette; no role for cath or stress test.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 42-year-old female with acute pericarditis develops jugular venous distention and hypotension. The ECG shows electrical alternans. Which of the following is the most likely additional physical finding?
options: Basilar rales halfway up both posterior lung fields
answer_text: Pulsus paradoxus Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, JVP, clear lungs, pulsus paradoxus; urgent echo and pericardiocentesis; RUQ tenderness from hepatic congestion.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 77-year-old man is under review on the ward after having a pacemaker inserted earlier that day. He initially presented to the emergency department two days ago with recurrent episodes of collapse, leading to a diagnosis of sick sinus syndrome. In the past hour, he has reported increasing chest discomfort and developed hypotension. On examination, he is cool and clammy peripherally, his jugular venous pressure (JVP) is at 5 cm above the sternal angle, and his heart sounds are indistinct. His current heart rate is 72 bpm with a blood pressure of 88/56 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Haemopericardium Post-pacemaker tamponade from myocardial perforation → Beck’s triad; treat with urgent pericardiocentesis. Lead fracture presents as device malfunction, not tamponade.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 65-year-old male presents to the emergency department with increased shortness of breath and a light-headed feeling. He reports some left shoulder pain and some ongoing mild chest pain, which improved when sitting up. The patient reports that the breathlessness has been increasing over the last 7 days, but has been significantly worse over the last 24 hours. The patient reports having had a STEMI (ST elevation myocardial infarction) 5 weeks ago with a stent inserted into the left anterior descending artery. The patient has a past medical history of type II diabetes mellitus. On examination, the patient is found to have a raised jugular venous pressure. Peripheral pulses are weak and the patient is tachycardic with a regular rhythm. The chest is clear on examination with good air entry throughout, and the heart sounds are muffled. Observations: - Heart rate: 101 bpm - Blood pressure: 89/50 mmHg - Temperature: 36.0°C - Oxygen saturations: 95% on air - Respiratory Rate: 20 bpm There is no discrepancy between the blood pressures in each arm. An ECG is done which shows Q waves in V1-V3 with no ST change. The complexes are small amplitude. What is the most likely diagnosis for the patient’s symptoms?
answer_text: Cardiac tamponade Beck’s triad after recent STEMI → tamponade; PE would desaturate and not muffle heart sounds; dissection has tearing pain; small QRS voltage also supports effusion.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a one-day history of central chest pain. The pain is described as severe, non-radiating and eases on expiration. Clinical examination of her cardiorespiratory system is unremarkable other than a heart rate of 96/min. An ECG shows widespread ST elevation in the anterior, inferior and lateral leads. Bloods show the following: Full blood count: Normal Urea and electrolytes: Normal Troponin I: 0.8 ng/mL (< 0.2 ng/mL) What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Acute pericarditis Acute pericarditis: sharp central pain better when sitting forward; widespread ST elevation; troponin may be mildly raised; ACS usually territorial.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with several days of progressive chest pain, pleuritic in nature and worse on lying down. He achieves some relief from the pain by sitting forward. On examination, a pericardial rub is noted when leaning forward. Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following electrocardiogram (ECG) findings is most specific?
answer_text: PR depression Acute pericarditis ECG: most specific sign is PR depression; ST elevation is diffuse; QRS widening suggests other pathology.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Which of the following is bad prognostic sign regarding acute rheumatic fever:
answer_text: Old age. Old age is considered a bad prognostic sign in acute rheumatic fever.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A patient with history of mitral valve replacement 3 weeks ago developed infective endocarditis. Which of the following microorganisms is responsible for this endocarditis?
answer_text: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis) Coagulase-negative staphylococci are a common cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: In rheumatic fever, the most condition considered as a sequel and end damage for organ is
answer_text: Carditis Carditis is the most significant sequelae in rheumatic fever.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: The lower risk condition for infective endocarditis is
answer_text: Mitral valve prolapse without regurgitation Mitral valve prolapse without regurgitation carries a lower risk for infective endocarditis.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with pyrexia and found to have infective endocarditis. Which one of the following is most associated with a good prognosis?
answer_text: Streptococcus viridans infection Streptococcus viridans endocarditis generally has a favorable prognosis.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: which one of the following is bad prognostic sign of rheumatic fever
answer_text: Old age Old age is considered a bad prognostic sign in rheumatic fever.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a history of fever, chills, night sweats, and a pansystolic murmur over the apex radiating to the axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Infective endocarditis The prolonged fever with a new murmur, particularly a pansystolic murmur at the apex, is highly suggestive of infective endocarditis.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which investigation is most indicated to confirm the diagnosis of infective endocarditis in this patient?
answer_text: Blood cultures and echocardiography Blood cultures combined with echocardiography are the mainstays in diagnosing infective endocarditis.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which clinical sign is often associated with infective endocarditis?
answer_text: Janeway lesions Janeway lesions (non-tender, erythematous lesions on the palms and soles) are a well-known sign of infective endocarditis.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: What is the most appropriate initial treatment approach for infective endocarditis in this patient?
options: Empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy tailored after culture results
answer_text: Empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy tailored after culture results Early initiation of empirical IV antibiotics—later tailored to culture results—is crucial in the treatment of infective endocarditis.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 50 year old man is assessed because of 3 weeks of fever and influenza-like symptoms. Examination findings are tachycardia (heart rate 105 beats/min), and a large pulse pressure, BP 140/45 mmHg. Initially it was thought a murmur was present but repeat examination reveals no murmur. Investigations reveal no evidence of chest or urinary infection. What are these findings most compatible with?
options: Infective endocarditis affecting the aortic valve
Infective endocarditis affecting the tricuspid valve
answer_text: Infective endocarditis affecting the aortic valve A wide pulse pressure suggests aortic incompetence, which can be seen in infective endocarditis of the aortic valve.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: An 18 year old woman presents with a sore throat and suspected acute rheumatic fever. Which of the following is a minor manifestation of acute rheumatic fever?
answer_text: Raised C-reactive protein Raised C-reactive protein is a minor criterion in the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: An 18 year old woman has a raised C-reactive protein, a rash consistent with erythema marginatum and pyrexia. However, the clinician remains uncertain about the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever. Rapid response to which treatment will help to confirm the diagnosis?
answer_text: Aspirin A rapid clinical response to high- dose aspirin supports the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 65 year old man presents with a 4-week history of general malaise and lethargy. He has had two courses of antibiotics that have temporarily improved his symptoms but he continues to feel worse over time. His family physician notices he has become anaemic. He attends the emergency department and he is admitted to hospital with a fever. He has some blood cultures taken and he undergoes an echocardiogram, which shows a mass on his mitral valve. What is the most likely organism that will be grown from his blood cultures?
answer_text: Viridans streptococci Viridans streptococci are the most common cause of native valve endocarditis.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Considering the patient in Question 16.72, before the blood culture results are known, the junior doctor reviews the 65 year old man and examines him for evidence of endocarditis. What is the commonest sign that the doctor is likely to find?
answer_text: Haematuria Haematuria, often microscopic, is the most common sign in endocarditis.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 45-year-old man attends the emergency department with worsening breathlessness and fevers. The medical team suspects a diagnosis of infective endocarditis. Which of the following is the most suggestive feature of infective endocarditis?
answer_text: Appearing and changing murmurs A new or changing murmur is a major criterion for infective endocarditis.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 35-year-old IV drug abuser presents with night sweats and weight loss. On examination he is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.5°C. You suspect a diagnosis of infective endocarditis. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for his condition?
answer_text: Staphylococcus aureus Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infective endocarditis in IV drug abusers.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with night sweats. On examination you detect a systolic murmur. She has severe gum and tooth decay and has recently had two teeth taken out. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for her condition?
answer_text: Streptococcus mutans Streptococcus mutans, associated with dental infections, is a likely cause of endocarditis in this context.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 40-year-old man with an underlying cardiac condition is about to undergo a root canal treatment with a new crown to be fitted in the dentist’s office. Which one of the following conditions strongly warrants antibiotics prophylaxis?
options: Previous coronary artery bypass grafting involving the use of the internal mammary arteries
Presence of a dual chamber pacemaker
answer_text: None of the above Current guidelines do not recommend antibiotic prophylaxis for these conditions.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: You are attending a seminar on infective endocarditis. The lecturer comments that some clinical features of the condition result from immune complex deposition. The following features are all the result of immune complex deposition EXCEPT?
answer_text: Splenic abscess Splenic abscess is not a result of immune complex deposition in infective endocarditis.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 35-year-old man complains of fatigue, night sweats and weight loss. On examination you note a systolic murmur and evidence of splenomegaly. Which investigation is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?
answer_text: Blood cultures Blood cultures are essential in the diagnosis of infective endocarditis.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A previously fit and well 45-year-old man presents to AE with fevers and malaise. On examination he has multiple splinter haemorrhages and a systolic murmur. A diagnosis of infective endocarditis is suspected. Dukes criteria is used to help with the diagnosis of the condition. Which of the following statements is INCORRECT in Dukes criteria?
options: Presence of Osler nodes is a minor criterion
Positive blood for rheumatoid factor is a minor criterion
Echocardiographic evidence of prosthetic valve dehiscence is a major criterion
Serological evidence of active infection with an organism consistent with infective endocarditis (IE)
Definite diagnosis can be made with three minor criteria
answer_text: Definite diagnosis can be made with three minor criteria A definite diagnosis of IE requires either two major, or one major and three minor, or five minor criteria; three minor criteria alone are not sufficient.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 45-year-old teacher with known mitral valve prolapse presents to his GP with a 2-week history of fevers, rigors, chest pain and breathlessness. He recently underwent a tooth extraction. On examination he is febrile with multiple splinter haemorrhages. A systolic murmur is heard and appears to have increased in intensity since his last GP visit. What is the most likely causative agent in this case?
answer_text: Streptococcus viridans Streptococcus viridans, a normal oral flora, is the most common cause of endocarditis following dental procedures.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 41-year-old man with fever and transient pain in both knees and elbows. The right knee was red and swollen for 1 day during the week prior to presentation. On physical examination, the patient has a low-grade fever. He has a III/ VI, high-pitched, apical systolic murmur with radiation to the axilla, as well as a soft, mid-diastolic murmur heard at the base. A tender nodule is palpated over an extensor tendon of the hand. There are pink erythematous lesions over the abdomen, some with central clearing. The following laboratory values are obtained: Hct 42%, WBC 12,000/µL with 80% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 20% lymphocytes, ESR 60 mm/h. Which investigation is most likely to provide a definitive diagnosis?
answer_text: Antistreptolysin O antibody An elevated ASO titer is needed to confirm a recent streptococcal infection in rheumatic fever.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of high fever and left ankle and knee joint swelling. She had a sore throat 3 weeks ago. There is no family history of serious illness. Her immunizations are up-to- date. She had an episode of breathlessness and generalized rash when she received dicloxacillin for a skin infection 2 years ago. She appears ill. Her temperature is 38.8°C (102.3°F), pulse is 87/min, and blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg. Examination shows left ankle and knee joint swelling and tenderness with limited range of motion. Breath sounds are normal. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answer_text: Clarithromycin Clarithromycin is the antibiotic of choice for patients with beta-lactam allergy in the treatment of rheumatic fever.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 25-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse develops low grade fever, malaise, and night sweats after a dental procedure. Which investigation is most likely to provide a definitive diagnosis?
answer_text: Blood culture Blood cultures are definitive in diagnosing subacute bacterial endocarditis.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A nurse prepares a list of patients for dental procedures. Which patient is most likely to ben efit from antibiotic prophylaxis?
answer_text: 65-year-old man with prosthetic aortic valve Only patients with prosthetic valves, prior IE, or unrepaired cyanotic heart disease require prophylaxis.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 43-year-old man with HIV and IV drug use presents with fever, night sweats, and a holosystolic murmur. What is the most likely sequela of his condition?
options: Asymptomatic hemorrhages on palms and soles
answer_text: Pulmonary embolism IV drug users with IE are at high risk for septic emboli to the lungs.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: Blood cultures and TEE in a patient with tricuspid vegetations reveal the organism responsible for IE. Which organism is most likely?
answer_text: Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is the most common cause of acute IE in IV drug users.
