heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 34-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve presents with fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, low-grade fevers, and nail hemorrhages. Blood cultures grow Cardiobacterium hominis. What is the next step in management?
answer_text: Switch to IV ceftriaxone Targeted therapy with ceftriaxone is indicated for Cardiobacterium hominis, a HACEK organism.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 64-year-old man, 7 days post-admission for traumatic pancreatitis, develops fever, dyspnea, and a new holosystolic murmur. There is purulent discharge at his central line site. Which organism is most likely responsible?
answer_text: Staphylococcus aureus Healthcare-associated IE is most commonly caused by S. aureus.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 41-year-old man with IV drug use presents with a 10-day history of weakness, headache, and night sweats, and a holosystolic murmur on exam. What is the most likely consequence of his condition?
options: Painless macules and papules on palms and soles
answer_text: Pulmonary embolism Right-sided IE in IV drug users commonly leads to septic pulmonary emboli.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: An autopsy shows multiple nodules on the ventricular side of the mitral valve composed of immune complexes and thrombi. In which patient would these findings most likely be found?
options: A 71-year-old male with acute high fever and nail-bed hemorrhages
A 41-year-old female with a facial rash and nonerosive arthritis
A 28-year-old HIV-positive female IV drug user
A 6-year-old female with subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum
answer_text: A 41-year-old female with a facial rash and nonerosive arthritis These findings are characteristic of Libman-Sacks endocarditis seen in SLE.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: Three weeks after transurethral prostate resection, a 70-year-old man presents with fever, malaise, and extremity pain. He has subungual petechiae and tender red papules, with a new holosystolic murmur. The organism does not cause hemolysis and is PYR positive. Which organism is most likely responsible?
answer_text: Enterococcus faecalis Enterococcus faecalis, a PYR positive, gram-positive coccus, is known to cause endocarditis post GU procedures.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: An 18-year-old male complains of fever and transient pain in both knees and elbows. The right knee was red and swollen for 1 day during the week prior to presentation. On physical examination, the patient has a low-grade fever. He has a III/VI, high pitched, apical systolic murmur with radiation to the axilla, as well as a soft, mid-diastolic murmur heard at the base. A tender nodule is palpated over an extensor tendon of the hand. There are pink erythematous lesions over the abdomen, some with central clearing. The following laboratory values are obtained: Hct: 42, WBC: 12,000/μL with 80% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, 20% lymphocytes, ESR: 60 mm/h. The patient’s ECG is shown below. Which of the following tests is most critical to diagnosis?
answer_text: Antistreptolysin O antibody Acute rheumatic fever per Jones: prior strep + carditis/MR, arthritis, fever, erythema marginatum, nodules, PR prolongation; send ASO; DDx IE/SLE/MI less likely.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Which one of the following features is not part of the modified Duke criteria used in the diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
answer_text: Prolonged PR interval Rheumatic fever may prolong PR. IE diagnosis per modified Duke/ESC: pathology OR 2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor; majors = typical positive blood cultures or echo/endocardial involvement; minors = risk, fever, vascular, immunologic, microbiologic not meeting major.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old woman is due to have a tooth extracted next week. Her past medical history is significant for an aortic valve replacement 2 years previously. What antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended prior to this procedure?
answer_text: General oral hygiene advice No routine IE prophylaxis for dental work; emphasize oral hygiene. Chlorhexidine and pre-procedure antibiotics not recommended without specific indications.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 75-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of fevers, night sweats and lethargy. On examination, you note several Janeway lesions on his hands. There is a collapsing pulse and you note an early diastolic murmur. You take multiple sets of blood cultures and commence the patient on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for presumed infective endocarditis. A trans-thoracic echo identifies large vegetation on the aortic valve with associated aortic regurgitation. You note the patient has a background of metastatic colorectal cancer and is currently receiving palliative chemotherapy. In light of the patient’s past medical history, which of the following organisms are most likely to be responsible?
answer_text: Streptococcus gallolyticus Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis group) IE strongly linked to colorectal cancer; S. viridans common after dental sources.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old male who recently underwent cardiac surgery presents with fever, fatigue, and weight loss. The patient was discharged after a successful mitral valve replacement 4 months ago and as such an urgent echocardiogram is performed. The echo confirms the presence of a new valvular lesion, and a diagnosis of endocarditis is made. Three sets of blood cultures are taken. Which organism is most likely to be responsible for the patient’s diagnosis?
answer_text: Staphylococcus aureus Most IE now S. aureus; early post-valve (<2 mo) S. epidermidis dominates; >2 mo reverts to usual spectrum; S. bovis group links to colon cancer.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with aortic dissection?
answer_text: Bicuspid aortic valve Bicuspid aortic valve is most associated with aortic dissection.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: A 63-year-old man with a history of high blood pressure presents in AE with suddenonset tearing chest pain radiating to the back.
answer_text: Aortic dissection Tearing chest pain radiating to the back is indicative of aortic dissection.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 70-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a weak right radial pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Aortic dissection The described “tearing” chest pain with pulse deficit is most consistent with an aortic dissection.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of aortic dissection?
answer_text: CT angiography of the aorta CT angiography is the gold standard for diagnosing aortic dissection in hemodynamically stable patients.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: What is the best treatment strategy for a patient with aortic dissection (Type A) presenting in this manner?
options: Urgent surgical repair after blood pressure control
answer_text: Urgent surgical repair after blood pressure control Type A aortic dissection requires urgent surgical intervention along with aggressive blood pressure management.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which of the following is a common complication of aortic dissection?
answer_text: Cardiac tamponade Aortic dissection may lead to rupture into the pericardial space, causing cardiac tamponade.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 55 year old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents with a history of sudden-onset central chest pain. There are no diagnostic electrocardiogram (ECG) abnormalities, and an interval troponin concentration is not diagnostic of myocardial infarction. What diagnosis should be confirmed or excluded next?
answer_text: Aortic dissection Aortic dissection should be considered in hypertensive patients with acute chest pain because antithrombotic drugs given before excluding it may cause fatal bleeding.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Which of the following pathologies can be associated with an early diastolic murmur?
answer_text: Marfan’s syndrome Marfan’s syndrome predisposes to aortic regurgitation, which produces an early diastolic murmur.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 75 year old man is incidentally found to have a pulsatile swelling in his abdomen on a routine health check. He is sent for an abdominal ultrasound scan, which confirms the presence of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which risk factor is protective against the formation and expansion of an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
answer_text: Diabetes mellitus Diabetes mellitus has been shown to be protective against AAA formation and expansion.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 65 year old smoker with hypertension is found to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm on population screening with ultrasound. Which intervention will most reduce his future risk of aortic aneurysm rupture?
answer_text: Smoking cessation Smoking cessation is the most effective intervention to reduce the risk of aneurysm rupture.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 65 year old man with known hypertension presents with severe central chest pain that radiates between his shoulder blades. He is sweaty with a BP of 200/100 mmHg in his right arm, a pale left arm and an ECG showing sinus tachycardia. His chest X-ray shows mediastinal widening and a computed tomography scan shows a type A aortic dissection. Which of the following is known to reduce mortality?
options: Emergency repair of the ascending aorta
Prevention of limb or renal ischaemia
answer_text: Emergency repair of the ascending aorta Surgical repair of the ascending aorta is the definitive treatment to reduce mortality in type A dissection.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A short young woman presents with severe chest pain, vomiting and a sinus tachycardia. She is in the last trimester of pregnancy and has had normal blood pressure and observations at antenatal care. She is admitted for observation but is later found collapsed and in cardiac arrest. Despite attempts at resuscitation, mother and child die. Postmortem reveals an aortic dissection. What is the most likely underlying cause for the dissection?
answer_text: Pregnancy Pregnancy-associated dissection, though rare, can occur in the third trimester.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 23 year old woman is referred for evaluation because she is very tall, has problems with her vision and has a heart murmur. Her family physician is concerned that she may have Marfan’s syndrome. What structural gene is associated with an abnormality in Marfan’s syndrome?
answer_text: Fibrillin Marfan’s syndrome is caused by mutations in the fibrillin gene.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: A 67-year-old former heavy smoker is postoperative day 4 from an open aortobifemoral bypass operation for severe claudication. On routine postoperative CT scan prior to discharge, a pseudoaneurysm is noted just proximal to the aortic origin of the bypass grafts. Which of the following best defines a pseudoaneurysm?
options: A focal dilation in a vessel in which the intimal and medial layers are disrupted and the dilated segment is lined by adventitia only
A focal dilation of a vessel only involving one portion of the circumference
Apparent dilation of a vessel due to intrinsic narrowing proximal and distal to the point of apparent narrowing
Dilation of a vessel, though not to the size necessary to be diagnosed as a true aneurysm
The appearance of an aneurysmal dilation of a vessel on imaging due to the angulation of the artery and imaging technique
answer_text: A focal dilation in a vessel in which the intimal and medial layers are disrupted and the dilated segment is lined by adventitia only This definition describes a pseudoaneurysm, where the vessel wall is disrupted and only the adventitia contains the dilation.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: All of the following factors are associated with elevated risk for the development of an aortic aneurysm EXCEPT:
answer_text: Female sex Female sex is not a risk factor; in fact, males are at higher risk for degenerative aortic aneurysms.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: You are seeing Mr. Walker in clinic for follow-up. He is a 22-year-old man with a family history of sudden death and arterial aneurysms. He is quite tall with widely spaced eyes and a broad uvula. On his first visit, you order a transthoracic echocardiogram to investigate a diastolic murmur and note an aortic root aneurysm of 4.9 cm. He most likely has a mutation in which of the following genes?
answer_text: TGF-B receptor Loeys-Dietz syndrome is associated with mutations in the TGF-B receptor genes.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: Which of the following patients with aortic dissection or hematoma is best managed without surgical therapy?
options: A 45-year-old female with a dissection involving the aorta distal to the great vessel origin but cephalad to the renal arteries
A 74-year-old male with a dissection involving the root of the aorta
A 58-year-old male with aortic dissection involving the distal aorta and the bilateral renal arteries
A 69-year-old male with an intramural hematoma within the aortic root
All of the above patients require surgical management of their aortic disease.
answer_text: A 45-year-old female with a dissection involving the aorta distal to the great vessel origin but cephalad to the renal arteries Uncomplicated distal dissections can be managed medically.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: A 32-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department for acute shortness of breath. A helical CT shows no evidence of pulmonary embolus, but incidental note is made of dilatation of the ascending aorta to 4.3 cm. All the following are associated with this finding EXCEPT:
answer_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus SLE is not typically associated with ascending aortic dilation.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 46-year-old man develops sudden severe central chest pain after lifting heavy cases while moving house. The pain radiates to the back and both shoulders but not to either arm. His BP is 155/90 mmHg, pulse rate is 92 beats per minute and the ECG is normal. He is distressed and sweaty, but not nauseated. What would you consider the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Aortic dissection The most likely diagnosis – and the one that must be urgently excluded – is an aortic dissection. The other options do not fit the clinical picture.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old man presents to accident and emergency with a 3-day history of increasingly severe chest pain. The patient describes the pain as a sharp, tearing pain starting in the centre of his chest and radiating straight through to his back between his shoulder blades. The patient looks in pain but there is no pallor, heart rate is 95, respiratory rate is 20, temperature 37°C and blood pressure is 155/95 mmHg. The most likely diagnosis is:
answer_text: Aortic dissection The description is typical of an aortic dissection, which presents with a severe, tearing pain radiating to the back.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 67-year-old male presents to your office after community ultrasound screening revealed an aortic aneurysm measuring 3.0 × 3.5 cm. Physical examination confirms a palpable, pulsatile, nontender abdominal mass just above the umbilicus. The patient’s medical conditions include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco use. What is the best recommendation for the patient to consider?
options: Watchful waiting is the best course until the first onset of abdominal pain.
Surgery is indicated except for the excess operative risk represented by the patient’s risk factors.
Serial follow-up with ultrasound, CT, or MRI is indicated, with the major determinant for surgery being aneurysmal size greater than 5 to 6 cm.
Serial follow-up with ultrasound, CT, or MRI is indicated, with the major determinant for surgery being involvement of a renal artery.
Unlike stents in coronary artery disease, endovascular stent grafts have proven unsuccessful in the management of AAAs.
answer_text: Serial follow-up with ultrasound, CT, or MRI is indicated, with the major determinant for surgery being aneurysmal size greater than 5 to 6 cm. AAA: smoking/HTN risk; rupture risk by size; repair if >5.5 cm, rapid growth, or symptoms; endovascular option; renal artery involvement complicates repair only.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 70-year-old female has been healthy except for hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic. She presents with sudden onset of a severe, tearing chest pain, which radiates to the back and is associated with dyspnea and diaphoresis. Blood pressure is 210/94. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral basilar rales. A faint murmur of aortic insufficiency is heard. The BNP level is elevated at 550 pg/mL (Normal < 100). ECG shows nonspecific ST-T changes. Chest x-ray suggests a widened mediastinum. Which of the following choices represents the best initial management?
options: IV furosemide plus IV loading dose of digoxin
Percutaneous coronary intervention with consideration of angioplasty and/or stenting
Blood cultures and rapid initiation of vancomycin plus gentamicin, followed by echocardiography
IV beta-blocker to control heart rate, IV nitroprusside to control blood pressure, transesophageal echocardiogram
IV heparin followed by CT pulmonary angiography
answer_text: IV beta-blocker to control heart rate, IV nitroprusside to control blood pressure, transesophageal echocardiogram Aortic dissection with AR and HTN → IV beta-blocker first, then nitroprusside; diagnose by TEE/MRA/CTA; urgent surgery for Type A; avoid anticoagulation and digoxin.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 67-year-old male presents to your clinic to establish primary care; he is asymptomatic. He has a history of hypertension for which he takes hydrochlorothiazide. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 62. The patient smoked until 5 years ago, but has been abstinent from tobacco since then. His blood pressure in the office today is 132/78. Aside from being overweight, the remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following preventive health interventions would be most appropriately offered to him today?
options: Carotid ultrasound to evaluate for carotid ar tery stenosis
Abdominal ultrasound to evaluate for aortic aneurysm
Lipoprotein(a) assay to evaluate coronary heart disease risk
Exercise (treadmill) stress testing to evaluate for coronary artery disease
Homocysteine level to evaluate coronary heart disease risk
answer_text: Abdominal ultrasound to evaluate for aortic aneurysm USPSTF: one-time AAA ultrasound for men 65–75 who ever smoked; no carotid US/ treadmill screening in asymptomatic; do not order Lp(a)/homocysteine.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 38-year-old lady presents to the emergency department with increased shortness of breath for the last 5 days. On full history taking, you find she has also recently had some episodes of chest pain on exertion. She is normally fit and well but does report generalized aching and a high temperature approximately 2 weeks ago. On examination you find that she is haemodynamically stable with a blood pressure on 100/65 mmHg in the right arm and a heart rate of 95 bpm. The radial pulse on the right side is absent. Heart sounds are normal and the apex beat is non displaced. Her oxygen saturations are 95% on air and her respiratory rate at rest is 20 breaths per minute. Given the history and examination findings given, what is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Takayasu’s arteritis Absent radial pulse + systemic features best explained by Takayasu arteritis; alternatives each miss key findings.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following drugs is not first line antihypertensive?
answer_text: Beta blockers Beta blockers are no longer considered first-line for primary hypertension in many guidelines.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: Which of the following is not considered as a first line treatment for hypertension?
answer_text: Beta blockers Beta blockers are not considered first line treatment for hypertension.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: A 45-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is reviewed in the diabetes clinic. Blood pressure was 145/95 mmHg. Lisinopril was started to treat her hypertension. Her blood tests were S.K 4.5 mmol/l, Creatinine 1.8 mg/ dl and eGFR was 47 ml/min. Three months later S.K 4.9 mmol/l, screatinine 2 mg/dl and eGFR was 44 ml/min. Which of the following options is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Stop lisinopril and arrange investigations to exclude renal artery stenosis
answer_text: No action No action is appropriate as the changes in renal parameters are minimal.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 42-year-old man with known hypertension who ran out of his medication presents with a blood pressure of 230/140 mmHg, severe headache, dizziness, and blurred disc margins on fundoscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Hypertensive emergency The very high blood pressure with end-organ damage (blurred disc margins) indicates a hypertensive emergency.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: How would you best label this patient’s hypertensive state?
answer_text: Hypertensive emergency End-organ damage (e.g., retinal changes) in the context of severely elevated blood pressure defines a hypertensive emergency.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which of the following is an appropriate first-line intravenous antihypertensive agent in this scenario?
answer_text: Intravenous nitroprusside IV nitroprusside (or alternatively IV labetalol) is often used for rapid blood pressure control in hypertensive emergencies.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 56 year old man presents with a history of headache. He is noted to have a loud second heart sound on auscultation. Which of the following pathologies could explain this finding?
answer_text: Essential hypertension A loud second heart sound may result from high diastolic pressures as seen in essential hypertension.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 35 year old executive has a reproducible BP of 180/100 mmHg. She is referred for assessment in the clinic. You perform a range of tests to determine whether there is an underlying cause for her hypertension. What is the commonest cause of secondary hypertension?
answer_text: Renal disease Renal disease is the most common cause of secondary hypertension.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 60 year old man is referred by his family physician because despite four drugs he continues to have uncontrolled blood pressure. The doctor feels that the patient needs further investigation for a potential secondary cause of hypertension. What is the commonest cause of poorly controlled hypertension?
answer_text: Poor adherence with medication Poor adherence to antihypertensive therapy is the most common cause of uncontrolled blood pressure.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: All of the following statements regarding the epidemiology of hypertension are true EXCEPT:
options: Among individuals age 60 years or older, average systolic blood pressure is higher in women.
Diastolic blood pressure increases steadily with age throughout life.
Hypertension prevalence is lower in Mexican Americans than non-Hispanic whites.
In industrialized nations, blood pressure increases steadily during the first two decades of life.
In the United States, approximately 30% of adults have hypertension.
answer_text: Diastolic blood pressure increases steadily with age throughout life Diastolic BP actually declines after age 55, making this statement false.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: Disease of which organ is the most common cause of mortality in hypertensive patients?
answer_text: Heart Heart disease is the leading cause of death in hypertensive patients.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: A 28-year-old woman has hypertension that is difficult to control. She was diagnosed at age 26. Since that time, she has been on increasing amounts of medication. Her current regimen consists of labetalol 1000 mg twice a day, lisinopril 40 mg once a day, clonidine 0.1 mg twice a day, and amlodipine 5 mg once a day. On physical examination, she appears without distress. Blood pressure is 168/100 mmHg, and heart rate is 84 bpm. Cardiac examination is unremarkable. She has good peripheral pulses and no edema. Her physical appearance does not reveal any hirsutism, fat maldistribution, or abnormalities of genitalia. Laboratory studies reveal a potassium of 2.8 mEq/dL and a serum bicarbonate of 32 mEq/dL. Fasting blood glucose is 114 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Conn syndrome Resistant hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis suggests primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome).

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: What is the best way to diagnose the disease in the patient described in Question V-143?
answer_text: Plasma aldosterone/renin ratio The plasma aldosterone/renin ratio is the preferred diagnostic test for Conn syndrome.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: Mr. Wilkins is a 65-year-old aeronautics engineer who has never been to the doctor and takes no medications. He is brought to the emergency department by his wife for worsening headache over the last day and confusion starting about an hour ago. His blood pressure on presentation is 230/140 mmHg, and heart rate is 90 bpm. Arterial oxygen saturation is 95%. On examination, he is moving all extremities equally, and there are no obvious cranial nerve deficits, but he is clearly delirious. Cardiac examination reveals an enlarged and forceful PMI and an S4 gallop; his lungs are clear to auscultation. Laboratory studies show a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL, 2+ protein in his urine with hematuria, and a hematocrit of 32% with normal platelet count. Peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes. Emergent brain MRI shows old microvascular changes but no acute infarct or hemorrhage. Regarding his blood pressure management, which of the following would be the most reasonable therapeutic course?
options: 20 mg of IV labetalol and initiation of a continuous parenteral drip for goal mean arterial pressure of 125 mmHg in the first hour
answer_text: 20 mg of IV labetalol and initiation of a continuous parenteral drip for goal mean arterial pressure of 125 mmHg in the first hour In malignant hypertension, rapid yet controlled blood pressure reduction using IV agents is warranted.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: Which of the following statements regarding the physiology of renal perfusion is true?
options: Due to tight precapillary regulation, the glomerular capillary endothelium is relatively shield ed from pressure injury.
Renal cortical blood flow is less than renal medullary blood flow, and coupled with the high metabolic needs of the renal cortex, this leaves that region bordering on hypoxemia.
Renal perfusion is tightly regulated to the metabolic needs of the kidney.
Urinary albumin excretion is predictive of systemic atherosclerotic events and can present years in advance of clinical atherosclerotic disease.
Venous blood returning from the renal cortex has a lower oxygen content than venous blood returning from the renal medulla.
answer_text: Urinary albumin excretion is predictive of systemic atherosclerotic events and can present years in advance of clinical atherosclerotic disease. Increased urinary albumin excretion is an early marker for systemic atherosclerotic events.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: Which of the following statements regarding renal artery stenosis is true?
options: An abnormally reduced renal artery flow velocity by Doppler ultrasound is predictive of hemodynamically significant stenosis.
Early in the course of renal artery stenosis, elevated systemic renin levels are typical.
In the general population, the presence of fibromuscular dysplasia is rare (<1% prevalence).
Levels of renin activity observed in renal artery stenosis are predictive of response to medical therapy.
Usually the first clinical presentation of renal stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia is reduced renal function.
answer_text: Early in the course of renal artery stenosis, elevated systemic renin levels are typical. Elevated renin levels are an early indicator of hemodynamically significant renal artery stenosis.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A man has been diagnosed with essential hypertension by his GP and needs to commence on the appropriate treatment. In the treatment of essential hypertension, which of the following statements is true?
options: Alpha-blockers such as prazosin are unlikely to cause postural hypotension
Patients of Afro-Caribbean descent respond well to ACE inhibitors
ACE inhibitors are indicated if there is unilateral renal artery stenosis
Treatment with bendrofluazide may result in hypokalaemia
ACE inhibitors may cause ankle swelling as a side effect
answer_text: Treatment with bendrofluazide may result in hypokalaemia Thiazide diuretics like bendrofluazide can cause hypokalaemia.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 50-year-old man has persistently elevated blood pressure of about 185/110 mmHg. He has been complaining of headaches for a few weeks but otherwise well. ECG reveals abnormal voltage changes and ST segment depression in the left ventricular leads. He was also found to have evidence of arteriovenous nipping on fundoscopy. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Advise weight loss and see again in 2 months
Hospitalize and give urgent IV antihypertensive medication
Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 2 months
Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 3 days
answer_text: Begin oral antihypertensives and see in 3 days This is hypertensive urgency with minor end-organ damage; blood pressure should be reduced over hours using oral agents.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 50-year-old Caucasian man sees his GP for a blood pressure check as he has recently been diagnosed with essential hypertension. His only other medical history is type II diabetes mellitus with no end-organ damage, which is well controlled on oral hypoglycaemic agents. His blood pressure has been 145/90 mmHg persistently despite diet and exercise for 3 months. Which of the following is the first-line medication for blood pressure control in this patient?
answer_text: Start on enalapril ACE inhibitors like enalapril are first-line in hypertensive diabetic patients.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a mild headache. He is known to have poorly controlled hypertension and is on multiple antihypertensive medications. On examination his blood pressure is 205/110 mmHg and there is no evidence of end-organ involvement. His headache is still present but there is no focal neurology identified. Which of the following is the least appropriate in the management of this patient’s blood pressure?
options: Rapidly lowering blood pressure in the emergency department
Adjust treatment and follow-up within 24 to 48 hours of presentation in the community
Initiate a maintenance dose of an oral medication before discharge
Consider a short observation period before discharge
Discharge the patient, emphasizing the importance of close follow-up and compliance with medications
answer_text: Rapidly lowering blood pressure in the emergency department Rapid lowering of blood pressure in asymptomatic hypertensive patients may be harmful and is not recommended.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old man has been recently diagnosed with hypertension and commenced on treatment. He attends his GP to find out more about the condition. Which of the following is the commonest cause of hypertension?
answer_text: Undetermined cause Primary or essential hypertension, with an undetermined cause, accounts for the majority of cases.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 63-year-old retired doctor presents with nausea and headaches. His past medical history includes type II diabetes mellitus. On examination you note his blood pressure is 165/76 mmHg. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
answer_text: ACE inhibitors ACE inhibitors are the first- line treatment for hypertension in diabetic patients.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 65-year-old hypertensive patient is reviewed in the outpatient clinic complaining of visual disturbances. On examination you note flame-shaped haemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Grade 3 retinal disease Flame-shaped haemorrhages are characteristic of Grade 3 hypertensive retinal changes.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old African American female presents to the ER with lethargy and blood pressure of 250/150. Her family members indicate that she was complaining of severe headache and visual disturbance earlier in the day. They report a past history of asthma but no known kidney disease. On physical examination, retinal hemorrhages are present. Which of the following is the best approach?
options: Clonidine by mouth to lower blood pressure
Nifedipine sublingually to lower blood pressure
answer_text: Continuous-infusion nitroprusside Hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy → ICU IV nitroprusside or alternatives; avoid labetalol in asthma; no SL nifedipine; clonidine too slow; loops not acute control.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 50-year-old construction worker continues to have elevated blood pressure of 160/95 even after a third agent is added to his antihypertensive regimen. Physical examination is normal, electrolytes are normal, and the patient is taking no over-the-counter medications. Which of the following is the best next step for this patient?
options: Check chest x-ray for coarctation of the aorta.
answer_text: Check pill count. Resistant HTN most often nonadherence; check history/pill count; also salt, alcohol, sleep apnea; secondary causes less likely without clues.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: You are seeing a 45-year-old female patient of your partner for the first time in your clinic. A quick review of the patient’s medical record shows that her systolic blood pressure was greater than 140 mm Hg at both of her last clinic appointments. Her medical history is otherwise significant only for diabetes mellitus. Her blood pressure today is 164/92. What is the best next step in her blood pressure management?
options: Ask the patient to keep a written record of her blood pressure and bring with her to a return appointment.
Advise the patient to begin a heart healthy, low sodium diet and refer to a nutritionist.
Prescribe an ACE inhibitor in addition to heart healthy diet.
Prescribe a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker in addition to a heart healthy diet.
Arrange for echocardiogram to assess for end-organ damage.
answer_text: Prescribe an ACE inhibitor in addition to heart healthy diet. Diabetes + HTN target ≤130/80; start ACEi (renal benefit) over lifestyle alone; thiazides are general first line; CCB acceptable but not preferred initially.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 45-year-old man with high blood pressure attends his GP practice for a review. His blood pressure readings have been persistently raised. His blood pressure on the previous clinic reading was 156/80 so the GP organised for him to have ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, which revealed a daytime average blood pressure of 138/85 mmHg. He is on the maximum dose of ramipril. Which second-line agent would be most appropriate to add?
answer_text: Indapamide ACEi + uncontrolled HTN → add CCB or thiazide-like diuretic; resistant HTN 4th line: K>4.5 bisoprolol or doxazosin; K<4.5 spironolactone; avoid verapamil for primary HTN.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Which one of the following statements is not correct regarding hypertension in pregnancy?
options: An increase above booking readings of > 30 mmHg systolic or > 15 mmHg diastolic suggests hypertension
Pre-eclampsia occurs in around 5% of pregnancies
Urine dipstick showing protein + is consistent with gestational hypertension
A rise in blood pressure before 20 weeks suggests pre-existing hypertension
With gestational hypertension the blood pressure rises in the second half of pregnancy
answer_text: Urine dipstick showing protein + is consistent with gestational hypertension Proteinuria suggests pre-eclampsia not gestational HTN. Gestational HTN = ≥20 w high BP without protein. Rise >30 systolic or >15 diastolic from booking suggests HTN. Pre-eclampsia ~2–8%. BP rise before 20 w = chronic HTN.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: All of the fallowing drugs improve the prognosis in heart failure Except:
answer_text: Diguxin. Diguxin does not improve prognosis in heart failure.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: Digitalis toxicity may be precipitated by all except one:
answer_text: Hepatic impairment Hepatic impairment does not precipitate digitalis toxicity as the liver plays a minimal role in its elimination.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: A 47-year-old man is admitted to hospital following an acute coronary syndrome. He has a history peptic ulcer disease and his cardiologist decides to use clopidogrel. What is the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
options: Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor
answer_text: Inhibits ADP binding to its platelet receptor Clopidogrel works by inhibiting ADP binding to its platelet receptor.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide have which of the following effects?
options: Diuresis due to inhibition of potassium and water reabsorption
Diuresis due to inhibition of sodium and water reabsorption
Diuresis due to inhibition of water reabsorption only
Increased serum potassium levels due to enhanced distal tubule function
answer_text: Diuresis due to inhibition of sodium and water reabsorption Loop diuretics act in the loop of Henle to inhibit sodium and water reabsorp tion.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: B-Adrenoceptor antagonists (B-blockers) are used in which of the following situations?
answer_text: Chronic left ventricular systolic dysfunction Beta blockers improve survival in chronic LV dysfunction but are contraindicated in acute failure or shock.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A 71 year old woman with a history of hypertension presents with fatigue and rapid, irregular palpitations. She normally takes enalapril for blood pressure control. Clinical examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse, rate 125 beats/min, and BP 128/86 mmHg. Cardiovascular examination is otherwise normal. A 12- lead ECG is performed, which shows atrial fibrillation with poor ventricular rate control, but no other abnormality. Which of the following drugs is the most suitable agent to control heart rate in this patient?
answer_text: B-blocker B-blockers are the first-line therapy for rate control in atrial fibrillation.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Which of the following drugs is known to be effective in preventing stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation?
answer_text: Apixaban Apixaban, an oral factor Xa inhibitor, has been shown to prevent stroke in AF patients.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Which of the following antiplatelet drugs is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor?
answer_text: Dipyridamole Dipyridamole works by inhibiting phosphodiesterase, thereby increasing cAMP in platelets.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Considering the patient in Questions 16.72 and 16.73, blood cultures demonstrate viridans streptococci. What is the most appropriate antibiotic regime to commence the patient on?
answer_text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin Benzylpenicillin combined with gentamicin is the recommended regimen for viridans streptococcal endocarditis.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: The B-blockers represent the most-studied drug in the history of HFrEF. Initially avoided for their negative inotropic and chronotropic effects, they now form the foundation of neurohormonal-targeted therapy in the treatment of chronic HFrEF. However, the benefit of B-blockers is not a blanket class effect and indeed has only been demonstrated for three drugs in the numerous clinical trials: metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, and carvedilol. Importantly, metoprolol tartrate has never been found to have mortality benefit in HFrEF, nor have B-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (nebivolol, xamoterol).
answer_text: Answer: C. Metoprolol succinate. The B-blockers represent the most-studied drug in the history of HFrEF. Initially avoided for their negative inotropic and chronotropic effects, they now form the foundation of neurohormonal-targeted therapy in the treatment of chronic HFrEF. However, the benefit of B-blockers is not a blanket class effect and indeed has only been demonstrated for three drugs in the numerous clinical trials: metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, and carvedilol. Importantly, metoprolol tartrate has never been found to have mortality benefit in HFrEF, nor have B-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (nebivolol, xamoterol).

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: All of the following medications used in the acute management of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction are appropriately matched to their mechanism of effect EXCEPT:
options: Abciximab – inhibition of the glycoprotein IIb/ IIIa receptor
B-Adrenergic antagonists – reduced myocardial oxygen consumption
Clopidogrel – inhibition of the platelet adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor
answer_text: Nitroglycerin – reduced cardiac afterload Nitroglycerin primarily reduces preload rather than afterload.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 64-year-old female comes to your surgery with a past medical history of hypertension. She is on an ACE inhibitor as well as on a range of other medications. Which one of the following would be most likely to blunt the antihypertensive effects of an ACE inhibitor?
answer_text: Ibuprofen Ibuprofen, an NSAID, can blunt the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors by reducing renal excretion.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 48-year-old woman with essential hypertension, treated for 3 months, presents with a persistent dry cough despite linctus and antibiotics. Which antihypertensive is responsible?
answer_text: Lisinopril ACE inhibitors like lisinopril are known to cause a dry cough.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 66-year-old man is diagnosed with a transient ischaemic attack and commenced on clopidogrel. He already takes a statin. After a week of treatment, he presents to his GP complaining of severe diarrhoea. His GP suspects that clopidogrel is the cause and decides to switch him to combination antiplatelet treatment. This includes modified-release dipyridamole. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
answer_text: Phosphodiesterase inhibitor Dipyridamole: non-specific PDE inhibitor; decreases adenosine uptake; antiplatelet with aspirin if clopidogrel intolerant. GP IIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen; tirofiban blocks it. GPIb binds vWF. P2Y12 blocked by clopidogrel.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old man is admitted following an acute coronary syndrome. He receives aspirin, clopidogrel, nitrates and morphine. His 6-month risk score is high and percutaneous coronary intervention is planned. He is therefore given intravenous tirofiban. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Inhibits the production of thromboxane A2
answer_text: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist Tirofiban is GP IIb/IIIa antagonist that blocks fibrinogen binding and platelet aggregation; not COX-1 inhibition; not AT-III activation; not a vasodilator.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 78-year-old man presents with a hot, red, swollen leg. On examination, the left leg is tender and hot to touch, with evidence of a recent superficial laceration he sustained whilst gardening. His blood tests show raised inflammatory markers and a negative D-dimer. He is treated for cellulitis with clarithromycin due to being penicillin-allergic. Which of his regular medications should be concurrently suspended?
answer_text: Simvastatin Clarithromycin increases simvastatin exposure → myopathy risk; notable interactions of clarithromycin with SSRIs etc; no key interaction with aspirin or clopidogrel.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: A 24-year-old man with no prior medical problems faints while having exercise. He has a quick recovery and has no neurologic deficits. ECG shows a normal sinus rhythm. Which of the following is the most useful diagnostic test?
answer_text: Echocardiogram. Echocardiogram is used to detect underlying structural heart issues.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: The following are recognized causes of prolonged PR interval except
answer_text: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is not a cause of prolonged PR interval.

heading: Previous CVS
stem: Common causes of empyema are the following EXCEPT:
options: Rupture of sub-phrenic abscess through the diaphram
answer_text: Rheumatic fever Rheumatic fever is not a common cause of empyema.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: In the management of cardiac arrest, which of the following most accurately describes basic life support (BLS)?
options: Administration of intravenous drugs and external defibrillation (the two ‘D’s)
Support of airway, breathing and circulation (ABC)
Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure (ABCDE)
Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure, treatment of fibrillation (ABCDEF)
answer_text: Support of airway, breathing and circulation, and assessment of disability and exposure (ABCDE) BLS involves ensuring airway, breathing, circulation and a quick assessment of disability and exposure.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Which of the following statements is true of a pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest?
options: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be carried out for 1 minute before the rhythm is reassessed
Intravenous amiodarone will restore cardiac output
It is initially managed with immediate defibrillation
Reversible causes include hyperthyroidism and hypercalcaemia
Reversible causes include hypothermia and hypoxia
answer_text: Reversible causes include hypothermia and hypoxia PEA is associated with reversible causes such as hypothermia and hypoxia; defibrillation is not effective.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumour. Which of the following is true of atrial myxoma?
options: It occurs more commonly in the right atrium than in the left atrium
Surgery is not indicated because atrial myxomas are benign
Surgery is usually indicated to prevent embolic complications such as stroke
The tumour commonly obstructs the aortic valve
answer_text: Surgery is usually indicated to prevent embolic complications such as stroke Although benign, atrial myxomas require surgical removal to prevent embolism.

heading: Davidson CVS
stem: A patient presents with an incidental finding of a mass in the left atrium whilst undergoing an echocardiogram for hypertension. What is the most likely cardiac tumour in this situation?
answer_text: Atrial myxoma Atrial myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumour.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: You are appointed as a cardiac epidemiologist advisor on an international committee setting global health policy. Your committee is assigned to predict health trends in a Pacific East Asian nation with a population and environment very similar to China. At this point in history, the nation is just moving from the first classic stage in the epidemiologic transition (“pestilence and famine”) to the second classic stage (“receding pandemics”). In regard to the anticipated patterns of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in this nation, which of the following is true?
options: As this nation enters the stage of receding pandemics, you would expect the majority of CVD morbidity and mortality to be due to cardiomyopathies secondary to infectious agents.
Each nation or geographical location progresses through the five stages of epidemiologic transition identically in regard to CVD risk.
In this nation, when CVD mortality peaks, you would expect stroke mortality to be greater than coronary heart disease mortality.
One would expect a very homogeneous epidemiologic pattern of CVD risk throughout this nation over time.
You anticipate that CVD mortality will inexorably climb as this nation progresses through the five stages of the epidemiologic transition.
answer_text: In this nation, when CVD mortality peaks, you would expect stroke mortality to be greater than coronary heart disease mortality. Epidemiologic transition studies show that in countries similar to China, stroke mortality predominates over CHD at the peak of CVD mortality.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: You are evaluating Mr. Estebez, a 67-year- old owner of a wildly successful chain of sushi restaurants. He complains of shortness of breath with exertion, lower extremity edema, and awakening at night feeling acutely short of breath. You wish to assess his volume status, and know that jugular venous pulse (JVP) assessment is the single most important physi cal examination measurement to aid you in this component of your evaluation. Which of the following statements regarding JVP measurement is true?
options: If done properly, the angle of inclination matters little to the measurement of JVP.
In normal patients, the JVP rises with inspiration due to the augmented volume loading of the right heart.
Measurement of the elevation of the top of the JVP and the sternal inflection point (angle of Louis) will provide a highly accurate measurement of central venous pressure.
The external jugular is preferred over the internal jugular vein due to its ease of visibility.
Venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are abnormal.
answer_text: Venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are abnormal. Because the internal jugular is the true reflection of right atrial pressure, visible pulsations above the clavicle indicate abnormal elevation.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following statements regarding blood pressure measurements is true?
options: Systolic pressure increases and diastolic pressure decreases when measured in more distal arteries.
Systolic leg blood pressures are usually as much as 20 mmHg lower than arm blood pressures.
The concept of “white coat hypertension” (blood pressures measured in office or hospital settings significantly higher than in nonclinical settings) has been shown to be a myth.
The difference in blood pressure measured in both arms should be less than 20mmHg.
Using a blood pressure cuff that is too small will result in a marked underestimation of the true blood pressure.
answer_text: Systolic pressure increases and diastolic pressure decreases when measured in more distal arteries. The blood pressure changes with distance from the heart due to pulse pressure amplification and damping of diastolic pressure.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following statements regarding normal depolarization patterns of the heart is true?
options: Each normal sinus beat is initiated by spontaneous depolarization in the atrioventricular (AV) node.
The normal order of depolarization is as follows: sinoatrial (SA) node - atrial myocardium - AV node - His bundle - Purkinje fibers - ventricular myocardium.
The right bundle branch bifurcates into an anterior and posterior fascicle.
The SA node is unique in its ability to spontaneously depolarize, a quality known as automaticity.
Within the ventricular myocardium, depolarization sweeps from epicardium to endocardium.
answer_text: The normal order of depolarization is as follows: sinoatrial (SA) node - atrial myocardium - AV node - His bundle - Purkinje fibers - ventricular myocardium. This reflects the normal conduction sequence initiating at the SA node and propagating through the specialized conduction system.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: All of the following ECG waveforms are matched correctly to the cardiac cycle that they represent EXCEPT:
answer_text: P wave - atrial repolarization Atrial repolarization is typically not visible on the ECG, making this pairing incorrect.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following mean QRS vectors in the frontal electrocardiographic plane is matched appropriately to its designation?
options: All of the above are incorrect.
answer_text: -20 degrees - normal axis A normal QRS axis is generally defined between -30° and +90°; -20° falls within this range.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following options describes the primary finding in the ECG shown in Figure V-14?
options: ST elevation in the anterior precordial leads; suspect anterior myocardial ischemia
answer_text: Normal ECG The ECG is normal with appropriate rate, intervals, and waveform morphology.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A large snowstorm hits your area on a Thursday, and the roads are largely impassible until the following Monday. On Monday morning, a 48-year-old man is brought by EMS to the emergency department after being found with altered mental status by a neighbor. He is obtunded and unable to provide a history. You note a left brachial artery hemodialysis fistula in place. His initial ECG is shown in Figure V-19. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities would you expect to find in this patient?
answer_text: Hyperkalemia Missed dialysis sessions commonly lead to hyperkalemia, as reflected by peaked T waves on ECG.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: The SA node serves as the dominant pacemaker of the heart in normal sinus rhythm. What property of SA nodal cells allows it to act as the primary pacemaker?
options: Location near the superior lateral area of the right atrium
More numerous intercalated discs of any other myocardial tissue
Only cells with the ability to spontaneously depolarize
Spontaneous depolarization during phase 4 of the action potential at a more rapid rate than any other myocardial cells
answer_text: Spontaneous depolarization during phase 4 of the action potential at a more rapid rate than any other myocardial cells The SA node’s intrinsic automaticity during phase 4 is the key factor in pacemaking.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 76-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes mellitus, and osteoporo sis presents to the emergency department after a fall at home followed immediately by intense left hip pain. She was found by a neighbor after several hours. The patient cannot remember if she lost consciousness. She is exquisitely tender to palpation over the left hip, and her leg is shortened and externally rotated. Her mucous membranes are dry, and her skin tents easily. Blood pressure is 170/80 mmHg and heart rate is 130 bpm. Her rhythm strip is shown in Figure V-39. What is the most appropriate first step for her tachycardia?
answer_text: Pain control and IV hydration Tachycardia in this setting is most likely secondary to pain and dehydration; supportive care is appropriate.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: You are having a quiet shift in the local emergency department. For the past 4 days, there has been a large snowstorm limiting traffic, and people have generally stayed indoors and out of harm’s way. Suddenly, the emergency medical personnel arrive with a middle-aged woman who is obtunded. Her downstairs neighbors noted that they had not seen her for the past 4 days (since the snow started) and alerted the police who found her unconscious on her floor. On your assessment, you can barely feel a radial pulse. You note a dialysis fistula graft in her left arm. Blood pressure is 60/palp, and her ECG tracing is shown in Figure V-43. You rapidly set up for defibrillation and request a full chemistry panel. What electrolyte abnormality do you expect to find?
answer_text: Hyperkalemia The sinusoidal, bizarre ECG pattern is characteristic of severe hyperkalemia in a dialysis patient.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: An 87-year-old man with an orthotopic heart transplant presents with a mild resting tachycardia. Which of the following best explains his heart rate response?
options: The denervated donor heart responds only to circulating catecholamines.
The heart rate is due to rejection.
The transplant procedure damages the SA node permanently.
answer_text: The transplant heart is denervated and thus relies on circulating catecholamines for rate response. After transplant, the donor heart lacks autonomic innervation, causing a higher resting rate and delayed response to stress.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: Regarding donor heart allocation in the United States, which of the following statements is true?
options: Allocation is based solely on the severity of the recipient’s illness.
Donor hearts can be shared nationally without time constraints.
There is a physiologic limit of approximately 3 hours of ischemic time, necessitating regional allocation.
Time on the waiting list is not considered in allocation.
answer_text: There is a physiologic limit of approximately 3 hours of ischemic time, necessitating regional allocation. Donor hearts are allocated regionally based on ischemic time, illness severity, and wait time.

heading: Harrison MCQ’s
stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department for dyspnea on exertion. He had an orthotopic heart transplant for non-ischemic cardiomyopathy 5 years ago and, in general, has done quite well except for one cytomegalovirus reactivation within the first year. He reports that for the past 3 months, he has noticed that with decreasing amounts of exertion he has been having limiting dyspnea. He is adamant that he is experiencing no chest pain or pressure during these episodes. He has been perfectly compliant with his regimen of tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and low-dose prednisone. Echocardiography reveals a normal LV function with normal LV wall thickness. His resting ECG shows normal sinus rhythm at a rate of 80 bpm. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
answer_text: specifically cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV), a common long-term complication after heart transplantation. It causes diffuse, progressive narrowing of coronary arteries, often without angina due to cardiac denervation. Symptoms like exertional dyspnea are typical and may be the only sign.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: You are evaluating a 19-year-old woman in a travel clinic who complains of a nonpainful swelling of the lower extremity. On examination, the leg shows thickened skin with a woody texture. A bedside ultrasound confirms patent lower extremity veins without thrombus. You suspect lymphedema likely due to the most common cause of secondary lymphedema worldwide. What cause do you suspect?
options: Cancer involving the inguinal lymph nodes
answer_text: Lymphatic filariasis Lymphatic filariasis is the most common cause of secondary lymphedema globally.

heading: Harrison CVS
stem: You are taking care of a patient who suffers from chronic lymphedema due to recurrent streptococcal lymphangitis in childhood. She finds her leg swelling unsightly and asks about therapeutic options. All of the following are reasonable therapeutic options for chronic lymphedema EXCEPT:
answer_text: Diuretic therapy Diuretics are contraindicated in lymphedema as they may lead to intravascular depletion and metabolic disturbances.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: While on call you are bleeped to see a patient who has had a massive bleed PR. On examination you note he is drowsy with a blood pressure of 65/40 mmHg and pulse rate of 130 beats/min. While you obtain IV access, he arrests. The nurse calls the crash team and you commence cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). After 2 minutes, you note QRS complexes on the cardiac monitor but no evidence of a pulse. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
answer_text: Administration of colloid In pulseless elec trical activity due to hypovolaemia, volume resuscitation with colloid is the next appropriate step.

heading: Crash CVS MCQ’s
stem: A 44-year-old female comes to your office with chest pain of several days’ duration. She describes the pain as sharp and stabbing, and indicates that it is located at the left sternal border; it is increased by coughing and palpation. There is no family history of heart disease, nor is there a personal history of diabetes, hypertension, smoking or hyperlipidaemia. A physical examination, an ECG and chest radiographs are all normal. Further diagnostic studies should include which of the following?
options: A treadmill exercise test with ECG and blood pressure monitoring
answer_text: No additional tests In the absence of risk factors and with normal investigations, no further cardiac tests are indicated.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mr. George is a 52-year-old man with longstanding hypertension and poorly controlled diabetes. He presents complaining of several months of breathlessness with exertion, acute episodes of shortness of breath when recumbent, and lower extremity edema. On examination, he has an elevated jugular venous pulse and an S4 on auscultation. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55% with a large left atrium. You suspect this patient has the syndrome of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Drugs targeting which of the following have convincingly demonstrated mortality reduction for patients with HFpEF?
answer_text: None of the above No drug has convincingly demonstrated mortality reduction in HFpEF.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are evaluating a 64-year-old woman with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy. She presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath. You note that she has gained 11 kg since her last cardiology appointment 2 months ago. Physical examination confirms findings associated with acute decompensated heart failure, including pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pulse, abdominal ascites, lower extremity edema, and a square wave blood pressure Valsalva response. Her extremities are warm, and blood pressure is 110/78 mmHg with a heart rate of 75 bpm. Her laboratory studies return with a sodium of 128 mEq/L and creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL (which is increased from her prior level of 1.2 mg/dL). Chest x-ray shows a diffuse alveolar filling pattern consistent with pulmonary edema. What is the next most appropriate step?
options: Insert a large-bore central IV line and prepare for ultrafiltration
Insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic monitoring
Start dobutamine at 5 µg/kg/min and titrate to a urine output of 1 mL/kg/hr
answer_text: Administer furosemide 40 mg IV Diuretics are first-line in acute decompensated heart failure.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Which of the following statements regarding nesiritide is true in patients with acute decompensated heart failure requiring invasive hemodynamic monitoring?
options: Nesiritide has no significant effect on blood pressure.
Nesiritide improves renal perfusion in states of acute decompensated heart failure.
Nesiritide is associated with a decreased rate of rehospitalization, but not death, from acute decompensated heart failure.
Nesiritide reduces pulmonary capillary wedge more rapidly than IV nitrates.
None of the statements are true.
answer_text: None of the statements are true None of the given statements regarding nesiritide have been convincingly demonstrated.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mr. Jones is a 21-year-old man who presents to the emergency department with several days of worsening shortness of breath and lethargy 1 week after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. His family brought him in after he lacked the energy to rise from the couch unassisted. His blood pressure is 88/72 mmHg, heart rate is 115 bpm, and room air oxygen saturation is 90%. Physical examination reveals pulmonary crackles, elevated jugular venous pressure, an audible S3 gallop, and cool extremities. He is lethargic and slow to respond to questions. Laboratory analysis reveals a creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL, elevated BNP level, and mildly elevated lactate. Bedside echocardiography reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15% with global hypokinesis. You start dobutamine at 5 µg/kg/ min and prepare to insert a pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic monitoring. Which of the following hemodynamic parameters is most likely increased?
answer_text: Systemic vascular resistance In cardiogenic shock, compensatory vasoconstriction leads to increased systemic vascular resistance.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Which of the following medications has been shown to reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
answer_text: Metoprolol succinate Only metoprolol succinate (along with bisoprolol and carvedilol) has shown mortality benefit in HFrEF.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are seeing a patient with newly diagnosed nonischemic cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%. He is euvolemic and New York Heart Association (NYHA) class I in terms of symptoms severity. His blood pressure is 120/78 mmHg, and heart rate is 80 bpm. You know that, eventually, you would like him on optimal doses of a B-blocker and an ACE inhibitor. Which of the following represents the appropriate order of initiation and dose titration of these medications?
options: Co-initiate ACE inhibitor and B-blocker at low dose. Titrate each up every 2–4 weeks to highest tolerated dose.
Initiate ACE inhibitor and titrate to highest tolerated dose. Then initiate B-blocker and titrate to highest tolerated dose.
Initiate ACE inhibitor at low dose. Then initiate B-blocker at low dose. Alternate titrating the dose up for each drug to the highest tolerated dose for both.
Initiate B-blocker and titrate to highest tolerated dose. Then initiate ACE inhibitor and titrate to highest tolerated dose.
The specific strategy does not matter so much as the goal of initiating both ACE inhibitor and B-blocker in a timely manner and titrating both to their optimal, highest tolerated doses.
answer_text: The specific strategy does not matter so much as the goal of initiating both ACE inhibitor and B-blocker in a timely manner and titrating both to their optimal, highest tolerated doses. Studies have shown that the order of initiation does not significantly affect outcomes, as long as both are titrated optimally.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are seeing a 72-year-old woman with a history of ischemic cardiomyopathy and left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%. She is NYHA class II in terms of symptoms. She is on lisinopril 40 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, and spironolactone 25 mg daily. Her blood pressure is 102/82 mmHg, and heart rate is 60 bpm. Which of the following additional medications will further reduce her mortality?
answer_text: None of the above In patients on optimal neurohormonal therapy, no additional medication has demonstrated further mortality benefit.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are following a 57-year-old man who suffered a large anterior myocardial infarction 8 months ago. Despite a late presentation, he underwent primary coronary intervention with an excellent result. Currently, his heart rate is 65 bpm, blood pressure is 104/82 mmHg, and he is asymptomatic. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with a right bundle branch block and QRS duration of 135 msec. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 25% with a large area of anterior dyskinesis consistent with aneurysm. Which of the following therapies is indicated to reduce this patient’s mortality?
options: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator with cardiac resynchronization capability (coronary sinus lead)
answer_text: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator Primary prevention with an ICD is indicated in patients with reduced EF post-MI.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are evaluating a 25-year-old man with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy who underwent an orthotopic heart transplant 18 months ago. His heart rate has been consistently around 90 bpm. What is the most appropriate next step for his elevated resting heart rate?
options: Exercise treadmill ECG testing to evaluate for chronotropic competence
Initiate metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily
Refer for electrophysiology study to evaluate for ectopic atrial tachycardia
answer_text: Reassurance Elevated resting heart rate is common in denervated transplanted hearts, and no intervention is needed.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are appointed to an advisory position with the government’s committee on organ transplantation. The committee chairman is curious about enacting a nationwide organ-sharing strategy for heart transplants. You advise that this strategy is not beneficial because:
options: Blood types are grouped nonrandomly nationally, precluding true nationwide sharing
The different regions have highly variable criteria for severity of illness determination
The financial structure of reimbursement/payment nationwide would not allow it
There is a physiologic limit on ‘cold ischemic’ time for harvested hearts that would preclude nationwide sharing
None of the above are true
answer_text: There is a physiologic limit on ‘cold ischemic’ time for harvested hearts that would preclude nationwide sharing The limited allowable cold ischemic time restricts nationwide sharing of donor hearts.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department for dyspnea on exertion. He had an orthotopic heart transplant for non-ischemic cardiomyopathy 5 years ago and, in general, has done quite well except for one cytomegalovirus reactivation within the first year. He reports that for the past 3 months, he has noticed that with decreasing amounts of exertion he has been having limiting dyspnea. He is adamant that he is experiencing no chest pain or pressure during these episodes. He has been perfectly compliant with his regimen of tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and low-dose prednisone. Echocardiography reveals a normal LV function with normal LV wall thickness. His resting ECG shows normal sinus rhythm at a rate of 80 bpm. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
answer_text: Coronary artery disease Cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a form of coronary artery disease, is a common long-term complication post-transplant.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mrs. Block is a 68-year-old woman with chemotherapy-related cardiomyopathy (EF 15%) and frequent hospitalizations for acute decompensated heart failure. She is not a candidate for heart transplant. Which of the following is an appropriate response regarding other options available to prolong her life?
options: Continuous infusion of milrinone will improve cardiac function and survival.
A left ventricular assist device can improve quality of life but provides no survival benefit over optimal medical care.
A left ventricular assist device can improve survival over the initial 2–5 years more than optimal medical therapy.
Stem cell implantation has been shown to prolong life in patients with end-stage cardiomyopathy.
There are no other options for prolonging life, and we should consider palliative measures in the future.
answer_text: A left ventricular assist device can improve survival over the initial 2–5 years more than optimal medical therapy. LVAD support has been shown to improve survival in patients not eligible for transplantation.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Which of the following statements regarding the epidemiology of congenital heart disease (CHD) in the United States is true?
answer_text: Given advances in surgical techniques and pre- and postnatal care, survival for a neonate with CHD now approaches 90%. Advances in care have dramatically improved survival in neonates with CHD.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: 1% of all live births. B. Given advances in surgical techniques and pre- and postnatal care, survival for a neonate with CHD now approaches 90%. C. Given the declining rates of pregnancy in women with CHD, the incidence of CHD in neonates is declining. D. The population of adults with CHD is declining given improved prenatal screening efforts. E. Women with CHD are at no increased risk for complications during pregnancy compared with the normal population.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 62-year-old man is being evaluated for mitral valve replacement for severe mitral regurgitation. Transesophageal echocardiogram demonstrates a small jet of right-to-left flow during systole across the atrial septum, occurring when a small flap of tissue swings open (<1 mm). Which of the following explains this finding?
answer_text: Patent foramen ovale A patent foramen ovale is characterized by a small, flap-like opening in the atrial septum.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are evaluating a 21-year-old man with newly diagnosed ventricular septal defect (VSD). Echocardiography confirms a 5-mm VSD in the muscular interventricular septum. Right heart catheterization reveals a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 20 mmHg, pulmonary vascular resistance of 2 Wood units, and systemic vascular resistance of 6 Wood units, with a calculated Qp:Qs of 1.25. What therapeutic course do you recommend?
options: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing to define peak oxygen consumption
Closure with a percutaneously deployed septal occluder device
Consideration of heart and lung transplant
No intervention now; annual cardiology assessments and reimaging if any new symptoms emerge
Surgical correction via open heart surgery and patch repair
answer_text: No intervention now; annual cardiology assessments and reimaging if any new symptoms emerge Small VSDs with minimal shunting do not require immediate intervention.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are evaluating a 52-year-old patient who presented with chest pain and elevated cardiac enzymes. A superficial, continuous murmur is heard at the mid-sternal level that was not documented before. Echocardiography visualizes normal valves. Right heart catheterization shows an oxygen saturation step-up in the coronary sinus. What is the abnormality accounting for this patient’s symptoms?
options: Anomalous left coronary artery off the main pulmonary artery
Coronary arteriovenous fistula to the coronary sinus
answer_text: Coronary arteriovenous fistula to the coronary sinus The oxygen step-up in the coronary sinus indicates a coronary AV fistula.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mr. Jenson is a 40-year-old man with a congenital bicuspid aortic valve. Which other anatomic structure is important to follow on his biannual echocardiograms?
answer_text: Aortic root size Patients with a bicuspid aortic valve are at risk for dilation of the aortic root.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: All of the following are classic definitional features of the tetralogy of Fallot EXCEPT:
answer_text: Tricuspid atresia Tetralogy of Fallot does not include tricuspid atresia; it consists of RV outflow obstruction, overriding aorta, VSD, and RV hypertrophy.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 78-year-old man with a history of tobacco abuse, obesity, and diabetes mellitus is evaluated for dyspnea on exertion. Echocardiography confirms severe aortic stenosis. Which of the following most likely contributed to the development of his lesion?
answer_text: Diabetes mellitus Diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for calcific aortic stenosis in the elderly.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 63-year-old man presents with new-onset exertional syncope and is found to have aortic stenosis. Untreated patients with his presentation have a predicted average life span of:
answer_text: 3 years Exertional syncope in aortic stenosis is associated with a poor prognosis, with an average lifespan of about 3 years if untreated.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: An 82-year-old man with severe calcific aortic stenosis, who previously deferred surgery, now presents with hypotension, tachycardia, and signs of multi-organ dysfunction. Which of the following would be a reasonable therapeutic option to improve his short-term perfusion to permit aortic valve replacement?
options: Digoxin 250 µg IV once and 125 µg orally daily thereafter
Metoprolol 5 mg IV serial dosing targeting a resting heart rate of 60–70 bpm
Phenylephrine continuous IV infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure of >65
answer_text: Percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty Balloon valvuloplasty can temporarily improve perfusion in severe aortic stenosis.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: An 85-year-old former lawyer presents with accelerating dyspnea and lower extremity edema. Echocardiogram reveals an ejection fraction of 25% with global hypokinesis, a calculated aortic valve area of 0.8 cm2, and a mean gradient of 25 mmHg. What is the next most reasonable step to determine whether this patient would benefit from aortic valve replacement?
options: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to evaluate ventricular scar and aortic valve mor phology
Cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) to determine ventricular viability
Coronary angiography to evaluate for the presence of obstructive coronary disease
Right heart catheterization to document cardiac output and filling pressures
answer_text: Dobutamine stress echocardiography Dobutamine stress echo helps differentiate true severe AS from pseudo-severe AS in low-flow states.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Which of the following parameters is typically reduced in chronic severe aortic regurgitation?
answer_text: Diastolic blood pressure Chronic aortic regurgitation leads to a decrease in diastolic blood pressure due to regurgitant flow.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 21-year-old woman with connective tissue disease presents with acute shortness of breath and pulmonary edema. Echocardiogram shows severe aortic regurgitation with an avulsed right coronary cusp. While awaiting emergent surgery, what intervention is most likely to help maintain her end-organ perfusion?
options: Esmolol continuous IV infusion titrated to a heart rate of 60–70 bpm
answer_text: IV nitroprusside Nitroprusside reduces afterload and regurgitant flow, improving effective stroke volume.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: What is the most common cause of obstruction to left ventricular inflow?
options: Infective endocarditis with large mitral valve vegetations
answer_text: Rheumatic mitral disease Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis, which obstructs LV inflow.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: In cases of severe mitral stenosis, which of the following parameters is typically increased?
answer_text: Left atrial pressure Mitral stenosis leads to elevated left atrial pressure to maintain cardiac output.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: All of the following will result in an elevation of left atrial pressure and potential worsening of lung function EXCEPT:
answer_text: Metoprolol Metoprolol, a beta-blocker, does not increase left atrial pressure.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mrs. Bream, an 84-year-old woman with severe mitral stenosis, develops new onset atrial fibrillation. Which of the following therapeutic interventions will NOT help lower her left atrial pressure?
options: Transvenous pacemaker placement and pacing at a heart rate of 90 bpm
All of the above will help lower left atrial pressure
answer_text: Transvenous pacemaker placement and pacing at a heart rate of 90 bpm Increasing the heart rate with pacing can worsen the elevated left atrial pressure in mitral stenosis.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
