stem: A 34-year-old man with rheumatic mitral stenosis is asymptomatic with a mitral valve area of 1.7 cm2. On exercise, his pulmonary artery systolic pressure reaches 40 mmHg. What treatment plan do you recommend?
options: Periodic cardiology assessments and echocardiographic monitoring
answer_text: Periodic cardiology assessments and echocardiographic monitoring Asymptomatic moderate mitral stenosis is managed conservatively with regular monitoring.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 65-year-old man with a 15-year history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy and severe mi tral regurgitation asks whether his valve should be fixed to improve survival. What is your response?
options: If you were to have high pulmonary artery pressures or develop new atrial fibrillation, we would move forward with valve repair.
In patients like you, valve repair has never been shown to improve survival.
We should consider valve surgery only if repair is possible. Replacement would not improve your survival.
While surgical methods have not shown survival benefit, percutaneous mitral valve repair has been shown to reduce mortality in patients like you.
Yes, your valve should have been fixed years ago.
answer_text: In patients like you, valve repair has never been shown to improve survival. Repair of functional mitral regurgitation in the setting of dilated cardiomyopathy has not demonstrated a survival benefit.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are performing a right and left heart catheterization on a patient with stenosis involving two valves. Based on the pressure readings, which two valves are involved?
answer_text: Mitral and tricuspid The pressure gradients indicate combined stenosis of the mitral and tricuspid valves, commonly seen in rheumatic disease.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are evaluating a 50-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. She has severe tricuspid regurgitation, a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle, and signs of right heart failure. What is the best treatment for her severe tricuspid regurgitation?
options: Diuretics and salt restriction accompanied by medical therapy targeting her elevated pulmonary artery pressures
answer_text: Diuretics and salt restriction accompanied by medical therapy targeting her elevated pulmonary artery pressures Management of functional tricuspid regurgitation in the setting of pulmonary hypertension is primarily medical.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are seeing a 21-year-old woman in primary care who has never seen a physician before. She is found to have a systolic murmur in the left second interspace preceded by a presystolic click. Echocardiogram confirms pulmonic stenosis with a peak gradient of 60 mmHg and doming of the pulmonic valve without regurgitation. What is her best treatment option?
answer_text: Percutaneous balloon valvotomy Percutaneous balloon valvotomy is the treatment of choice for symptomatic pulmonic stenosis.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 77-year-old patient with severe aortic stenosis develops signs of acute pulmonary edema and is found to have a new soft, short apical systolic murmur consistent with acute severe mitral regurgitation due to ruptured chordae. Which parameter will likely increase as a result of the new severe mitral regurgitation?
answer_text: Ejection fraction The ejection fraction may increase due to a reduction in afterload when regurgitation occurs.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mr. Milsap, a patient with a history of rheumatic heart disease, presents with atrial fibrillation at a rate of 60 bpm. Which of the following options for thromboembolic prophylaxis is appropriate?
options: More information is needed prior to initiating thromboembolic prophylaxis
answer_text: Warfarin Warfarin remains the recommended anticoagulant for valvular atrial fibrillation.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: All of the following are risk factors for the development of peripartum cardiomyopathy EXCEPT:
answer_text: Primiparous Primiparity is not a risk factor for peripartum cardiomyopathy; multiparity is more common.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are evaluating a 25-year-old patient diagnosed with “heart failure” who has been wheelchair-bound for many years and has severe scoliosis. His ECG shows tall R waves in V1 and V2 with deep Qs in V5 and V6, and echocardiogram reveals severe global left ventricular dysfunction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy The patient’s longstanding neuromuscular issues and characteristic ECG findings point to Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Which of the following is the most common inheritance pattern for familial cardiomyopathies?
options: Autosomal dominant driven by exon duplication
Autosomal dominant driven by missense mutations
Autosomal recessive driven by exon deletion
Autosomal recessive driven by exon duplication
answer_text: Autosomal dominant driven by missense mutations Familial cardiomyopathies are most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with missense mutations.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 45-year-old man with obesity presents with dyspnea, fatigue, and a nocturnal cough over several months. Echocardiography reveals a globally depressed left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% with a dilated left ventricle. Which of the following tests is a Level I recommendation for further workup?
answer_text: Thyroid-stimulating hormone level TSH level is a Level I recommended test in the workup of new cardiomyopathy.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 22-year-old college student presents with lethargy and fatigue 3 days after a viral upper respiratory illness. He is obtunded, tachycardic, hypotensive, with cool extremities and elevated jugular venous pressure. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 30% and mild mitral regurgitation. Endomyocardial biopsy reveals lymphocytic myocarditis. Which of the following statements regarding his prognosis and implications for therapy is true?
options: His chance of survival is <10% without cardiac transplantation. Emergent transplant listing is warranted.

His chance of survival is >50%, with many similar patients having a full recovery in left ventricular function over the ensuing weeks to months. Aggressive pharmacologic and mechanical hemodynamic support is warranted.
Immunosuppression with high-dose systemic steroids will increase his chance of survival.
The presence and titer of anti-heart antibodies can help provide prognostic information for this patient.
answer_text: His chance of survival is >50%, with many similar patients having a full recovery in left ventricular function over the ensuing weeks to months. Aggressive pharmacologic and mechanical hemodynamic support is warranted. Fulminant viral myocarditis can have a good prognosis with aggressive support, with many patients recovering LV function.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are evaluating a 42-year-old woman with a history of Hashimoto thyroiditis treated with radioactive iodine. She presents after passing out at home and reports several days of worsening lethargy and chest discomfort. Echocardiogram reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 15%, and endomyocardial biopsy shows diffuse granulomatous lesions with inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following statements is true regarding her diagnosis?
options: Most patients with this etiology of cardiomyopathy recover with supportive care.
Steroids are highly effective in treating this form of cardiomyopathy.
The course of this cardiomyopathy is dire, often with rapid deterioration requiring urgent transplantation.
While seen occasionally, ventricular tachyar rhythmias are rare in this disease.
None of the above is true.
answer_text: The course of this cardiomyopathy is dire, often with rapid deterioration requiring urgent transplantation. Giant cell myocarditis presents with a fulminant course and often requires urgent transplantation.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: All of the following are associated with an elevated risk for development of cardiomyopathy during anthracycline chemotherapy EXCEPT:
options: All of the above are associated with elevated risk
answer_text: All of the above are associated with elevated risk of cardiomyopathy due to anthracyclines. Each listed factor increases the risk of anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mr. Kia is a 32-year-old bass guitarist who presents with chest pain after a week of coryza, cough, fever, and muscle aches. His pain is constant, radiates to his left shoulder, and is exacerbated by lying flat and during deep breaths. Examination reveals a rasping extracardiac sound present in three components per heartbeat. His ECG is shown and troponin I levels are undetectable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Aspirin 81 mg daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily, and atorvastatin 80 mg daily
Aspirin 1 g every 8 hours with omeprazole 20 mg daily
Heparin, aspirin, clopidogrel, and immediate coronary angiography
Prednisone 40 mg daily for 2 weeks followed by a taper over 2 months
answer_text: Aspirin 1 g every 8 hours with omeprazole 20 mg daily This presentation is consistent with acute pericarditis, for which high-dose aspirin is indicated.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are caring for a 45-year-old man in the cardiac intensive care unit who was initially treated for acute coronary syndrome but is now diagnosed with acute pericarditis. Shortly after admission, he becomes hypotensive with elevated neck veins and cool extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Cardiac tamponade The clinical findings of hypotension, elevated JVP, and pulsus paradoxus are indicative of cardiac tamponade.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: In a patient with cardiac tamponade, which of the following is likely to be increased during inspiration compared to expiration?
answer_text: Tricuspid inflow velocity In cardiac tamponade, tricuspid inflow velocity increases during inspiration due to ventricular interdependence.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: All of the following ECG characteristics aid in differentiating acute pericarditis from acute myocardial infarction EXCEPT:
options: Absence of the development of Q waves
T-wave inversions after return of the ST segments to baseline
answer_text: ST elevation in V2 ST elevation in V2 is not a distinguishing feature between pericarditis and MI.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 35-year-old woman with a history of Hodgkin disease treated with chemotherapy and mediastinal irradiation presents with signs of constrictive pericarditis. Echocardiogram shows pericardial thickening and an abrupt cessation of ventricular filling in early diastole. What is the best approach for treatment?
answer_text: Pericardial resection Pericardial resection is the definitive treatment for constrictive pericarditis.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 45-year-old accountant with a 3-month history of fevers, symmetric arthralgias, and fatigue experiences sudden left hand weakness that resolves within 1 hour. Echocardiogram shows a solitary 2-cm mass in the left atrium arising from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis that appears pedunculated. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Cardiothoracic surgical removal of the mass
Repeat blood cultures and evaluation for HACEK organisms
Serologies for ANAs, anti-DNA, and anticardiolipin antibodies
Whole-body PET scan to evaluate for malignancy
answer_text: Cardiothoracic surgical removal of the mass The mass is most consistent with an atrial myxoma, which should be surgically removed.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Which of the following malignancies carries the highest relative risk of metastasis to the heart?
answer_text: Malignant melanoma Malignant melanoma has the highest relative risk of cardiac metastases.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: You are attending your 12-year-old son’s Little League baseball game when the catcher fouls the ball into his chest, leading to collapse and cardiac arrest. What intervention is most critical for his survival?
options: Emergent transfer for percutaneous coronary intervention
Emergent transfer for repair of an acute aortic dissection
Prompt cardiac surgery to repair an avulsed aortic valve
answer_text: Prompt defibrillation Immediate defibrillation is crucial in commotio cordis to restore normal rhythm.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 47-year-old woman with a BMI of 37 kg/ m2 and type 2 diabetes is informed about her future risk of heart attack and stroke. What is the most common cause of death in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus?
answer_text: Coronary artery disease Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death in adults with type 2 diabetes.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mr. Daniels, a 49-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse, presents with signs of high-output heart failure. After treatment, his symptoms and left ventricular size improve rapidly. Which of the following most likely caused this improvement?
answer_text: Thiamine Thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi) can cause high-output heart failure that improves rapidly with thiamine administration.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 65-year-old former factory worker with rheumatoid arthritis presents with fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, brittle hair, and lower extremity swelling. Her TSH is 79.4 mIU/L. In regard to her cardiovascular system, which measurement is NOT expected to decrease?
answer_text: QT interval In hypothyroidism, most parameters decrease except the QT interval, which is often prolonged.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: In the current model describing the steps of atherosclerosis initiation and evolution, which of the following constitutes the first step?
options: Arterial endothelial cells overexpress adhesion receptors for leukocytes.
Low-density lipoproteins accumulate within the arterial intima.
Macrophages and other leukocytes are recruited to the arterial intima.
Macrophages become lipid-laden foam cells via endocytosis.
answer_text: Low-density lipoproteins accumulate within the arterial intima. The initial step in atherosclerosis is the accumulation of LDL within the arterial intima.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Which of the following statements regarding the pathophysiologic consequences of an atheroma is true?
options: An atheroma resulting in total vascular occlusion invariably causes infarction.
An enlarging atheroma does not generally encroach on the arterial lumen until the plaque exceeds 40% of the internal elastic lamina.
Most atheromas will eventually produce symptoms in the patient.
Upon initial formation, the atheromatous plaque usually grows inward toward the vessel lumen.
Vessels affected by atherogenesis tend to contract and get smaller in diameter.
answer_text: An enlarging atheroma does not generally encroach on the arterial lumen until the plaque exceeds 40% of the internal elastic lamina. Compensatory enlargement prevents luminal narrowing until advanced stages.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Based on the 2013 cholesterol guidelines from the ACC/AHA, all of the following groups are a definite statin benefit group EXCEPT:
options: All individuals who have clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)
Individuals with an elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) regardless of LDL cholesterol level or ASCVD risk
Individuals with LDL cholesterol ≥190 mg/dL without a secondary cause
Individuals without established ASCVD or diabetes who are 40–75 years old with LDL 70–189 mg/dL and ASCVD risk ≥7.5%
Patients with diabetes without established cardiovascular disease who are 40–75 years old and have LDL 70–189 mg/dL
answer_text: Individuals with an elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) regardless of LDL cholesterol level or ASCVD risk Elevated hsCRP alone is not an indication for statin therapy per the guidelines.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 50-year-old man presents for his yearly check-up. He has a history of vascular disease, obesity, and an ASCVD risk of 6%. He is concerned about his low HDL cholesterol. What can definitively lower his cardiovascular risk the most regarding his HDL?
options: An agonist of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor B
An inhibitor of cholesteryl ester transfer protein
answer_text: Weight loss and physical activity Lifestyle modifications remain the most effective means to improve HDL levels and reduce cardiovascular risk.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: All of the following are major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand EXCEPT:
options: All of the above are major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand.
answer_text: Heart rhythm Heart rhythm is not a primary determinant of myocardial oxygen demand.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mr. Jackson is undergoing an exercise stress test. How does the normal heart respond to meet its higher oxygen demand?
options: Increased myocardial oxygen extraction during near-constant coronary blood flow
Increased oxygen extraction from the ventricular chambers
Relative expansion of the diastolic time period allowing increased coronary flow
Vasodilation of epicardial coronary arteries leading to decreased resistance and increased flow
Vasodilation of intramyocardial coronary vessels leading to increased coronary flow
answer_text: Vasodilation of intramyocardial coronary vessels leading to increased coronary flow The primary mechanism is vasodilation of intramyocardial vessels to increase blood flow.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: As Mr. Jackson continues his exercise stress test and experiences angina, which of the following biochemical changes in his ischemic myocardium would NOT be observed?
options: A shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism
Depletion of myocardial stores of high-energy phosphates
answer_text: An increase in intracellular pH During ischemia, intracellular pH decreases due to anaerobic metabolism.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Which of the following sites is an unusual anatomic location for anginal pain radiation?
answer_text: Trapezius muscle Anginal pain rarely radiates to the trapezius muscle.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Ms. Wilson is a 66-year-old postmenopausal postal employee who experiences chest pressure and dyspnea while walking her mail route. What term and CCS functional class best describe her angina?
answer_text: Stable angina – CCS class II Her predictable symptoms at a certain level of exertion classify her as CCS class II stable angina.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: A 50-year-old accountant with a history of cigarette use completes an exercise treadmill ECG stress test. He develops upsloping ST depressions in leads II, III, and aVF. His peak heart rate is 130 bpm, and his blood pressure increases from 120/80 to 155/95 mmHg. What is the appropriate interpretation of this stress test?
options: Negative stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
Negative stress test; nonspecific ST changes
Nondiagnostic stress test; normal blood pressure response
Positive stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
Positive stress test; normal blood pressure response
answer_text: Positive stress test; normal blood pressure response The ST changes and blood pressure response are consistent with a positive stress test.

heading: Other Harrison MCQ’s :
stem: Mr. Brian, a 57-year-old hockey team coach with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco abuse, presents with chest discomfort that initially occurred with vigorous exertion but now at rest. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
options: More information is required before making a diagnosis.
answer_text: Unstable angina The progression of symptoms from exertional to rest suggests unstable angina. E. Hepatopulmonary syndrome

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 70-year-old male with a history of mild chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, and CHF is admitted to your inpatient service with decreased urine output, weakness, and shortness of breath. He takes several medications but cannot remember their names. Labs are pending; his ECG is shown below. Based on the information available, what is the best initial step in management?
options: Administration of oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
answer_text: Administration of intravenous calcium gluconate Hyperkalemia ECG: peaked T, PR/QRS prolongation → sine wave risk; treat now with IV calcium, insulin ± glucose, ± bicarbonate; then remove K⁺; check glucose/renal status.

heading: Cardiology pre-test MCQ’s
stem: You are called by a surgical colleague to evaluate a 54-year-old woman with ECG abnormalities one day after a subtotal thyroidectomy for a toxic multinodular goiter. Her only medication is fentanyl for postoperative pain control. The patient denies any history of syncope, and has no family history of sudden cardiac death. Physical examination is unremarkable except for a clean postoperative incision at the base of the neck. Her ECG is reproduced below. What is the best next step in evaluation and management of this patient?
options: Stat noncontrast CT scan of the brain
Reassure the patient that her ECG is normal for a woman her age
answer_text: Measurement of serum ionized calcium Prolonged QT post-thyroid surgery → suspect hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism; check ionized calcium; magnesium for torsades only.

heading: Cardiology Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 56-year-old man attends his GP surgery for a routine blood pressure check and examination. He has no immediate concerns and his past medical history includes hypertension and asthma. He feels well in himself. On examination, he appears well and observa tions are normal except for a raised blood pressure of 155/87 mmHg. Upon auscultation of the heart, the GP notices an S4 heart sound. The GP then requests an ECG recording. Which part of the ECG does this sound coincide with?
answer_text: P wave S4 = atrial kick against stiff ventricle; aligns with ECG P wave; not QRS, ST, T, or U.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Asthma is characterized by all the following EXCEPT:
options: The patient can be completely free between the episodes.
The disease can start at any age.
In adults it is more common and more severe in men than women.
answer_text: In adults it is more common and more severe in men than women. Asthma in adulthood is more common in women.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: Dyspnea that associate with wheezing can be caused by the following EXCEPT:
answer_text: Pneumothorax. Pneumothorax usually does not present with wheezing.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: Asthma is characterized by all the following EXCEPT:
options: Rare before five years of age.
The disease can start at any age.
The patient can be completely free between the episodes.
answer_text: Rare before five years of age. Asthma can occur before five years of age, hence this statement is incorrect.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: which feature is incorrect regarding asthma
options: Patient can be complete free between episodes
In adults it is more severe in male than female
answer_text: In adults it is more severe in male than female Asthma in adults is typically more severe in females.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 53 year old woman with a 30-year history of asthma, now with worsening control despite maximal inhaled therapy, chronic productive cough of green sputum, breathlessness and wheeze is sent for a CT scan. What is shown on the image?
answer_text: Bronchiectasis CT demonstrates bilateral, proximal bronchiectatic changes consistent with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 37 year old asthmatic woman presents with difficult asthma control that worsens in April and May. Serum allergy testing reveals: Total IgE 1241 kU/L; Specific IgE to dog 24 kU/L; cat
answer_text: The patient’s asthma is triggered by seasonal pollens (specific IgE to oilseed rape and grass positive) Seasonal allergens are implicated given the positive specific IgE and seasonal pattern.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: 4 kU/L; tree pollen 0.2 kU/L; oilseed rape 34 kU/L; grass pollen 25 kU/L. What is the likely explanation for her presentation?
options: The patient has exercise-induced asthma (IgE testing irrelevant)
The patient has lied about exposure to animals (specific IgE to cats and dogs elevated)
The patient is non-adherent with medication (total IgE remains high)
The patient is sensitised to montelukast (IgE results represent cross-reactivity)
The patient’s asthma is triggered by seasonal pollens (specific IgE to oilseed rape and grass positive)
answer_text: Low dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) Asthma with reversible obstruction after SABA failure → start low-dose ICS; COPD less likely given minimal pack-years; LABA/LAMA, LABA alone, omalizumab, and oral steroids are not first-line maintenance.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 45 year old smoker with cough, wheeze and productive sputum undergoes pulmonary function testing. Spirometry pre-bronchodilator: FEV1 2.6 L, FVC 4.4 L, FEV1/FVC 0.59. Post-bronchodilator: FEV1 3.2 L, FVC 4.4 L, FEV1/FVC 0.73. What does the testing reveal?
options: A mixture of obstruction and restriction
answer_text: A reversible obstructive defect The marked reversibility confirms an asthma diagnosis despite a smoking history.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 27 year old woman with severe atopic asthma, 26 weeks pregnant, presents with worsening nocturnal cough and breathlessness. PEFR is 240 L/min (best 450 L/min). Her medications include high-dose ICS/LABA, oral montelukast, and as-needed SABA. What should be the next step in her management?
answer_text: Oral prednisolone The patient is experiencing a significant asthma exacerbation; systemic steroids are indicated.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 48 year old asthmatic with increased exacerbations, nocturnal cough, and eosinophilia is on Flixotide/salmeterol and salbutamol as required. He has started a 5-day course of prednisolone. In line with BTS guidelines, what should be added to step-up therapy?
answer_text: Add montelukast Montelukast is recommended as an add-on therapy for difficult-to-control asthma.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 43 year old woman presents with cough, shortness of breath and wheeze. A smoker working in a bakery, she experiences deterioration after 3 weeks back at work. To assess for occupational asthma, which test is most helpful?
answer_text: Peak expiratory flow rate diary A detailed PEFR diary over several weeks is key for diagnosing occupational asthma.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Which of the following is the major risk factor for asthma?
answer_text: Atopy Atopy is the strongest risk factor for asthma development.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 24-year-old woman with eczema and allergic rhinitis has asthma. Which statement regarding her disease is true?
options: Confirmation of the diagnosis requires methacholine challenge testing.
Mortality due to the disease has been increasing over the past decade.
The most common risk factor in individuals with the disorder is genetic predisposition.
The prevalence of the disorder has not changed in the past several decades.
The severity of the disease does not vary significantly within a given patient with the disease.
answer_text: The severity of the disease does not vary significantly within a given patient with the disease Individuals with mild disease generally stay mild, and severe disease remains severe over time.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 38-year-old woman dies of status asthmaticus. All of the following pathologic findings are likely EXCEPT:
options: Infiltration of the airway mucosa with eosinophils and activated T lymphocytes
Infiltration of the alveolar spaces with eosinophils and neutrophils
Occlusion of the airway lumen by mucous plugs
Thickening and edema of the airway wall
Thickening of the basement membrane of the airways with subepithelial collagen deposition
answer_text: Infiltration of the alveolar spaces with eosinophils and neutrophils Asthma is primarily an airway (bronchial) disease; alveolar spaces are usually spared.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Which of the following patients is appropriately diagnosed with asthma?
options: A 24-year-old with cough and wheeze 6 weeks after a viral infection
A 26-year-old with cold-exercise cough and occasional wheeze
A 34-year-old with chronic cough and FEV1 increasing from 1.68 L to 1.98 L (18%) after albuterol
A 44-year-old with workplace mouse allergen exposure only at week’s end
A 60-year-old heavy smoker with airway hyperreactivity and chronic dyspnea
answer_text: A 34-year-old with chronic cough and an 18% improvement in FEV1 after albuterol Diagnosis requires reversible airflow obstruction (≥12% and 200 mL improvement in FEV1).

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 24-year-old woman with mild intermittent asthma uses albuterol 4-7 times/week. What do you advise?
options: Add inhaled salmeterol twice a day
Think of a new name for the goldfish
answer_text: Add inhaled beclomethasone Using a rescue inhaler more than twice per week indicates the need for a low-dose inhaled steroid.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with mild persistent asthma is on inhaled corticosteroids and albuterol prn. Which statement is correct?
options: She should continue her current therapy and follow symptoms.
She should switch to inhaled tiotropium as needed.
She should switch from inhaled beclomethasone to salmeterol.
There is >70% chance her asthma will lessen in pregnancy.
There is >70% chance her asthma will worsen in pregnancy.
answer_text: She should continue her current therapy and follow symptoms. Inhaled steroids and short-acting B-agonists are safe and effective in pregnancy.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 34-year-old man with severe persistent asthma, brown mucous plugs, and high eosinophils. Which test is indicated next?
answer_text: Serum immunoglobulin (Ig) E level Evaluation for ABPA requires checking total serum IgE and Aspergillus sensitivity.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A known asthmatic presents to the GP complaining of gradually worsening of her symptoms. She is already taking a regular B2 agonist inhaler. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
answer_text: Low-dose inhaled steroid The next step in the management plan is to add on a low- dose inhaled steroid. If this is inadequate, then a long-acting B2 agonist is added. Further escalation may involve high-dose inhaled steroids or additional therapies.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A woman is admitted to hospital with acute severe asthma. Her respiratory rate is greater than 25 breaths/min and peak flow is less than 50% of her predicted value. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
answer_text: Nebulized salbutamol Nebulized salbutamol or terbutaline in addition to oral steroids are the initial treatment of acute severe asthma. Intravenous magnesium is added in life-threatening exacerbation.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 30-year-old woman known to have asthma presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of worsening breathlessness and chest tightness despite regular salbutamol inhalers. She has been suffering from an upper respiratory tract infection for the past few days. Which of the following findings on clinical examination would be an ominous sign for an impending respiratory failure in this patient?
answer_text: Silent chest A silent chest (absence of wheezing) is an ominous sign indicating severe airway obstruction and impending respiratory failure in asthma.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 36-year-old woman with a history of moderate persistent asthma presents to the emergency department with progressive worsening of SOB, wheezing and cough over 3 days. She has been compliant with her maintenance asthma regimen, which consists of an inhaled corticosteroid and a leukotriene receptor antagonist for maintenance therapy and salbutamol as rescue therapy. Which one of the following is most consistent with a diagnosis of asthma?
options: Reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FEV1 and normal FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FEV1 and increased FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FVC1 and normal FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FVC1 and increased FEV1:FVC ratio
answer_text: Reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1:FVC ratio Asthma is typically associated with an obstructive impairment that is reversible with bronchodilators; a reduced FEV1 and FEV1:FVC ratio indicates airflow obstruction.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 28-year-old male with a long history of severe asthma presents to the emergency room with shortness of breath. He has previously required admission to the hospital and was once intubated for asthma. Which of the following findings on physical examination would predict a benign course?
answer_text: Pulsus paradoxus of 5 mm Hg Severe asthma red flags: silent chest, hypercapnia, thoracoabdominal paradox, AMS; these warrant ventilatory support; pulsus paradoxus 5 mmHg is normal.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 30-year-old athlete presents to your office complaining of intermittent wheezing. This wheezing begins shortly after running. The patient admits to smoking 1-2 packs of cigarettes per day for 5 years. What finding would be consistent with asthma?
options: Low oxygen saturation on finger oximetry
Dyspnea on assuming a supine position
answer_text: Improvement in FEV1 after bronchodilator Exercise-induced asthma → reversible obstruction; CXR hyperinflation possible; hypoxia unusu al; restrictive pattern would lower FVC.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 28-year-old builder attends the respiratory clinic for review. He reports a 6-month history of progressive dyspnoea on exertion associated with coughing. He has been started on a salbutamol inhaler by his general practitioner which he is now using several times a day. He has been smoking since the age of 18 years and he has a 10 pack-year history. Additionally, he reports occupational exposure to asbestos. Further investigation with spirometry testing reports an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.68. FEV1 pre-bronchodilator therapy is 3.0L. FEV1 post-bronchodilator therapy is 3.4L. What is the most appropriate intervention for this patient?
options: Long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) and long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) inhaler
answer_text: Radiographic signs correlate with the severity of airflow limitation. Radiographic signs do not reliably correlate with the severity of airflow limitation in COPD.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 45-year-old woman who is a known asthmatic comes for review. In the past two years she has had around six exacerbations of asthma requiring oral steroids. Her current medication includes salbutamol 2 puffs prn and beclometasone 200 mcg 1 puff bd. You note from the records that her BMI is 31 kg/m^2, she is a non-smoker and has a good inhaler technique. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Increase beclometasone to 200 mcg 2 puffs bd
answer_text: Add oral montelukast Asthma uncontrolled on SABA+low-dose ICS → add LTRA before LABA per NICE 2017.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with an exacerbation of asthma. On arrival her peak flow is 30% of predicted, respiratory rate is 36/min and oxygen saturations are 98% on 100% high-flow oxygen. She is given back-to-back nebulisers, intravenous hydrocortisone and started on a magnesium infusion. Which one of the following would be the strongest indicator of a need for intubation and ventilation?
options: Oxygen saturations of 95% on 100% high- flow oxygen
answer_text: pH 7.33 pH <7.35 in acute asthma indicates rising CO2 and fatigue → ominous; serial peak flows not useful in life-threatening attacks.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 37-years-old known asthmatic, presents to the emergency department with the complaint of severe shortness of breath. On examination, her respiratory rate is around 35/min. She is unable to complete a full sentence. On auscultation, she has a global wheeze. Her initial arterial blood gas shows: pH 7.46 mmol/L (7.35-7.45); pCO2 3.9 kPa (4.0-6.0); pO2 11.2 kPa (10.0-
answer_text: Non-invasive ventilation Normal PaCO2 in acute severe asthma implies impending respiratory failure → treat as life-threatening.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 0); HCO3 22 mmol/L (22-26). She is given oral prednisolone, salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisation back to back. An hour later, chest auscultation reveals a silent chest. A repeat arterial blood gas shows: pH 7.35 mmol/L (7.35-
answer_text: Roflumilast 500 μg daily Roflumilast, a PDE4 inhibitor, reduces exacerbation frequency in COPD.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 45); pCO2 5.7 kPa (4.0-6.0); pO2 11.0 kPa (10.0-13.0); HCO3 24 mmol/L (22-26). Chest X-ray was unremarkable. Which of the following is the best step in the management of this patient?
answer_text: A Asthma Obstructive spirometry with raised volumes and normal TLCO in a never-smoker → asthma more likely than COPD.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of breathlessness on exertion, which has been worsening for one year. This is accompanied by wheeze which worsens with exercise, and during the course of the summer when she also has severe hayfever. She has never smoked. The chest X-ray shows mild hyperinflation but is otherwise unremarkable. Her lung function test results are shown below: | Test | Result | Predicted | | FEV1 (I) | 1.1 | 1.7–3.0 | | FVC (I) | 2.7 | 2.0–3.5 | | FRC (I) | 4.2 | 1.7–3.4 | | TLC (I) | 6.5 | 3.6–5.6 | | Tico (mmol/min per kPa) | 5.86 | 5.7–9.5 | | Kco (mmol/min per kPa per I) | 1.63 | 1.66 | What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Smoking cessation and pulmonary rehabilitation Smoking cessation and pulmonary rehabilitation are proven to improve outcomes and quality of life in COPD.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted with dyspnoea. Pulmonary function tests show a PEFR of 300 L/min and FEV1/FVC ratio reduced. He is otherwise healthy, smokes five cigarettes per day and keeps a pet cat. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: A Asthma PEFR reflects large-airway obstruction → useful for asthma diagnosis and monitoring.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: Common stage of disease is one sees cough and sputum as an important feature in ? (filled with standard approach)
answer_text: COPD (chronic bronchitis) Chronic bronchitis is clinically characterized by chronic cough and sputum production for at least 3 months in two successive years.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Which of these actions increase survival in COPD?
options: Stop smoking and long term 02 therapy.
Stop smoking and regular combined LABA/ICS inhalation
Stop smoking and intermittent short courses of steroids
answer_text: Stop smoking and long term 02 therapy. Long term oxygen therapy along with smoking cessation improves survival in COPD.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: The following are true in COPD EXCEPT:
options: Radiographic signs correlate with the severity of airflow limitation.
Measurement of lung volumes provides an assessment of hyperinflation.
In severe COPD, and with large bullae, body plethysmography is preferred to estim lung volumes.
A low peak flow is consistent with COPD but is non-specific.
answer_text: Haemophilus influenzae AECOPD pathogens: H. influenzae most common; also S. pneumoniae and M. catarrhalis.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: Regarding treatment of acute exacerbation of COPD, the following are true EXCEPT:
options: In most cases, simple regimens of antibiotics are advised, such as amoxicillin or a macrolide.
Oral prednisolone reduces symptoms, but cannot improve lung function,
Mechanical ventilation may be considered in those with a reversible cause for deterioration (e.g.pneumonia), or if there is no prior history of respiratory failure.
Nebulized short-acting B2-agonists, combined with an anticholinergic agent can be administered.
answer_text: In most cases, simple regimens of antibiotics are advised, such as amoxicillin or a macrolide. Antibiotics are not recommended in COPD exacerbation unless there is an associated infection.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 66-year-old heavy smoker presents with chronic productive cough, progressive dyspnea, pursed-lip breathing, and a barrel chest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) The history and physical findings (smoking history, barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing) are typical for COPD.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which pulmonary function test finding is most consistent with COPD?
options: Increased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
Isolated reduced FVC with normal FEV1
answer_text: Reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (obstructive pattern) COPD is characterized by an obstructive pattern with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which two management strategies have been shown to improve the prognosis in COPD?
options: Surgical lung volume reduction and beta-blockers
answer_text: B Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease ABG consistent with severe COPD exacerbation (acute on chronic).

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 55 year old man has smoked 30 cigarettes per day since he was 15 years old. He is a taxi driver. He finds he is increasingly breathless on exertion. Oxygen saturations are 98% on room air. Examination reveals tracheal tug, reduced cricosternal distance and a barrel chest. He has reduced cardiac dullness and symmetrically reduced air entry. CXR reveals hyperinflation and spirometry reveals moderate airways obstruction. The patient walks 300 m on an incremental walk test before becoming breathless; oxygen saturations are maintained. What pathological change best explains why he is breathless on exertion?
answer_text: Loss of elastic recoil Loss of elastin fibers in COPD cause dynamic hyperinflation on exertion.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 67 year old ex-smoker woman with progressive exertional breathlessness, normal spirometry but CT showing emphysema is evaluated. What is the most likely cause of her breathlessness?
answer_text: COPD Despite normal spirometry, emphysema can cause significant dyspnoea.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 65 year old man with known COPD and mild obstruction presents with increasing exertional breathlessness despite LAMA and SABA. He does not desaturate on walk test. What is a reasonable addition to escalate therapy?
answer_text: LAMA/LABA combination inhaler A dual bronchodilator regimen can improve symptoms in COPD patients with exertional dyspnoea.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: All of the following are typically characterized as an obstructive lung disease EXCEPT:
answer_text: Asbestosis Asbestosis is a fibrotic, restrictive lung disease, not an obstructive disorder.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Which of the following pulmonary function test results is consistent with Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
options: Increased TLC, decreased vital capacity, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio
Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/ FVC ratio, decreased MIP
Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
answer_text: Increased TLC, decreased vital capacity, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio Obstructive pattern with air trapping includes increased TLC and a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 69-year-old man with COPD has frequent exacerbations. Which treatment decreases exacerbation frequency?
answer_text: “Signet ring” sign. The signet ring sign is highly characteristic of bronchiectasis.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: All of the following are risk factors for COPD EXCEPT:
options: Use of biomass fuels in poorly ventilated areas
answer_text: Recurrent respiratory infections Recurrent respiratory infections are not a proven risk factor for COPD compared to the others.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 65-year-old woman is suspected of COPD. What are the expected PFT findings?
options: Increased FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased TLC, decreased DLCO
Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, increased TLC, increased RV, decreased DLCO
Normal FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased TLC, normal DLCO
Normal lung volumes, normal DLCO, normal FEV1/FVC ratio
Increased FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased DLCO, decreased TLC
answer_text: Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, increased TLC, increased RV, decreased DLCO COPD is characterized by airflow obstruction with hyperinflation and air trapping.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 70-year-old man with moderate COPD on albuterol only. Next best step in management?
options: Trial of oral glucocorticoids for 4 weeks
Perform exercise/nocturnal oximetry and start oxygen if needed
answer_text: Initiate inhaled tiotropium 18 μg daily Long-acting anticholinergics (tiotropium) are recommended in moderate COPD with symptoms.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 56-year-old with severe COPD exacerbation in respiratory failure. Which therapy shows greatest reduction in mortality?
answer_text: Use of noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation NIPPV reduces mortality and intubation rates in COPD exacerbations with hypercapnia.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 63-year-old with COPD has progressive dyspnea, JVP elevation, pedal edema, Hct 49%. Which therapy prolongs survival?
answer_text: Oxygen Long-term oxygen therapy improves survival in COPD patients with resting hypoxemia.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 65-year-old lifelong smoker presents with a wheeze, breathlessness and cough with sputum production. On examination you note reduced chest expansion bilaterally. He has lived in central London since the age of 10. Which of the following is most likely to be causing his symptoms?
answer_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) Tobacco smoking is the most common cause of COPD. Other factors, such as air pollution and genetics, play a smaller role. Long-term exposure to these irritants causes an inflammatory response in the lungs, which results in the breakdown of lung tissue and narrowing of airways. Diagnosis is based on lung function tests.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 60-year-old man with severe COPD is admitted with an acute exacerbation. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
answer_text: Arterial blood gas When the patient arrives in hospital, arterial blood gases should be measured and the inspired oxygen concentration noted in all patients with an exacerbation of COPD, so that controlled oxygen therapy can be tailored. These measurements should be repeated regularly, according to the response to treatment.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted under your care with increasing breathlessness, wheeze and sputum production. She has COPD. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
answer_text: 24% oxygen Individuals with COPD typically depend on a degree of hypoxia to maintain respiratory drive, so it is best to commence low oxygen concentrations via a Venturi mask. The oxygen saturation and arterial blood gas results should be regularly assessed to determine correct oxygen therapy.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A child is admitted with a cough and sputum production, which is thick, foul smelling and green in colour. The mother notes episodes of him coughing up blood. On examination he has notable finger clubbing with coarse crackles in both lung bases on auscultation. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
answer_text: Cystic fibrosis A typical presentation of cystic fibrosis. The presence of clubbing suggests a chronic respiratory disease process as opposed to acute infections or inhaled foreign body. It is an autosomal recessive disorder which affects the lungs, pancreas, liver, kidneys and gastrointestinal tract.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: You suspect bronchiectasis in a young patient. Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
answer_text: High-resolution CT High-resolution CT of the chest is the most frequently used imaging test to establish the diagnosis of bronchiectasis. Other investigations may also need to be performed to determine the underlying cause.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A child recently diagnosed with cystic fibrosis is admitted following an exacerbation of his symptoms. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
answer_text: Antibiotics Exacerbations of pulmonary symptoms in patients with cystic fibrosis must be recognized early and treated vigorously to maintain pulmonary function and relieve symptoms. Antibiotic treatment is prescribed based on new symptoms or worsening of existing symptoms.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A teenager presents to the GP with symptoms indicative of cystic fibrosis. A sweat test is performed. Which of the following is diagnostic?
options: A chloride value between 40 and 60 mmol/L
A chloride value less than 40 mmol/L
A sodium value of less than 60 mmol/L
A sodium value between 40 and 60 mmol/L
answer_text: A sodium value above 60 mmol/L Because of defective chloride channels (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR)), the concentration of chloride in sweat is elevated in patients with cystic fibrosis. The sweat test measures the amount of chloride excreted in sweat. A chloride level of greater than or equal to 60 mmol/L means that cystic fibrosis is likely to be diagnosed.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old male has had a chronic cough with clear sputum production for over 5 years. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes per day for 20 years and continues to do so. X-ray of the chest shows hyperinflation without infiltrates. Arterial blood gases show a pH of 7.38, PCO2 of 40 mm Hg, and PO2 of 65 mm Hg. Spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC of 45% without bronchodilator response. Which of the following is the most important treatment modality for this patient?
answer_text: Smoking cessation program Chronic bronchitis (smoker) → smoking cessation key; bronchodilators for symptoms; LTOT if PaO₂ ≤55 mmHg; antibiotics/steroids only for exacerbations; theophylline last-line.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: You are reviewing a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) who remains breathless despite using a salbutamol inhaler as required. Their FEV1 is 60%. There is no history of asthma, eosinophilia or FEV1 variation. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) + inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) in a combination inhaler or long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA)
Long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA) or LABA + inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) in a combination inhaler
Long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA) or regular combined short-acting beta2-agonist + muscarinic antagonist (e.g. Combivent)
Combined long acting beta agonist and long acting muscarinic antagonist (LABA/LAMA)
answer_text: Combined long acting beta agonist and long acting muscarinic antagonist (LABA/LAMA) COPD still breathless on SABA/SAMA without steroid-responsive features → step to LABA+LAMA; stop SAMA if used and keep SABA PRN.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 65-year-old man attends the emergency department with a cough productive of green sputum. He has recently been diagnosed with COPD and is an active smoker. On examination, he is saturating at 94% on room air and is wheezy bilaterally. A chest X-ray does not reveal any consolidation. Blood tests: CRP 26 mg/L; Na+ 133 mmol/L; K+ 3.6 mmol/L; Bicarbonate 34 mmol/L; Urea 6 mmol/L; Creatinine 100 μmol/L. What is the most likely underlying organism causing this clinical picture?
answer_text: Age between 20–25 years Young age alone is not a recognized major risk factor, while the others are established risk factors.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 58-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with a 1-week history of increased breathlessness and reduced exercise tolerance. His COPD is usually managed with a salbutamol inhaler as required and a salmeterol inhaler. He has a chronic cough productive of clear sputum but denies any recent change in this. He appears breathless and his respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute, but there is no use of accessory muscles at rest. All other clinical observations were normal. On auscultation of his chest you note expiratory wheeze throughout but good air entry and no other added sounds. Other than encouraging the use of his salbutamol inhaler, what is the most appropriate management?
options: Give a course of oral prednisolone for 5 days
Give a course of oral prednisolone for 7 days and oral amoxicillin for 5 days
Give a course of oral prednisolone for 7 days and oral clarithromycin for 5 days
Give a course of oral prednisolone for 5 days and oral amoxicillin for 5 days
Give a course of oral prednisolone for 7 days and oral furosemide for 7 days
answer_text: Give a course of oral prednisolone for 5 days AECOPD without purulent sputum or pneumonia signs → no antibiotics; increase bronchodilators; give 7–14 days oral prednisolone if significantly breathless; furosemide only if fluid overload.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 62-year-old woman with recently diagnosed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents for review. Her FEV1 is 65% of the predicted value. She has managed to give up smoking and was prescribed a salbutamol inhaler to use as required. Despite this, she is still symptomatic and complains of wheeze and shortness of breath. There is no history of asthma, eosinophilia or FEV1 variation. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Add a combined long-acting beta2-agonist and long-acting muscarinic antagonist inhaler
Refer for consideration of long-term oxygen therapy
Add a combination long-acting beta2-agonist and corticosteroid inhaler
answer_text: Add a combined long-acting beta2-agonist and long-acting muscarinic antagonist inhaler COPD persistent symptoms on SABA/SAMA without steroid-responsive features → escalate to LABA+LAMA per NICE 2018.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 69-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents to the Emergency Department with dyspnoea. Three days ago he was started on amoxicillin and prednisolone by his GP. Since arriving in the department he has been given back-to-back nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium bromide. The oxygen concentration has been titrated to 28% to achieve a saturation of 88-92%. Due to his poor response to treatment an aminophylline infusion is started. Thirty minutes later, his arterial blood gases show the following (taken on 28% oxygen): pH 7.30; pCO2 7.6 kPa; pO2
answer_text: Non-invasive ventilation IV magnesium sulfate benefits acute severe asthma, not COPD; extra IV hydrocortisone adds little after several days of oral prednisolone.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 1 kPa. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
answer_text: C Hypercapnia without profound hypoxia Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure without contraindications → start NIV.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 75-year-old man with a body mass index (BMI) of 31 kg/m2 presents with a history of worsening breathlessness and cough of about 1 week’s duration. He is normally short of breath and has had to give up walking to the shops, which are only 300 m away. He has a chronic cough that is worse in the morning. He is a smoker and smoked 20 cigarettes per day until he became ill this time. His arterial blood gases in room air are as follows: pH 7.24, Pao2 6.2 kPa, Paco2 9.8 kPa, bicarbonate 33 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
answer_text: High-resolution CT scan of the chest. HRCT is the gold standard for diagnosing bronchiectasis.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 17-You review a 56-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, who is suffering an acute exacerbation. Which of the following features would suggest suitability for non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP?
answer_text: Post-infectious damage following severe measles. A history of severe measles predisposes to bronchiectasis.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 44-You review a 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), who asks about the provision of oxygen therapy at home. In which of the following settings have randomised controlled trials shown that long- term oxygen therapy (LTOT) reduces mortality?
options: Cor pulmonate caused by chronic airflow obstruction
answer_text: B Cor pulmonate caused by chronic airflow obstruction Only LTOT reduces mortality in hypoxemic COPD; oxygen relieves dyspnea but no survival benefit in listed non-COPD conditions.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 49-A 66-year-old retired boilermaker presents to the Respiratory Clinic. Spirometry shows post-salbutamol FEV₁ 1.81 l, post-salbutamol FVC 2.7 l; transfer factor 55%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: C Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease Obstruction with reduced TLCO → emphysematous COPD.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: Stress can complicate community-acquired pneumonia from the following:
answer_text: Staphylococcus pneumonia Staphylococcal pneumonia is known to be a severe form that can be complicated by stress and post-viral states.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: The reason why hypercapnia is not present in early pneumonia is that alveolar ventilation is still adequate (added for completion).
options: Because oxygen therapy is always provided
Because the body temperature is not high
Because pneumonia does not affect gas exchange
answer_text: Because alveolar ventilation remains compensated In early pneumonia, increased respiratory drive prevents CO2 retention, thus hypercapnia does not typically occur.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following is not patient-related risk factor for tuberculosis?
options: Close contacts with smear-positive pulmonary TB
answer_text: Bronchiolitis obliterans Obstructive spirometry in RA → bronchiolitis obliterans likely; RA lungs also: fibrosis, effusion, nodules, drug toxicity.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A patient with history of lobar pneumonia 4 weeks ago presented with high-grade fever, chills, rigors, left-sided chest pain, cough, sputum, and dyspnea. Which complication is the most probable?
answer_text: Empyema Persistence of fever and pleuritic chest pain after pneumonia suggests a purulent pleural effusion (empyema).

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Tuberculous granuloma contain the following cells EXCEPT:
answer_text: Neutrophils. Neutrophils are not typically found in a tuberculous granuloma.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with a six-month history of worsening breathlessness and a daily productive cough yielding approximately one cup of sputum. He has a past history of severe measles in childhood and a recent smoking history (10 cigarettes/day for 2 years). On examination, he appears ill with mild dyspnea, early clubbing, and bilateral coarse crepitations over the lower lung zones, while his cardiac examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Bronchiectasis. The clinical picture is most consistent with bronchiectasis.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: In the patient described above, what is the best diagnostic modality to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
options: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
answer_text: A Aspiration Aspiration pneumonia: poor dentition + aspiration risk; insidious course; dependent lobe infiltrates; putrid sputum; weight loss/ anaemia common.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Which of the following underlying causes is most likely responsible for this patient’s condition?
answer_text: D Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia Staphylococcal pneumonia post-viral → patchy consolidation → abscess, pneumo/empyema; severe criteria noted; treat IV cefuroxime + clarithromycin + add flucloxacillin for S. aureus.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Aside from post-measles lung damage, which of the following is another recognized underlying cause of bronchiectasis in young patients?
answer_text: Cystic fibrosis. Cystic fibrosis is a common cause of bronchiectasis in young patients.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Which of the following complications is commonly associated with bronchiectasis?
answer_text: Hemoptysis. Hemoptysis occurs due to chronic inflammation of the bronchial vessels.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Another frequent complication of bronchiectasis is:
options: Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart failure
Acute respiratory distress syndrome secondary to trauma
answer_text: Recurrent respiratory infections. Abnormal bronchial architecture predisposes to recurrent infections.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: A further long-term complication that may develop in patients with bronchiectasis is:
answer_text: Cor pulmonale. Chronic lung disease can lead to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Which HRCT finding is most specific for the diagnosis of bronchiectasis?
answer_text: A Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis = chronic sequela of pneumonia; others listed are acute complications.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: In a young patient with a history of severe measles, which mechanism is most likely involved in the development of bronchiectasis?
answer_text: Post-infectious airway damage. Severe measles can damage bronchial walls leading to bronchiectasis.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: The daily production of a large volume of sputum in bronchiectasis is primarily due to:
options: Chronic infection and inflammation of the bronchial walls
Excess mucus production secondary to heart failure
answer_text: Chronic infection and inflammation of the bronchial walls. Repeated infections and inflammation lead to excessive mucus production.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: A 43 years old female presented with chest pain, hemoptysis and epistaxis, the chest X-ray show multiple nodular lesions with shadowing . the ANCA is positive, the possible diagnosis is
answer_text: Wegener’s granulomatosis

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: There are important things to control and prevention of tuberculosis except one
answer_text: Direct observation therapy Direct observation therapy is a treatment measure, not a primary prevention method.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: A 22-year-old man presents with fever, night sweats, weight loss and cough productive of cupful of blood. Ziehl-Neelsen stain is positive for acid-fast bacilli
answer_text: Tuberculosis Clinical presentation and positive stain confirm tuberculosis.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: Regarding the causes of drug resistant TB, all of the following are correct EXCEPT:
options: Poor quality drugs and shortage of drugs
answer_text: Hepatic failure Hepatic failure is not a cause of drug resistant TB.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: patient related factors for TB are the follow ing except
options: Contact with positive smear TB patients
CXR evidence of self healed TB
answer_text: Age 30-40 Age 30-40 is not considered a patient-related risk factor for TB.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: Regarding anti TB drugs side effects:
options: Asymptomatic increases in transaminases are common but serious liver damage is rare.
answer_text: Asymptomatic increases in transaminases are common but serious liver damage is rare. Other statements are incorrect as INH does not cause optic neuritis, Ethambutol causes optic neuritis, and Streptomycin is contraindicated in pregnancy.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: Which of following is least useful in assessing the prognosis of community acquired pneumonia?
options: Age of patient is above 75 years
answer_text: C-Reactive protein is very high CRP is not part of the CURB-65 prognostic score.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: The important diagnosis for tuberculosis is
answer_text: Sputum culture Sputum culture is the definitive diagnostic test for TB.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: A 34-year-old woman originally complaining of nasal obstruction develops cough, haemoptysis and pleuritic chest pain. Her chest x-ray shows multiple nodular masses.
answer_text: Wegener’s granulomatosis Nasal obstruction with lung nodules and hemoptysis is typical of Wegener’s granulomatosis.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: The following may be features of primary tuberculosis EXCEPT:
answer_text: Erythema marginatum. Erythema marginatum is not a feature of primary tuberculosis.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: Which one of the following suggest active pulmonary TB:
answer_text: Cavitation on chest X-ray. Cavitation on chest X-ray is indicative of active pulmonary TB.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with high continuous fever, rigors, shortness of breath, and a productive cough with rusty-colored sputum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Lobar pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae
answer_text: Lobar pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae The classic presentation of high fever with rusty sputum is most consistent with lobar pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: If sputum is sent for Gram stain in this patient, which of the following is the expected finding?
answer_text: Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci Streptococcus pneumoniae appears as gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci on Gram stain.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: What is the typical chest X-ray finding in a patient with lobar pneumonia?
answer_text: Lobar consolidation Lobar pneumonia is characterized by consolidation confined to one lobe of the lung.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 45 year old man returns from Spain with a week of fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, cough, and confusion. His CXR is shown. What abnormality is seen on his CXR?
answer_text: Extensive left-sided consolidation The CXR demonstrates dense consolidation of the left lung consistent with pneumonia.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: For the same patient described in Question
answer_text: 2 The patient scores 2 on CURB-65 based on confusion and elevated urea.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: 17, what is his CURB-65 score?
answer_text: B Corticosteroids EAA management: eliminate antigen exposure; use corticosteroids for progressive disease.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: For the same patient described in Question
answer_text: Legionella pneumophila The clinical picture with delirium, hyponatraemia and deranged LFTs is most consistent with Legionella pneumonia.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: 17, which of the following is the causative organism likely to be?
answer_text: Cirrhosis Cirrhosis typically causes transudative effusions, not exudative.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 38 year old man presents with cough productive of blood-streaked sputum, fever, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. He also has cold sores. His CXR is shown. What does his CXR show?
answer_text: Left-sided basal consolidation The CXR demonstrates basal consolidation typical of lobar pneumonia.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 49 year old patient returns from Portugal with fever, dry cough, breathlessness and con fusion. His wife reports an episode of unrecognition. In Spain he stayed in a hotel and was exposed to a nephew diagnosed with influenza. CXR shows bilateral infiltrates. What is the most useful diagnostic test?
options: Differential cell count in bronchial lavage
Nucleic acid amplification testing for respiratory pathogens
Paired serology for mycoplasma and legionella
answer_text: Nucleic acid amplification testing for respiratory pathogens Rapid molecular testing will quickly differentiate pathogens in this pneumonia presentation.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 53 year old man with a 3-month history of non-productive cough, normal spirometry and on omeprazole for reflux presents for evaluation. Which statement is true?
options: A trial of an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) is warranted
He should see an ENT surgeon
His cough has become a habit and he must get used to it
His reflux medication should be increased
answer_text: A CXR should be performed A chest X-ray is essential to exclude parenchymal lung disease.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A patient in the asthma clinic presents with deteriorating control characterized by a productive cough of green sputum and right-sided pleuritic chest pain for 48 hours. CXR is shown. What is the likely cause of the deterioration?
answer_text: Fungal infection The clinical picture and radiographic findings suggest allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 32 year old man presents with a 5-day history of left-sided pleuritic chest pain, fever and cough productive of rusty sputum. He also has nasolabial cold sores. Which organism is likely responsible?
answer_text: Streptococcus pneumoniae The presentation is most consistent with lobar pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 53 year old businessman returns from the Middle East with fever, chills, cough and shortness of breath. His CXR shows diffuse infiltrates. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Burkholderia pseudomallei needs to be covered
He should be isolated and tested for CPE
He should be isolated and tested for MERS
He should be isolated and tested for SARS
Local antibiotic protocol for CAP should be followed
answer_text: He should be isolated and tested for MERS Travel history and clinical features warrant MERS evaluation.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 73 year old man in hospital for 3 days post-hip surgery becomes acutely confused with a new right-sided infiltrate on CXR. What is the appropriate approach?
answer_text: Local antibiotic policy for HAP The scenario is most consistent with hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), warranting appropriate antibiotic therapy.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 72 year old man initially improving from COPD exacerbation spikes a fever with green, blood-streaked sputum and a dense left-sided consolidation on CXR. Late-onset HAP is most often attributable to which microorganism?
answer_text: Acinetobacter Late-onset HAP is commonly caused by Gram-negative bacteria such as Acinetobacter.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: The mortality from hospital-acquired pneumonia is approximately which of the following?
answer_text: 30% HAP carries a mortality rate of around 30%.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 34 year old woman who is an intravenous drug-user presents with high fever, pleuritic chest pain, cough productive of foul sputum and a fluctuant groin swelling. CXR shows multiple nodules and CT shows basal nodules, some cavitating. What is the likely explanation?
answer_text: Infective endocarditis Septic emboli from right-sided endocarditis in an IV drug-user cause multifocal lung lesions.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 54 year old man due to start monoclonal antibody therapy for Crohn’s disease has a minor CXR abnormality. With a history of childhood BCG vaccination, what is true regarding the IGRA?
options: A positive result should prompt antituberculous chemotherapy
It is more specific than tuberculin skin testing
It is now the first-line test for active TB
It is only positive with systemic mycobacterial infection
It measures the release of interferon-alpha from sensitised T cells
answer_text: It is more specific than tuberculin skin testing IGRA is less affected by BCG vaccination and is more specific than TST.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 64 year old woman with back pain, weight loss and a flank mass that is fluid-filled under goes aspiration of pus. What is an important additional test?
answer_text: Mycobacterial testing Extrapulmonary TB should be considered in psoas abscess formation.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 28 year old woman develops a painful lower limb rash, arthralgia and fever, then a CXR is performed. At 4-week review, she feels well except for mild lethargy. What is the most likely cause?
answer_text: Sarcoidosis The systemic symptoms and CXR with hilar lymphadenopathy are typical of sarcoidosis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 72 year old woman with a 20-year history of rheumatoid arthritis is found on CXR and CT to have multiple smooth nodules that have been present for at least 5 years. What is the likely cause?
answer_text: Rheumatoid nodules Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis can cause pulmonary nodules that remain stable over time.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 64 year old man presents with high fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. After chest drain placement for an empyema with typical fluid values, he re-presents two weeks later with right-sided changes, pleuritic pain, fever, and symmetrical arthritis. What is the likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Rheumatoid arthritis The recurrent contralateral effusion with joint swelling suggests rheumatoid arthritis-associated pleural disease.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 45 year old non-smoking man with fever, weight loss, and breathlessness develops stridor on admission; CXR shows multiple bilateral nodules. His history includes sinusitis and conductive deafness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Granulomatous polyangiitis The multisystem involvement with sinusitis and subglottic stenosis suggests granulomatous polyangiitis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 55 year old geologist with cough, breathlessness, and arthralgia since home renovation (with damp and dust exposure) and beryllium handling at work presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Berylliosis Berylliosis should be excluded in patients with beryllium exposure and a sarcoid-like picture.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 69 year old woman undergoing a CT coronary angiogram is incidentally found to have diffuse ground glass and centrilobular nodules. She has a pet parrot. What is the likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Exposure to avian proteins in a parrot is suggestive of bird fancier’s lung.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: Which of the following associations regarding lung disease is correct?
options: Chlamydia psittaci and hide factory workers
answer_text: Francisella tularensis and muskrat contact Francisella tularensis is associated with muskrat exposure.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 78-year-old woman has multilobar pneumonia requiring intubation. Her blood gas on high FiO2 shows a PO2 of 54 mmHg. What is the cause of the hypoxemia?
answer_text: Shunt In pneumonia, alveoli are filled with exudate, producing perfusion without ventilation (shunt).

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 38-year-old woman with acute eosinophilic pneumonia and rapid respiratory failure. What is the best treatment now?
options: Consult thoracic surgery for lung biopsy
Continue IV antibiotics while awaiting cultures
Initiate methylprednisolone 60 mg IV every 6 hours
answer_text: Initiate methylprednisolone 60 mg IV every 6 hours Acute eosinophilic pneumonia responds dramatically to corticosteroids.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 51-year-old woman has 7 years of cough with thick green sputum, Pseudomonas. Next test?
answer_text: High-resolution chest CT HRCT is the diagnostic standard for confirming bronchiectasis.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 62-year-old woman with focal bronchiectasis post-MAC infection. Cultures now negative but daily sputum persists. Best treatment?
options: Initiate airway clearance with oscillating positive expiratory pressure flutter valve
answer_text: Initiate airway clearance with oscillating positive expiratory pressure flutter valve Airway clearance techniques are key in managing bronchiectasis after infection clearance.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: What finding is expected on bronchoalveolar lavage in diffuse alveolar hemorrhage?
answer_text: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage typically shows hemosiderin-laden macrophages.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 56-year-old with subacute fevers, patchy alveolar infiltrates, histology with granulation tissue filling airways (COP). Best therapy?
answer_text: Prednisone 1 mg/kg daily Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia generally responds well to corticosteroids.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 52-year-old with dyspnea and extensive mediastinal calcifications encasing structures. Which of the following is true?
options: A urine Histoplasma antigen test will be positive.
The most common cause is histoplasmosis or TB.
Patient should be referred for surgical resection.
answer_text: The most common cause of the condition is histoplasmosis or tuberculosis Fibrosing mediastinitis is most often due to granulomatous infections like TB or histoplasmosis.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 35-year-old farmer presents with acute wheeze, cough and shortness of breath (SOB). He has smoked 10 cigarettes a day for 6 months. He likes to keep fit by running marathons. His grandfather had asthma as a child. He has lived in central London for the past year. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his condition?
answer_text: Occupation Farmer’s lung is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis induced by the inhalation of biologic dusts coming from hay dust or mould spores. Acute farmer’s lung starts about 4 to 8 hours after exposure.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A middle-aged woman is admitted to hospital with a cough, sputum production, fever and dyspnoea. A diagnosis of pneumonia is made. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for her symptoms?
answer_text: Streptococcus pneumoniae S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia where a pathogen is isolated, accounting for about 50% of cases.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: An elderly woman is admitted to hospital with pneumonia. The following are all risk factors used in predicting mortality in community-acquired pneumonia EXCEPT?
options: Respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min or more
Systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg
answer_text: Respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min or more The mortality associated with community-acquired pneumonia is dependent on the CURB 65 score. A respiratory rate of 30 breaths/ min is a key risk factor, not 20.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A middle-aged man presents with a cough, sputum production, fever and dyspnoea. Red-coloured papules are noted on the back of his hands. Routine blood investigations demonstrate that he is anaemic. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for his condition?
answer_text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes a form of atypical pneumonia which can cause extra-pulmonary symptoms including erythema multiforme, haemolytic anaemia, Guillain–Barré syndrome, renal failure and pericarditis.

heading: Crash Respiratory
