stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the GP with symptoms suggestive of pneumonia. He also complains of generalized muscular pains. He has many pets at home and mentions he recently bought two parrots. Which of the following organisms would account for his condition?
answer_text: Chlamydia psittaci Chlamydia psittaci is an intracellular bacterial species found in birds. Transmission is by inhalation or contact and the illness often starts with flu-like symptoms.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 23-year-old known intravenous drug abuser is admitted with a fever, productive cough and dyspnoea. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for his condition?
answer_text: Staphylococcus aureus Intravenous drug users have an increased risk of community-acquired pneumonia, with S. aureus pneumonia being common and potentially leading to lung abscess formation.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the GP with a fever, productive cough and chest pain. He has recently been abroad to Dubai and stayed at a newly built hotel. He mentioned that he had bouts of diarrhoea in the last few days of his trip, which he put down to the foreign food. Which of the following organisms is most likely to account for his condition?
answer_text: Legionella pneumophila Legionella is transmitted via inhalation of contaminated water droplets, often from hotel cooling towers, and is associated with gastrointestinal symptoms.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 40-year-old man is diagnosed with a mild pneumonia. He has no known drug allergies. What is the most appropriate treatment?
answer_text: Amoxicillin Mild pneumonia is usually managed at home with a 5–7-day course of oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: You suspect pneumonia in a 35-year-old woman. Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
answer_text: CXR CXR is the gold-standard investigation in pneumonia, showing airspace opacity, lobar consolidation/air bronchograms or interstitial opacities.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: An Asian man presents with a 2-month history of fever and a cough productive of blood- tinged sputum. He has recently moved to the United Kingdom from abroad. What is the most likely causative organism?
answer_text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis Mycobacterium tuberculosis is often seen in Asian immigrants. Classic symptoms include chronic cough with blood-containing sputum, fever, night sweats and weight loss.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A West Indian immigrant has recently been diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB). Which of the following cells are solely responsible for engulf ing bacilli and forming granulomatous lesions?
answer_text: Macrophages TB infection begins when mycobacteria invade pulmonary alveoli and are engulfed by macrophages, which then form granulomatous lesions.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: An Asian immigrant presents with a fever and a cough productive of blood-tinged sputum. On examination you note an enlarged liver and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. A CXR shows patchy shadowing in the upper zones. You suspect TB. What is the next most appropriate investigation you would order to confirm your suspicion?
answer_text: Sputum smear Multiple sputum cultures (or induced sputum samples) are usually taken to look for acid-fast bacilli using sensitive staining techniques.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A middle-aged man is diagnosed with TB. He has no known drug allergies. Which is the least likely drug to be included in the initial treatment?
answer_text: Streptomycin The standard treatment for new-onset pulmonary TB is 6 months of quadruple therapy; streptomycin is typically reserved for previously treated cases due to resistance concerns.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 55-year-old man has recently been diagnosed with TB. He has been started on quadruple therapy and complains of a colour change in his urine. What drug is most likely to be responsible for this?
answer_text: Rifampicin Rifampicin can cause bodily fluids such as urine, sweat and tears to become orange-red, alongside other side effects.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: An outbreak of pneumonia involving over 20 cases, some fatal, has occurred in one town and most of the sufferers have stayed in the same hotel. Features of the illness were high fever, rigors, confusion, myalgia, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. Chest radiograph showed bilateral shadowing. The clinical diagnosis was confirmed by a fluorescent antibody titre, which showed a significant rise in paired sera taken a month apart. What is the most likely pathogen?
answer_text: Legionella pneumophilia The atypical presentation with gastrointestinal symptoms and association with a hotel outbreak is characteristic of Legionella.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 50-year-old patient with long-standing chronic obstructive lung disease develops the insidious onset of aching in the distal extremities, particularly the wrists bilaterally. There is a 10-lb weight loss. The skin over the wrists is warm and erythematous. There is bilateral clubbing. Plain film is read as periosteal thickening, possible osteomyelitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
answer_text: Obtain chest x-ray. HOA: clubbing + periosteal reaction + arthralgia → search intrathoracic malignancy/suppurative lung disease; first test CXR; RA and osteomyelitis less likely; no empiric antibiotics.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 63-year-old man presents to the emergency department with haemoptysis. He has a past medical history of antiphospholipid syndrome and is on warfarin. On examination, chest auscultation is normal. There is evidence of nasal crusting. The sensation is reduced bilaterally to the ankles. A chest x-ray demonstrates cavitating nodules in both midzones. Blood tests: WBC
answer_text: Granulomatosis with polyangittis ENT + lung + renal involvement → consider GPA (granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: 5*10^9/L (4.0 - 11.0); Hb 138 g/L Male: (135-180); Urea 15.6 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0); Creatinine 240 μmol/L (55 - 120); CRP 145 mg/L (0-5); INR 1.4 (0.9-1.1). What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Oral glucocorticoids Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → treat with oral glucocorticoids.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 46-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid arthritis is investigated due to progressive shortness of breath. She is currently treated with methotrexate and ibuprofen. The following results are obtained from spirometry: FEV1/FVC 45%. What is the most likely cause of the dyspnoea?
answer_text: 354 mL Using 6 mL/kg of ideal body weight, 6 x 59 ≈354 mL is recommended.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 28-year-old presents to the emergency department with a dry cough, progressive dyspnoea, and recurrent chest infections. He was recently started on a salbutamol inhaler by his general practitioner which has had little effect. A diffuse wheeze is heard on auscultation. Investigations show eosinophilia and IgE 2300 kU/mL. Chest x-ray: bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. What is the treatment of choice for this patient?
options: Low dose inhaled corticosteroids (Low-dose ICS inhaler)
answer_text: Increase PEEP to 12 cmH2O Increasing PEEP above the lower inflection point helps recruit alveoli and improve oxygenation.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A middle aged woman presents with progressive shortness of breath. Chest X ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Calcium 2.7mmol/l; Angiotensin converting enzyme 200μg/l (<40μg/l). Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following features would be associated with a good prognosis?
answer_text: Erythema nodosum Sarcoidosis prognosis better with HLA-B8 and Löfgren syndrome; other listed factors predict worse outcomes.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 20-year-old man with epilepsy presents to the Emergency Department with a three-day history of cough and increasing shortness of breath. He has foul-smelling sputum. He had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure one week ago. On examination his temperature is 40 °C, he has right-sided crepitations and his chest X-ray shows a right middle lobe infiltration. Which one of the following options is the most likely cause?
answer_text: E Pneumonia due to anaerobes Anaerobic pleuropulmonary infection from aspirated oropharyngeal flora → foul sputum; diagnose via invasive cultures (bronchoscopy or transthoracic aspiration).

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 47-year-old man has been admitted to hospital with increasing shortness of breath, sweats and purulent sputum. He is known to the team to be homeless and has a history of alcohol misuse. His Emergency Department records indicate that he was admitted in an unconscious state a few days ago but self-discharged when he woke up. On examination there is pyrexia and dullness at the apex associated with bronchial breathing. His chest X-ray shows right middle-lobe consolidation. What is the most likely cause?
answer_text: Left-sided pneumothorax The CXR reveals a clear visceral pleural line with absent lung markings indicating a left-sided pneumothorax.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: An 81-year-old woman who had consulted her GP with symptoms of flu 2 weeks earlier now presents to the Emergency Department. For the past few days she has had increasing cough, associated with purulent sputum and haemoptysis. Her daughter visited and noticed that she had become acutely confused and arranged an ambulance. On arrival to the department she is found to be agitated, with a respiratory rate of 35/min. Blood gases reveal that she is hypoxic, her white blood cell count is 20 × 10^9/L predominantly neutrophils. Her creatinine concentration is 250 µmol/L. Chest X-ray reveals patchy areas of consolidation, with necrosis and empyema formation. What diagnosis best fits this clinical picture?
answer_text: Therapeutic aspiration The CXR shows a large left-sided pneumothorax in a symptomatic patient; therapeutic aspiration is indicated.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a long history of productive cough and breathlessness. He also complained of halitosis and reported having exacerbations that consisted of productive sputum, chest pain and occasional haemoptysis. Examination in the clinic reveals bilateral inspiratory crackles. Which of following treatments is the most likely to decrease the frequency of his exacerbations?
answer_text: D Postural drainage Bronchiectasis management cornerstone = postural drainage taught by physiotherapy, 10–20 min, ≥3 times/day.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 16-A 26-year-old office secretary who smokes 10-15 cigarettes per day presented in the clinic after a couple of episodes of haemoptysis. She also said that she had felt tired recently and gave a history of passing cola-coloured urine with blood. A full blood count showed anaemia and the chest X-ray showed blotchy shadows over the lung fields. She is ANCA negative. What is your probable diagnosis?
answer_text: B Goodpasture syndrome Hemoptysis + renal involvement pattern → Goodpasture syndrome (typically >16 years).

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 25-A 25-year-old patient with epilepsy aspirated gastric juice after a seizure (Mendelson syndrome). What is the most likely clinical symptom or sign?
answer_text: B Bronchospasm Mendelson syndrome = chemical pneumonitis after gastric aspiration; early bronchospasm typical.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 26-A 35-year-old woman who has been treated for asthma presents with worsening cough, wheeze and recurrent fleeting pulmonary infiltrates. She produces brownish plugs and her chest X-ray shows evidence of pulmonary infiltration and some lobar consolidation. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
answer_text: A Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis Asthma + fleeting infiltrates + brown plugs with stable exposure → ABPA from Aspergillus.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 28-A 22-year-old student attends the clinic for his 6-week check after admission with pneumonia. Which of the following complications of pneumonia is most likely to be a chronic rather than an acute complication of the infective process?
answer_text: Intercostal chest drain Failure of aspiration indicates the need for chest drain insertion to resolve the pneumothorax.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 19-year-old army cadet is admitted to hospital with cough, fever and malaise. On examination there is fever and coarse crepitations at the bases of the lungs. Cold agglutinins are positive. A chest X-ray shows bibasal shadowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: C Mycoplasma pneumonia Atypical LRTI with slow progression in healthy young adult → think Mycoplasma.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 69-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is referred with chronic cough productive of purulent sputum and recurrent chest infections. On examination she had coarse crepitations at both the bases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: A Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis associated with RA; HRCT is diagnostic test of choice.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with suspected pneumonia. Her observations are: temperature 38.3 °C, respiratory rate 27/min, BP 100/70 mmHg. She is confused during the consultation. Her urea is 5.2 mmol/l on arterial blood gas. Which of the following according to CURB-65 criteria is associated with a worse prognosis?
answer_text: B Confusion CURB-65 severity: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, RR ≥30, BP low, Age ≥65.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A young adult was referred because of cough and shortness of breath. Extrinsic allergic alveolitis was diagnosed. Apart from reduction of exposure to the allergen, which other therapy is most likely to be successful?
answer_text: All of the above Silicosis increases the risk for TB, fungal infections, lung cancer, and rheumatoid arthritis.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 42-Which one of the following does not increase the risk of death in patients with severe pneumonia?
options: Atrial fibrillation with fast ventricular response
answer_text: A Age 49 years CURB-65 mnemonic restated: C, U>7, R≥30, BPs<90 or BPd≤60, age ≥65.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 45-A 48-year-old man is reviewed in the Respiratory Clinic. He c...and regular; BP is 122/72 mmHg. There is wheeze on auscultation. You suspect extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA). Which of the following would be most consistent with EAA due to parrot antigen exposure?
answer_text: A Bilateral upper lobe fibrosis EAA classically causes bilateral upper-lobe fibrosis.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 47-A 32-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner complaining of cough and fever. You suspect tuberculosis. He is from an area where high levels of drug resistance are present. Which of the following blood tests is most desirable before starting therapy?
answer_text: C Liver function testing INH, rifampin, pyrazinamide → hepatotoxic; get baseline and periodic LFTs. ria for severe ARDS.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 68-year-old with multilobar pneumonia, shock, and hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ≤100). Which diagnosis fits best?
answer_text: Severe acute respiratory distress syndrome A PaO2/FiO2 ratio ≤100 mmHg meets the crite

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: An ARDS patient with a lower inflection at 12 cmH2O, current PEEP is 8, plateau 26. SaO2 is 86%. Best step?
answer_text: Narcotic overdose A normal alveolar-arterial gradient indicates hypoventilation is the cause of hypercapnia and hypoxemia, consistent with overdose.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: In which of the following situations is noninvasive mechanical ventilation contraindicated?
options: Post-extubation in COPD A. Acute interstitial pneumonia B. Mild ARDS C. Moderate ARDS D. Multilobar CAP E. Severe ARDS
answer_text: Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in an individual with acute respiratory distress syndrome NIV has a high failure rate in severe ARDS and is generally contraindicated.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 62-year-old intubated for pneumonia is considered for weaning. Which is a contraindication to a spontaneous breathing trial?
answer_text: Ongoing need for vasopressor support Hemodynamic instability precludes a safe spontaneous breathing trial.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: If a lung biopsy were taken 4 days after admission in severe ARDS, which finding is expected?
options: Patient breathing above set rate by 8 breaths/ min A. Desquamative interstitial pneumonia B. Eosinophil-rich infiltrates C. Extensive fibrosis with bullae D. Homogeneous neutrophil infiltrates E. Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes
answer_text: Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes Early ARDS is characterized by diffuse alveolar damage with formation of hyaline membranes.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 48-year-old with ARDS weighs 90 kg but
answer_text: Lobar collapse Lobar collapse can cause V/Q mismatch leading to type I failure.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 30-year-old male is admitted to the hospital after a motorcycle accident that resulted in a fracture of the right femur. The fracture is managed with traction. Three days later the patient becomes confused and tachypneic. A petechial rash is noted over the chest. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Arterial blood gases show PO2 of 50, PCO2 of 28, and pH of 7.49. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Fat embolism Post-fracture hypoxemia + neuro decline + petechiae at 12–36 h → fat embolism; PE unlikely to cause petechiae.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Which one of the following is not part of the diagnostic criteria of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)?
answer_text: Respiratory rate > 24/min ARDS Berlin criteria exclude respiratory rate; requires acute onset, bilateral infiltrates, non-cardiogenic edema, and PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 mmHg (≤200 = severe).

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: Type 2 Respiratory Failure may result from the following EXCEPT:
answer_text: Pulmonary oedema Pulmonary oedema typically causes type 1 respiratory failure.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: An 83 year old woman was passenger in a car that collided with a lamppost in the city centre. She was initially complaining of pain in her right hip and ribs but has become increasingly drowsy since the paramedics administered 2 mg of morphine. She is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. Urgent X-rays reveal a pelvic fracture, and a single right-sided rib fracture. Having, initially been drowsy but responsive she is now unresponsive. Oxygen saturations are 87% on 2 L/min oxygen via nasal cannulae. She is apyrexial. BP is 110/66 mmHg, pulse is 65 beats/min. There are no new findings on examination. An urgent CT brain reveals only small vessel disease. Arterial blood gas: H+ 60 nmol/L (pH 7.22), PaO2 8.7 kPa (65 mmHg), PaCO2 10 kPa (75 mmHg), HCO3- 26 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause of her deteriorating conscious level?
options: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with oxygen toxicity – loss of hypoxic drive
Flail segment due to rib fracture – loss of elastic recoil
Opiate toxicity – suppression of the respiratory centre
Undetected fracture of C3 – diaphragmatic failure
answer_text: Undetected fracture of C3 – diaphragmatic failure A fracture at C3 can paralyse the diaphragm leading to type II respiratory failure with a normal A–a gradient.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: In which of the following conditions might acute type I respiratory failure be expected?
answer_text: Pneumothorax Increased resonance and reduced expansion suggest pneumothorax.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 25-year-old man is brought in unresponsive with pH 7.16, PCO2 70 mmHg, and PO2 55 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Empyema The D-shaped opacity and clinical presentation are typical of an empyema requiring drainage.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A patient with mild ALS has PaCO2≥45 mmHg plus which symptom indicates NIV therapy?
answer_text: All of the above Any symptom of hypoventilation with hypercapnia warrants noninvasive ventilation.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 70-year-old patient with chronic obstructive lung disease requires 2 L/min of nasal O2 to treat his hypoxia, which is sometimes associated with angina. The patient develops pleuritic chest pain, fever, and purulent sputum. While using his oxygen at an increased flow of 5 L/min he becomes stuporous and develops a respiratory acidosis with CO2 retention and worsening hypoxia. What would be the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Observe patient 24 hours before changing therapy.
answer_text: Intubate and begin mechanical ventilation. Severe COPD with CO₂ narcosis after high O₂ → acute ventilatory failure; treat with ventilation (consider NIV if alert); bicarbonate not indicated.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: The following can cause exudative pleural effusion EXCEPT:
answer_text: Nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome typically causes a transudative effusion.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: The following can cause exudative pleural effusion EXCEPT: A) Pulmonary infarction. B) Malignancies. C) Para-pneumonic effusion. D) Liver cirrhosis.
answer_text: Liver cirrhosis. Liver cirrhosis is typically associated with transudative pleural effusion.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: A 21-year-old high-jumper presents with acute-onset dyspnoea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Examination reveals increased resonance and reduced expansion on the right side.
answer_text: Hyper-resonance, decreased breath sounds in the left chest with trachea deviation to right PTX → hyperresonance, ↓breath sounds, ↓fremitus; tension shifts mediastinum away; rales/ wheeze suggest alternate pathology.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 52 year old man presents with a 1-week history of fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain and increasing shortness of breath. He has a past history of alcohol dependency, alcoholic liver disease and chronic pancreatitis. He has smoked 10 cigarettes per day for 30 years and still drinks 28 units a week. He worked as a casual labourer on building sites where asbestos was removed in his 20s. What is most likely to be causing the CXR shown below?
answer_text: Stop smoking After spontaneous pneumothorax: stop smoking; fitness-to-fly typically 1–2 weeks post-resolution with clear CXR and no residual air.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 71 year old man presents with increasing breathlessness with no cough or systemic symptoms. He has atrial fibrillation and a recent echocardiogram with preserved LV function. What does his CXR show?
options: Right middle and lower lobe collapse
answer_text: Right-sided pleural effusion The CXR demonstrates a homogenous right-sided opacification with a meniscus sign, typical of a pleural effusion.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: For the patient described in Question 17.11, what would be the best next step in his management?
options: Bedside thoracic ultrasound and pleural aspiration
Thoracic ultrasound scan-guided intercostal chest drain
answer_text: Stop apixaban The isolated effusion in a patient on apixaban requires cautious intervention; stopping the anticoagulant is necessary before aspiration.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 35 year old man has been unwell for a week with fever, productive cough, rhinitis and aching muscles. He now presents with left-sided pleuritic chest pain. His CXR is shown. What is shown on the CXR?
answer_text: Ambulatory device Symptomatic primary pneumothorax without high-risk features → options: conservative care, needle aspiration, or ambulatory one-way valve device.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 29 year old man presents with progressive shortness of breath over a week, new central chest discomfort, and a productive cough. He is a cannabis smoker with no significant past medical history. His CXR is shown. What would be the next step in his management?
answer_text: B Chest drain insertion initially COPD with symptomatic pneumothorax, rim >2 cm → initial chest drain (no aspiration) per BTS.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 75 year old man with asbestos exposure presents with a large right-sided pleural effusion. Pleural aspiration is exudative but cytology is negative and CT shows circumferential pleural thickening. Which test is most likely to give a diagnosis?
answer_text: Thoracoscopy Direct visualisation and biopsy of pleural lesions via thoracoscopy is the gold standard.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: Which of the following is a cause of a transudative pleural effusion?
answer_text: Hypothyroidism Hypothyroidism can cause a transudative effusion.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: Which one of the following statements is true regarding Light’s criteria?
options: Pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
Pleural fluid LDH < two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH
answer_text: Pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH Light’s criteria use thresholds of protein and LDH ratios to define an exudate.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 64 year old man presents with fever, sweats, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. He is an ex-smoker with a history of alcohol excess. Pleural fluid aspiration under ultrasound guidance is performed. Which value might be expected?
answer_text: Pleural fluid pH 6.9 (H+ 126 nmol/L) The low pH with high LDH and protein is typical for empyema.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 34 year old man presents with acute-onset shortness of breath and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Examination reveals O2 saturations of 94% on room air and a hyper-resonant left chest. CXR shows a large left-sided pneumothorax. Therapeutic aspiration of 2.5 L of air is performed with no radiographic improvement. What should be the next step?
answer_text: Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP IPF is a restrictive disease with reduced lung volumes, but normal muscle strength, increasing the FEV1/FVC ratio.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 53-year-old with pneumonia, gross pus in the pleural space (empyema). A large-bore chest tube is placed. What else helps?
answer_text: Intrapleural instillation of alteplase plus DNase Combination therapy improves drainage in empyema.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 44-year-old on mechanical ventilation has sudden hypotension, peak airway pressure 55, absent right breath sounds. Next step?
options: Needle decompression of the right chest
answer_text: Place a large-bore needle into the right second anterior intercostal space to alleviate a tension pneumothorax. High airway pressures, absent breath sounds, and hypotension indicate tension pneumothorax.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 62-year-old with pneumonia and a pleural effusion. Which finding does NOT indicate a complicated effusion?
options: Recurrence of fluid after initial thoracentesis
answer_text: Recurrence of fluid following the initial thoracentesis Recurrence alone does not indicate complexity if pH, glucose, and loculation are not present.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A moderate right-sided pleural effusion is exudative. Which is NOT likely a cause of this pleural fluid?
answer_text: B Interstitial lung disease Systemic sclerosis may present first with lung disease; bibasal fine crackles; HRCT shows interstitial changes almost universally.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 28-year-old tall, thin male smoker has a 20% spontaneous pneumothorax on the right. Which statement is true?
options: CT scan is likely to show emphysematous changes.
If recurrent, thoracoscopy with pleural abrasion nearly 100% prevents recurrence.
Most patients need tube thoracostomy to resolve it.
Tall, thin habitus is the primary risk factor.
answer_text: If the patient were to develop recurrent pneumothoraces, thoracoscopy with pleural abrasion has a near 100% success rate for prevention of recurrence. Video-assisted thoracoscopic pleurodesis is highly effective in preventing recurrences.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: With regard to pleural fluid, which of the following is most important in determining whether an effusion is a transudate or exudate?
answer_text: Protein levels Transudative effusions have low protein/albumin levels compared with exudative effusions, as determined by Light’s criteria.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: Which of the following typically causes a transudative pleural effusion?
answer_text: Heart failure Heart failure is a common cause of transudative pleural effusions due to increased hydrostatic pressure.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: You are called to review a 70-year-old man admitted for treatment of pneumococcal pneumonia, who has become more unwell with swinging fevers, worsening breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. His inflammatory markers are rising and a repeat CXR shows a new right-sided pleural effusion. What is the next most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
options: Recheck the sputum for resistant organisms
answer_text: Ultrasound-guided diagnostic pleural tap Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis is diagnostic, as it yields pleural fluid for culture, Gram stain, and analysis, and reduces complications.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 76-year-old man with COPD was admitted to accident and emergency department with acute on chronic SOB. He has a chest drain inserted for a pneumothorax. Which of the following is true of chest drain management?
options: He should have his drain clamped if he has to travel to the radiology department without a medical escort.
The drain should only be removed when it has stopped bubbling.
The drain may be clamped if it only bubbles on coughing.
The drain should only be removed when it has stopped swinging.
Pain relief is usually not necessary in the first few days after insertion.
answer_text: The drain should only be removed when it has stopped bubbling. The drain can only be removed when bubbling in the underwater seal has ceased, indicating resolution of the air leak.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted to intensive care unit (ICU) for potassium replacement. A central venous line is inserted via the subclavian vein. During the procedure he becomes acutely breathless with decreasing oxygen saturation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: The wire has threaded into the left ventricle
His chronic obstructive airways disease has been exacerbated
A myocardial infarction has been induced
answer_text: A pneumothorax has been created Pneumothorax is a known complication of subclavian vein cannulation due to inadvertent lung puncture.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 58-year-old man with longstanding emphysema presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of breathlessness and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. On arrival, he is hypoxic, tachypnoeic, hypotensive and tachycardic. His trachea is deviated to the right and breath sounds are markedly reduced on the left side of his chest. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
options: Insert large bore cannula into the left second intercostal space
Insert chest drain with negative suction on the left side
answer_text: Insert large bore cannula into the left second intercostal space The clinical picture is suggestive of a tension pneumothorax, which is an emergency treated with immediate needle decompression in the second intercostal space.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 40-year-old nonsmoker presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset breathlessness and left-sided chest pain. On examination, he is unable to complete sentences and has low oxygen saturation levels. He has diminished breath sounds on the left side with tracheal deviation towards the right. Heart sounds are normal. What is the most likely explanation for these findings?
answer_text: Pneumothorax Unilateral diminished breath sounds with tracheal deviation strongly indicate a pneumothorax.

heading: Other MCQ’s
stem: A 66-year-old woman presents to accident and emergency with a 2-day history of shortness of breath. The patient notes becoming progressively short of breath as well as a sharp pain in the right side of the chest which is most painful when taking a deep breath. The patient also complains of mild pain in the right leg, though there is nothing significant on full cardiovascular and respiratory examination. Heart rate is 96 and respiratory rate is 12. The patient denies any weight loss or long haul flights but mentions undergoing a nasal polypectomy 3 weeks ago. The most likely diagnosis is:
answer_text: Pulmonary embolism Pulmonary embolism is most likely given the acute onset of pleuritic chest pain with associated leg pain and recent surgery; other options are less consistent with the clinical findings.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A patient with low-grade fever and weight loss has poor excursion on the right side of the chest with decreased fremitus, flatness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds all on the right. The trachea is deviated to the left. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Pleural effusion Poor excursion + dullness + ↓fremitus on right with contralateral tracheal shift → large right pleural effusion; not PTX (hyperresonant) or consolidation (↑fremitus).

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 64-year-old woman is found to have a right-sided pleural effusion on chest x-ray. Analysis of the pleural fluid reveals pleural fluid to serum protein ratio of 0.38, a lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level of 110 IU (normal 100-
answer_text: Congestive heart failure Light’s criteria define exudate (protein ratio >0.5, LDH >2/3 ULN, LDH ratio >0.6); exudates = inflammatory causes; transudates = CHF, nephrotic, cirrhosis, etc.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: , and pleural fluid to serum LDH ratio of

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: 46. Which of the following disorders is most likely in this patient?

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 50-year-old male with emphysema develops the sudden onset of shortness of breath and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Pneumothorax is suspected. Which of the following physical examination findings would be consistent with the diagnosis?
options: Localized wheezes at the left base
Hyper-resonance, decreased breath sounds in the left chest with trachea deviation to right
Increased tactile fremitus on the left side
Decreased breath sounds on the left side with deviation of the trachea to the left
answer_text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Presentation suggests Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis as per note.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 29-year-old man is admitted with sudden onset dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain. He is a smoker but has no history of respiratory disease. He considers himself healthy and regularly plays rugby. On admission he has a chest x-ray that shows a pneumothorax with a 3cm rim of air. Aspiration is successful and he is discharged. A follow-up chest x-ray two weeks later shows a complete resolution. What is the single most important piece of advice to reduce his risk of further pneumothoraces?
options: Arrange a course of respiratory physiotherapy
Seek prompt medical advice for potential respiratory infections
answer_text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis The CT reveals bilateral basal honeycombing and reticular changes consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old woman is referred to ambulatory care with a 3-month history of increasing breathlessness. She has no significant respiratory past medical history. On examination, observations are normal but there is decreased air entry to the right lung base. A chest x-ray confirms a large right-sided pleural effusion. The results of the pleural aspirate are shown below: Pleural fluid protein 134 g/L; Serum protein 61 g/L (60 - 80); White cell count 13,000 cells/ μL (< 1000); Microscopy No organisms seen; Culture No growth on routine culture after 48 hours. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s pleural effusion?
answer_text: Lung cancer Exudative pleural effusion with high protein and negative cultures in older adult → malignancy most likely (lung cancer common).

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 35-year-old married woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath associated with the start of her menstrual period. This occurred during her last menstrual period but resolved. Now the pain is more severe with some radiation to her shoulder. She has two young children; first born via spontaneous vaginal delivery and the other by emergency caesarean section. What is the likely cause of the patient’s symptoms?
answer_text: Catamenial pneumothorax Catamenial pneumothorax: cyclical, right-sided, around menses due to thoracic endometriosis.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 32-year-old man with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset left-sided chest pain. He denies any trauma or recent respiratory infections. His observations are as follows: respiratory rate 21 /min, sats 96% on room air, BP 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 88 bpm, and he is apyrexial. On examination, his trachea is central, the chest on the left side is hyper-resonant on percussion and there is reduced breath sound. The right side of the chest is normal. A chest x-ray reveals a 2.5cm apical rim of air. What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
answer_text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis The HRCT features are classical for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 70-year-old man with moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) attends the Emergency Department with increasing dyspnoea. He has been found to have a 3-cm pneumothorax. What would be the optimal management for this patient?
options: Chest drain insertion if needle aspiration fails
Conservative management, with observation and repeat chest X-ray after 4 hours
Conservative management, with observation and repeat chest X-ray after 12 hours
answer_text: Smokers RBILD is typically seen in smokers, usually between 40 and 60 years of age.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 27-A 43-year-old woman has a pleural effusion and evidence of photosensitive rash and arthralgia. She also reports exposure to sun that has worsened over the past few months. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: E Systemic lupus erythematosus SLE can cause pleural effusion; confirm with immunologic tests (anti-dsDNA).

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: You are asked to see a 63-year-old man who was admitted to the ward for intravenous antibiotics. He has a central line in situ in the right subclavian vein. He suddenly develops worsening shortness of breath. His oxygen saturation drops to 89% and a portable chest film indicates a right lung collapse. Which of the following is the most likely complication of line insertion to have occurred?
answer_text: D Pneumothorax Post–subclavian line pneumothorax (≤15% incidence) → insert chest drain.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 41-After a tennis match, a thin 20-year-old woman complains of l...neralised tenderness. A few minutes later she develops cyanosis. What is the diagnosis?
answer_text: E Tension pneumothorax Tension pneumothorax: rising intrapleural pressure with one-way air entry → rapid decompensation; immediate needle decompression then chest tube.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: Which of the following is not typically associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
answer_text: Tremor or hyperreflexia Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis commonly presents with tachypnea, fine crackles, clubbing, and may cause some shift; tremor or hyperreflexia is not typical.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Which of the following best describe fibrosing alveolitis?
answer_text: Clubbing and Velcro crepitations. Clubbing and Velcro crepitations are characteristic of fibrosing alveolitis.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: A 72-year-old man presents with breathlessness, clubbing and prominent fine bi-basal crackles on auscultation of his chest. The most likely diagnosis is
answer_text: High-resolution CT scan Middle-aged man with progressive dyspnea, clubbing, restrictive spirometry → suspect IPF; order HRCT; normal BNP argues against HF.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 73 year old woman with a 1-year history of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough, finger clubbing and bi-basal crackles is imaged with CT. What is the likely cause of the CT appearance?
answer_text: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis Upper-zone fibrosis + bird exposure → EAA (hypersensitivity pneumonitis); asbestosis, RA, nitrofurantoin usually lower-lobe.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 71 year old man presents with increasing breathlessness without cough. CT chest reveals bilateral diffuse fibrotic change with basal honeycombing. What does his CXR show?
options: A typical CT appearance is sufficient for diagnosis
Blind transbronchial needle aspiration would likely give the diagnosis
Bronchoscopy with cytopathological analysis of washings would help
Endobronchial ultrasound of his subcarinal node would exclude more diffuse disease
Transbronchial lung biopsy would give a tissue diagnosis
answer_text: A typical CT appearance is sufficient for diagnosis A characteristic CT pattern in IPF permits diagnosis without biopsy in the appropriate clinical context.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 62 year old ex-smoker presents with breathlessness on exertion. Pulmonary function: FEV1
answer_text: No evidence of airways obstruction Normal spirometry with reduced gas transfer may warrant further evaluation but shows no clear obstruction.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: 2 L, FVC 3.8 L, FEV1/FVC 0.84, TLC 4.1 L, RV 0.6 L, TLCO 1.5 (44%), KCO 1 (56%). How should these tests be interpreted?
options: Gas transfer reduction indicates hypersensitivity pneumonitis
answer_text: Cor pulmonale In COPD, chronic pulmonary hypertension can lead to right-sided heart failure (cor pulmonale), manifesting as JVD and edema.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 79 year old woman with progressive exertional breathlessness, bilateral fine basal crackles and clubbing has an HRCT showing bilateral basal peripheral reticulation with honeycomb cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Spontaneous resolution Sarcoidosis with Löfgren syndrome → good prognosis; many resolve without treatment; relapses less common.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: Respiratory bronchiolitis–interstitial lung disease (RBILD) is more common in which group?
answer_text: Monitoring Sarcoidosis often remits without therapy in the majority of patients.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 55 year old man with a 2-year history of increasing breathlessness and dry cough, with restrictive PFTs and HRCT showing bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, bronchovascular nodules and extensive fibrosis is evaluated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Sarcoidosis stage IV The presence of extensive fibrosis with lymph node enlargement indicates end-stage (stage IV) sarcoidosis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 26 year old non-smoking woman presents for the second time with pneumothorax. CT identifies multiple lung cysts and an upper pole abnormality of the right kidney. What diagnosis should be considered?
answer_text: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis The combination of recurrent pneumothorax, cystic lung changes and a renal lesion is characteristic of LAM.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)?
options: Finger clubbing and basal crackles are characteristic
It has no impact on lung function
It may progress even after exposure ceases
answer_text: It may progress even after exposure ceas es PMF may progress and lead to respiratory failure despite removal from exposure.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 41 year old stonemason with shortness of breath is found to have silicosis on imaging. Silicosis results from the inhalation of which substance?
answer_text: Quartz Silicosis is caused by inhalation of crystalline silica (quartz).

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Which of the following pulmonary function test results is consistent with Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Increased TLC, decreased vital capacity, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio
Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/ FVC ratio, decreased MIP
Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
answer_text: E Usual interstitial pneumonitis Dyspnea + clubbing + inspiratory crackles → UIP/IPF; CXR subpleural reticulation; CT honeycombing.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 65-year-old man has progressive dyspnea with bibasilar crackles and suspected ILD. Which test is most likely to determine the etiology?
options: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
answer_text: High-resolution CT scan of the chest HRCT is the next best step to evaluate suspected interstitial lung disease.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 34-year-old woman works in a pet store, subacute dyspnea, diffuse ground-glass opacities, loose noncaseating granulomas on biopsy. Diagnosis?
answer_text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Subacute presentation with granulomatous inflammation and relevant exposure indicates hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: What treatment do you recommend for the patient in Question VI-21 with hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
answer_text: Glucocorticoids plus removal of antigen Management of hypersensitivity pneumonitis requires antigen avoidance and corticosteroids.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Chronic silicosis is related to increased risk of which conditions?
answer_text: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA) HPOA, a paraneoplastic syndrome, is known to cause painful periostitis.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: All of the following occupational lung diseases are correctly matched EXCEPT:
answer_text: Progressive massive fibrosis—Shipyard workers Progressive massive fibrosis is typically related to silica/coal dust exposure, not shipyard work (asbestos).

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 53-year-old farmer with sudden fever, chills, dyspnea after stacking moldy hay. Which organism is most likely responsible?
answer_text: Actinomyces species Farmer’s lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) is classically due to thermophilic actinomycetes.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 62-year-old man with exertional dyspnea and bibasilar crackles. HRCT suggests idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. What would pathology show?
answer_text: Usual interstitial pneumonia The histopathologic hallmark of IPF is the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: What is the recommended treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: No therapy is effective for IPF
answer_text: Nintedanib 150 mg twice a day Nintedanib slows disease progression in IPF.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: An Afro-Caribbean man presents with increasing dyspnoea. A CXR shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Routine blood investigations demonstrate a raised serum calcium. Which of the following is also likely to be affected?
answer_text: Eyes Up to 90% of patients with sarcoidosis complain of eye involvement, including uveitis, which can lead to loss of visual acuity.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: You suspect sarcoidosis in an Afro-Caribbean man who presents with a cough and evidence of lymphadenopathy. Which of the following investigations is likely to be most useful in confirming a diagnosis?
answer_text: Lymph node biopsy Tissue obtained from biopsy can confirm sarcoidosis by demonstrating noncaseating granulomas, while supporting investigations include CXR and raised serum ACE.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A middle-aged man presents with exertional dyspnoea and a nonproductive cough. On examination he has finger clubbing and fine inspiratory crackles are noted bibasally on auscultation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis Cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis is characterized by progressive dyspnoea, persistent cough and finger clubbing, with later fibrosis of alveolar walls.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of extrinsic allergic alveolitis?
options: Contaminated humidifier systems in air conditioners
answer_text: Forking mouldy hay Extrinsic allergic alveolitis is caused by hypersensitivity to a variety of inhaled organic dusts; forking mouldy hay (farmer’s lung) is the most common cause.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A shipbuilding yard worker presents with breathlessness. A CT chest scan is ordered, and a diagnosis of asbestos-induced lung damage is made. He is distraught with the diagnosis and wants to know if he is eligible for industrial injury benefits. Which of the following findings would allow him to pursue a claim?
answer_text: All of the above Prolonged inhalation of asbestos fibres can cause various serious conditions including pleural plaques, asbestosis, mesothelioma, and diffuse pleural thickening, each of which may support an industrial injury claim.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 35-year-old man who has recently been treated for Hodgkin lymphoma presents to you with a nonproductive cough. His CXR shows shadowing in one of the upper zones. His oxygen saturation is 95% on air. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Radiation pneumonitis Radiation pneumonitis is a common complication after radiotherapy, presenting with localized lung shadowing.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 56-year-old female is seen in the respiratory clinic with a 1-year history of breathlessness. Physical examination shows tachypnoea, widespread crackles and finger clubbing. Spirometry shows a low vital capacity and total lung capacity associated with a relatively well-preserved peak flow rate. Arterial blood gases reveal hypoxaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Pulmonary fibrosis Pulmonary fibrosis is associated with finger clubbing, hypoxaemia and a restrictive pattern on lung function tests.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 65-year-old retired rock miner sees his GP with worsening breathlessness, decreased exercise tolerance, dry cough and weight loss. He reports no past medical history. On examination he appears slightly tachypnoeic at rest. Fine inspiratory crackles are heard in the upper zones. Subsequent chest radiograph reveals multiple round opacities in the upper lobes with calcified hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Silicosis Silicosis is caused by inhalation of silica dust, with characteristic upper lobe involvement and calcified hilar lymphadenopathy in individuals such as rock miners.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 60-year-old nonsmoker presents to his GP with worsening breathlessness for several months, mainly on exertion. He has also developed a nonproductive cough and nonpainful deformities of his fingernails. He worked in the building industry for 30 years before his retirement this year. On examination, there are bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles and evidence of finger clubbing. A subsequent plain chest radiograph shows evidence of lower lobe fibrotic changes. What is the most likely cause in this patient’s condition?
answer_text: Asbestosis Asbestosis, a type of pneumoconiosis due to asbestos exposure, typically presents after a latent period with exertional dyspnoea, a nonproductive cough, and fibrotic changes on imaging.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 34-year-old black female presents to your office with symptoms of cough, dyspnea, and fatigue. Physical examination shows cervical adenopathy and hepatomegaly. Spleen tip is palpable. Her chest radiograph is shown below. Which of the following is the best approach in establishing a diagnosis?
answer_text: Bronchoscopy and transbronchial lung biopsy Symmetric hilar LAD + respiratory symptoms → sarcoidosis; diagnose via bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy; ACE supportive only.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the respiratory clinic with worsening shortness of breath. He is otherwise well and is a retired dockyard worker. He is a lifelong non-smoker. On examination he has fine crackles at both lung bases. A chest X-ray shows fine reticulonodular shadowing at both lung bases and several pleural plaques. He undergoes pulmonary function testing. Which of these pulmonary function tests fits with the likely diagnosis?
options: Transfer factor for CO (TLCO) 45% of predicted value
Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) 60%
answer_text: Transfer factor for CO (TLCO) 45% of predicted value Asbestosis → reduced TLCO from fibrosis; TLCO = KCO×VA; restrictive disease lowers VA and KCO; neuromuscular restriction lowers VA with ↑KCO and normal TLCO.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 67-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea. These symptoms have been getting progressively worse over the past nine months and are associated with a dry cough. He gave up smoking 20 cigarettes/ day around 30 years ago. On examination his oxygen saturations are 97% on room air, re spiratory rate is 14/min and there are some fine bibasal crackles. Finger clubbing is noted. Investigations show the following: B-type natriuretic peptide 88 pg/ml (< 100pg/ml). ECG: sinus rhythm, 72/min. Spirometry: FEV1 1.57 L (50% of predicted); FVC 1.63 L (39% of predicted); FEV1/FVC 96%. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
answer_text: D Primary pulmonary hypertension Primary pulmonary hypertension: young women, exertional dyspnea → later syncope/chest pain; RV failure and sudden death common.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 62-year-old man is referred to the respiratory clinic with exertional shortness of breath. He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis and recurrent urinary tract infections and takes methotrexate, folic acid and nitrofurantoin as prophylaxis against infection. He is a pigeon fancier and has worked as a roofer for 40 years. On examination, chest auscultation reveals crackles at the lung apices. The jugular venous pulse is not raised and there is no peripheral oedema. A chest radiograph demonstrates reticular shadowing of the lung apices. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the probable cause?
answer_text: Parasternal heave A parasternal heave reflects right ventricular hypertrophy, commonly seen in cor pulmonale.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old man is referred to the chest clinic by his general practitioner (GP). He initially presented to the GP 6 weeks ago with shortness of breath and an associated dry cough. He was also feverish and complained of malaise. The GP tried several courses of antibiotics but these did not help. There was no haemoptysis. He is previously fit and well and has never smoked. He works as an accountant. On examination, you note some inspiratory crackles on chest examination but otherwise, the examination is normal. Blood tests that the GP previously did showed a leukocytosis and increased ESR and CRP. A chest x-ray shows patchy bilateral opacities. Some pulmonary function tests have also been arranged, which show an FEV1/ FVC ratio of 0.65 with a transfer factor of 67%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Cryptogenic organising pneumonia Subacute “pneumonia” not improving with antibiotics, reduced TLCO → cryptogenic organizing pneumonia favored over CAP, HP, cancer, or hemorrhage.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 39-year-old woman presents to the GP with a painful rash affecting both shins. Multiple raised erythematous nodules are noted bilaterally and the patient reports they have been present for 3 weeks and appear to be worsening. Of note, she also reports a persisting cough for the preceding 6 weeks and a chest x-ray reveals hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is most likely to be abnormal?
answer_text: Serum ACE level Erythema nodosum + cough → think sarcoidosis; check serum ACE (often raised); c-ANCA suggests GPA; dsDNA SLE; p-ANCA nonspecific.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department with bilateral ankle swelling and a rash on his shins. He has no past medical history. On examination, there is synovitis of the bilateral ankles and a few erythematous tender lumps on his anterior tibiae. A chest x-ray demonstrates bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Progressive disability and death despite treatment
Resolution with need for maintenance therapy
Resolution with treatment but without need for maintenance therapy
answer_text: Bosentan Bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, is used in primary pulmonary hypertension.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 34-year-old Afro-Caribbean man presents to his GP with a 4-week history of fever, joint pains, lymphadenopathy and a tender red rash on his legs. Bloods show mild inflammatory markers; chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate management?
answer_text: Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/ FVC ratio, normal MIP Pulmonary hypertension often shows normal lung volumes and normal inspiratory pressures.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 58-year-old man originally from India presents with progressive shortness of breath. History includes ankylosing spondylitis and atrial flutter for which he takes naproxen, amiodarone, and omeprazole. He previously worked in stone and coal mines. Examination reveals fine basal crepitations bilaterally. What is the most likely underlying cause?
answer_text: Amiodarone Amiodarone lung toxicity → lower-zone pulmonary fibrosis; several other causes give upper-zone disease.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 68-year-old male patient presents with a 6-month history of shortness of breath worse on exertion and a dry cough. Examination shows fine crackles at both lung bases. You suspect idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and organise investigations. Which of the following investigation findings would support a diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Reticular changes on CT imaging that is worse at the bases
Extensive ground glass opacities on CT imaging
answer_text: Reticular changes on CT imaging that is worse at the bases IPF HRCT: basal-predominant honeycombing, reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, architectural distortion; restrictive spirometry with low TLCO.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: Which one of the following is responsible for farmer’s lung?
answer_text: Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula Farmer’s lung = EAA from Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula spores; type III ± IV hypersensitivity; other EAA: bird fancier’s, malt worker’s.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 62-year-old ceramics worker comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. He has suffered from progressively increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough over the past year, yet has failed to respond to salbutamol and low-dose beclomethasone inhalers prescribed by his GP. He smokes five cigarettes per day, but has no other significant past medical history. His BP is 149/89 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. O₂ saturation on air is 92% and there are coarse end expiratory crackles and scattered wheeze on auscultation. Spirometry shows a mixed obstructive/restrictive picture, and chest X-ray shows evidence of mediastinal lymph node calcification. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: D Silicosis Ceramics worker with silica exposure → silicosis causing mixed defect unresponsive to asthma therapy; no proven steroid benefit; prevention and O₂ support only.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old man who has a 30 pack-year smoking history comes to clinic with worsening shortness of breath over the last 6 months. He works as a baker and keeps racing pigeons. On examination, he is clubbed, has saturations of 91% on air and has widespread fine inspiratory crepitations. His chest X-ray shows reticulonodular shadowing and computed tomography (CT) confirms reticulation, mainly subpleural, and some honeycombing. What is the diagnosis?
answer_text: Mesothelioma His occupational exposure and chronic symptoms are most consistent with mesothelioma.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of dyspnoea on exertion and a non-productive cough. On examination, there is clubbing and crepitations are heard at the lung bases. There is no wheeze on lung auscultation. Lung function tests show a reduced vital capacity and an increased ratio of the forced expiratory volume in 1 second to the forced vital capacity (increased FEV1/FVC). What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: D Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, restrictive pattern → IPF/CFA; middle-aged male predominance; progressive and often fatal.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 72-year-old retired insulation fitter visits his General Practitioner for breathlessness. He has been suffering from increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough for the last four months. He is an ex-smoker of 25 pack years. He is concerned as one of his ex-colleagues is recently diagnosed with lung cancer. On examination, there is evidence of bilateral inspiratory crackles and clubbing. Chest X-ray reveals pleural plaques and reticular shadowing at both bases. His spirometry results are as follows: | Parameter | Percent predicted | | FEV1 | 65% | | FVC | 62% | | FEV1/FVC | 74 | What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: A Asbestosis Restrictive spirometry with exposure history → pulmonary asbestosis.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 20-A 30-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner for breathlessness and dry cough. She is an immigrant from Nigeria and has recently moved to the United Kingdom for work. She has history of type II diabetes mellitus which is well controlled. She denies smoking or using any illicit drugs. She denies any exposure to pets or birds. Her ophthalmological examination shows left anterior uveitis and slit-lamp examination confirms this. Serum ACE levels are normal and ANCA is negative. Her chest X-ray showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: E Sarcoidosis Acute sarcoidosis: pulmonary symptoms common; uveitis possible; hypercalcemia in ~10%.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 23-A 55-year-old patient with systemic sclerosis has been referred for breathlessness and a dry cough. On examination, fine crackles are heard at the lung bases. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
answer_text: CT pulmonary angiogram High clinical suspicion of pulmonary embolism warrants CT pulmonary angiography.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 29-A 67-year-old retired boilermaker is referred to the Respiratory Clinic complaining of shortness of breath. He also has a dry cough and weight loss. Examination shows inspiratory crackles to the mid-zones on both sides and clubbing. Which single investigation would be most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?
answer_text: C High-resolution computed tomography Suspected asbestos disease → HRCT best for pleural plaques and fibrosis.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 47-year-old woman presents with a chronic cough, weight loss, malaise and shortness of breath… General respiratory and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations show low albumin. A chest X-ray shows a right upper-lobe tumour with hilar extension… bronchoscopy performed but no biopsies were obtained (washings negative so far).
answer_text: C Methotrexate pneumonitis Restrictive pattern with bibasal crackles in context given → interstitial lung disease; corticosteroids may help.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 70-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis complains of progressive breathlessness… on examination there are inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields. Investigations show mildly reduced haemoglobin and elevated creatinine.
answer_text: C Methotrexate pneumonitis —

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 48-A 65-year-old man presents with a history of proximal muscle weakness and breathlessness. Investigations include an elevated CK of 890 U/L and an ESR of 75 mm/1st hour. What of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his interstitial lung disease?
answer_text: C Polymyositis Polymyositis/dermatomyositis can cause ILD; associated malignancy (lung/ ovary/breast/stomach) in 5–8%.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: 40-year-old woman develops sudden-onset dyspnoea at rest following hip replacement surgery. On examination she is tachycardic and her electrocardiogram (ECG) shows right axis deviation.
answer_text: Pulmonary embolism

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: A 35-year-old businessman returns from a trip abroad and collapses at the airport with haemoptysis and pleuritic chest pain. He has a sinus tachycardia and his ECG shows right axis deviation.
answer_text: Pulmonary embolism The clinical picture is suggestive of pulmonary embolism.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: The presence of distended neck veins and bilateral leg edema in a COPD patient is most suggestive of:
answer_text: Age Age is not considered an independent prognostic factor in CA lung as per note.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: On precordial examination in a patient with cor pulmonale, which finding is most likely?
answer_text: E Recurrent small pulmonary embolisms Pulmonary HTN from capillary bed loss; recurrent PEs cause precapillary arteriolar remodeling.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 26 year old woman with a diagnosis of primary pulmonary hypertension is evaluated for therapy. Which of the following therapies may be indicated?
answer_text: Bosentan Bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, is used in primary pulmonary hypertension.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 24 year old woman presents with worsening breathlessness and palpitations. Examination shows elevated JVP and a paucity of peripheral vasculature on CXR. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Dysfunctional breathing studies and Nijmegen questionnaire
answer_text: Transthoracic echocardiography Echocardiography is indicated to evaluate for pulmonary hypertension or cardiac causes.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 23 year old woman diagnosed with primary pulmonary hypertension is evaluated for therapy. Which of the following therapies may be indicated?
answer_text: CT chest, abdomen, pelvis The mediastinal widening and pleural effusion suggest a lympho matous process; CT is required for further evaluation and tissue sampling.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Which of the following pulmonary function test results is consistent with Familial pulmonary hypertension?
options: Increased TLC, decreased vital capacity, de creased FEV1/FVC ratio
Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/ FVC ratio, decreased MIP
Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
answer_text: PET scan In a nodule >8 mm in an at-risk patient, PET scan is indicated to assess metabolic activity.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 47-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension and right heart failure is referred for transplant. Which is true?
options: iPAH patients have worse 5-year survival than all others.
Her own RV function will recover after lung transplant.
She is at high risk of recurrent PAH post-transplant.
answer_text: Her own right ventricular function will recover after lung transplantation Lung transplantation can result in significant recovery of RV function by reducing pulmonary vascular resistance.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with SOB and chest pain. She comments that she has recently travelled to Australia. An electrocardiogram demonstrates evidence of right heart strain. You suspect a pulmonary embolus. Which investigation is most likely to lead to a diagnosis?
answer_text: CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) CTPA has the best diagnostic accuracy for pulmonary embolism; if contraindicated, a V/Q scan may be considered.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 40-year-old woman has had increasing fatigue and shortness of breath for years. Chest x-ray shows right ventricular hypertrophy and enlargement of the central pulmonary arteries. Pulmonary embolus is ruled out by spiral CT scan. Other causes of pulmonary hypertension have also been ruled out. Right heart catheterization reveals a pulmonary artery pressure of 75/30 mm Hg. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of the patient?
options: Acute drug testing with short-acting pulmonary vasodilators
answer_text: Acute drug testing with short-acting pulmonary vasodilators Confirmed PAH → acute vasoreactivity testing; CCBs if responsive; otherwise prostacyclin, PDE-5i, ERA; transplant for refractory advanced disease.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 35-year-old female complains of slowly progressive dyspnea. Her past history is nega tive, and there is no cough, sputum production, pleuritic chest pain, or thrombophlebitis. She has taken appetite suppressants at different times. Physical examination reveals jugular venous distention, a palpable right ventricular lift, and a loud P2 heart sound. Chest x-ray shows clear lung fields. Oxygen saturation is 94%. ECG shows right axis deviation. A perfusion lung scan is normal, with no segmental deficits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Primary pulmonary hypertension Young woman with appetite suppressant use, dyspnea, normal perfusion scan → primary PAH; exclude CTEPH; echo shows RV pressure overload; O₂ noncorrective shunt unlikely.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 19-A 30-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath. This began insidiously over several months. She has no cough and no chest pain. Spirometry shows a restrictive pattern. Arterial blood gases reveal hypoxia and hypercapnia; a lung perfusion scan is normal. Right heart catheterisation reveals that right-sided pressures are markedly raised. Which diagnosis best fits with this clinical picture?
answer_text: E Whispering pectoriloguy Whispering pectoriloquy → consolidation from tumor and retained secretions; likely bronchial carcinoma → get endobronchial biopsy.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 21-A 50-year-old woman patient presents with increasing dyspnoea. She has peripheral oedema and clinical evidence of right-sided heart failure without signs of left ventricular failure. What is the most likely cause for the cor pulmonale?
answer_text: Recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis Recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis causes hoarseness rather than dyspnea.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A 73-year-old heavy smoker man with bronchial carcinoma developed nausea, vomiting, irritability and confusion. Investigations revealed Hb 9.8 g/dl, serum Na+ 104 mEq/L (normal 135–145 mEq/L). Which of the following is the most probable cause?
answer_text: SIADH Small cell lung cancer commonly causes paraneoplastic SIADH leading to severe hyponatremia.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A 73-year-old heavy smoker man with bronchial carcinoma consults a physician because of progressive confusion and lethargy. Blood tests reveal serum Na+ 104 mEq/L, and chest imaging shows a central lung mass. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is most likely responsible?
answer_text: SIADH Severe hyponatremia in a heavy smoker with a central tumor is typically caused by SIADH from small cell lung cancer.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: the following affect prognosis of CA lung except
options: Type of cell (small cell worse than non small cell)
answer_text: Nebulised tobramycin is an effective treatment in chronic colonisation Chronic colonisation with Pseudomonas is best managed with nebulised tobramycin.

heading: Previous Respiratory
stem: Causes of dyspnoea in bronchial carcinoma may be the following EXCEPT:
answer_text: E Whispering pectoriloguy Whispering pectoriloquy → consolidation from tumor; bronchial carcinoma likely → endobronchial biopsy.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 46 year old woman has a recent diagnosis of adenocarcinoma of the lung made at bronchoscopy 1 week ago. She presents to the emergency department acutely short of breath with a non-productive cough. She has an ache in the centre of her chest that is made worse by breathing in. She is apyrexial. Oxygen saturations are 91% on 40% oxygen. Respiratory rate is 30 breaths/min. Blood pressure (BP) is 100/65 mmHg and pulse is 110 beats/min. Examination reveals decreased expansion of the right side with dullness to percussion throughout the right side. Her trachea is deviated to the right and the apex beat is not palpable. Breath sounds are reduced on the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Collapse of the right lung Examination findings indicate lung collapse with mediastinal shift due to a central obstructing lesion (likely a tumour).

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 52 year old man presents with 4 days of haemoptysis. Over the last 2 months he has lost weight without experiencing night sweats. He has smoked 30 cigarettes per day for 40 years and worked in construction. He thinks it is likely that he encountered asbestos at work but cannot recall any specific exposure. He returned home from holiday in Guyana 1 week ago. What is most likely to cause the CXR findings shown below.
answer_text: Bronchial carcinoma A central cavitating mass with associated nodules in a heavy smoker is most consistent with bronchial carcinoma.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 26 year old woman presents with 24 hours of central chest pain and progressive shortness of breath over a month. Examination reveals pulse 105 beats/min, BP 105/65 mmHg, oxygen saturations 96% on room air, apyrexial, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Chest clear; heart sounds dual, no murmurs. ECG: sinus tachycardia; no other abnormalities. Blood tests: haemoglobin 110 g/L, WCC 9 × 10^9/L, platelets 340 × 10^9/L, urea and electrolytes normal, CRP 67 mg/L. Given the CXR below, what should the next test be?
answer_text: Stop daptomycin and give prednisolone The clinical picture is consistent with daptomycin-induced eosinophilic pneumonia, requiring cessation of the drug and steroids.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 63 year old woman had a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) when she presented with left-sided pleuritic chest pain. There was no pulmonary thromboembolism but a small pulmonary nodule at the apex of the right lung was noted. The patient recovered spontaneously over 24 hours and is otherwise asymptomatic with a smoking history of 10 cigarettes per day for 40 years. What is the best next step?
answer_text: Nitrofurantoin lung disease Chronic nitrofurantoin use can lead to a pneumonitis mimicking interstitial lung disease.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 63 year old woman had a pulmonary nodule identified incidentally during a CTPA examination. She has a 20 pack-year smoking history but no past medical history and is asymptomatic with performance status 0. Pulmonary function testing is normal. A PET scan is performed and shows FDG avidity in the right upper lobe nodule. What should be the next step?
answer_text: Right upper lobectomy An early-stage FDG-avid nodule in a fit patient should be resected surgically.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 51 year old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She is a non-smoker with no significant past medical history. She requires 40% oxygen to maintain saturations at 92%, is apyrexial, BP 101/62 mmHg, pulse 112 beats/min, respiration rate 30 breaths/min. What is shown on the CXR?
answer_text: Right-sided lung collapse The CXR demonstrates complete right lung collapse with mediastinal shift, typical of a central obstructing lesion.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 54 year old woman attends the rapid-access lung cancer clinic with haemoptysis and an abnormal CXR. CT confirms a large cavitating right upper lobe mass and bronchoscopic biopsy confirms squamous lung cancer. The PET scan below was arranged. What does the CT- PET scan show?
options: Uptake confined to the right upper lobe lesion
Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion and a spinal metastasis
Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion and indeterminate uptake in pulmonary vessels
Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion and right hilar lymph node
Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion, a spinal metastasis and a sternal metastasis
answer_text: Uptake in the right upper lobe lesion and right hilar lymph node The PET scan demonstrates FDG uptake in the primary lesion and ipsilateral hilar node, upstaging the disease.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 59 year old smoker presents with a new cough. CT reveals a 4-cm peripheral tumour in the left lower lobe with an ipsilateral enlarged hilar lymph node. Due to emphysema, CT-guided biopsy is high risk. PET shows high FDG avidity in the tumour and indeterminate hilar uptake. What should be the next investigation?
answer_text: Endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EBUS-FNA) EBUS-FNA is preferred for sampling hilar nodes with lower pneumothorax risk in compromised lungs.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: An 84 year old man with a 3-month history of nagging left chest ache, worst in the axilla with radiation to the spine, and a history of pipe-smoking presents. Examination shows dullness from left lung base to mid-zone with erythema ab igne. Which is the most likely cause of his chest pain?
answer_text: Mycetoma A mycetoma developing in an old tuberculous cavity is the most common cause of haemoptysis in this setting.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 67 year old man undergoing CT colonogram is found to have a 6-mm nodule in the right lower lobe. Which factor increases the risk of malignancy in pulmonary nodules?
answer_text: Upper lobe distribution Nodules in the upper lobes are more suspicious for malignancy.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 65 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis undergoes CT for ILD evaluation which shows mild basal interlobular septal thickening and a 1.5 cm speculated right upper lobe nodule. What is true regarding PET scanning for pulmonary nodules?
options: It is not useful in nodules < 1 cm in diameter
It offers no more information than a standard CT
