answer_text: It is not useful in nodules < 1 cm in diameter PET is limited in small nodules and cannot replace histological diagnosis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 63 year old female non-smoker with a 5-cm lesion in the right mid-zone undergoes bronchoscopy with tumour biopsy. Which is the most common histological type of lung cancer?
answer_text: Adenocarcinoma Adenocarcinoma is now the most common form of lung cancer.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 73 year old woman with metastatic non- small cell lung cancer develops increasingly painful wrists. What is the most likely cause?
answer_text: Nifedipine High-altitude pulmonary edema → descend, give oxygen; nifedipine helpful; dexamethasone/acetazolamide/PDE-5 inhibitors are alternatives.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 56 year old smoker with a new cough has CT showing a 4-cm left lung peripheral mass with an ipsilateral hilar lymph node and a cytology-positive pleural effusion. What is the correct staging?
answer_text: IV A malignant pleural effusion automatically classifies the lung cancer as stage IV.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 36 year old non-smoker with isolated haemoptysis and a CT showing left upper lobe collapse with a vascular tumour at the LUL orifice. What is the most likely tumour type?
answer_text: Carcinoid A young non-smoker with localized haemoptysis and a vascular endobronchial mass is most consistent with a bronchial carcinoid.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 64 year old woman with breast cancer metastatic to liver, lungs and bone develops increasing breathlessness despite antibiotics. CT shows diffuse interstitial thickening radiating from the hila. What is the likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Lymphangitis carcinomatosa The CT pattern in a cancer patient with progressive dyspnoea is most consistent with lymphangitic carcinomatosis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 28 year old man with a large anterior mediastinal mass with cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy is evaluated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Lymphoma The clinical and imaging findings are most consistent with lymphoma.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 72 year old man with a history of benign asbestos pleurisy presents with a right-sided pleural effusion, pleural plaques and mediastinal pleural thickening. What is the most likely reason for his presentation?
answer_text: Mesothelioma The clinical and imaging findings in an asbestos-exposed patient with an effusion and thickening are most concerning for mesothelioma.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 72 year old man with a smoking history and occupational exposure (‘monkey dung’) has a 5-cm peripheral left lung mass, left hilar lymphadenopathy, and an indeterminate liver lesion. What should be the next diagnostic test?
answer_text: Supraclavicular lymph node biopsy Peripheral lymph node biopsy is the least invasive method to obtain tissue in suspected lung cancer.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 55 year old woman with left apical lung cancer and lymph node involvement undergoes radiotherapy after mediastinoscopy. She develops hoarseness but bronchoscopy reveals no vocal cord paralysis. What is the likely cause?
options: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement by the tumour
answer_text: Endotracheal intubation during mediastinoscopy The hoarseness is most likely due to trauma from intubation rather than tumour involvement.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Mrs. Wittstine has scleroderma and a suspicious 3 cm FDG-avid lesion on PET/CT. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The findings on PET/CT make infection very likely.
The findings on PET/CT make infection very unlikely.
The findings on PET/CT make malignancy very likely.
The findings on PET/CT make malignancy very unlikely.
answer_text: Additional diagnostic studies are indicated. FDG uptake can be seen in both infection and malignancy; further studies are required.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 75-year-old man with asbestos exposure and a pleural effusion suspicious for mesothelioma. Which statement is true?
options: Cigarette smoking increases the likelihood of developing the condition.
Death in this disease is usually due to diffuse metastases.
Exposure can be brief (1-2 yrs), latency may be up to 40 yrs.
Repeated pleural fluid cytology usually leads to a definitive diagnosis.
Combination surgical resection and chemo significantly improves survival.
answer_text: Exposure can be as brief as 1–2 years, and latency to disease can be 40 years or more. Mesothelioma can occur after minimal exposure with a long latency period.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 64-year-old man with facial swelling, distended neck veins, suspect SVC syndrome. Which CT finding is most likely?
options: A central mass obstructing right main bronchus
An apical mass invading the chest wall
Enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes compressing the SVC
answer_text: Enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes causing obstruction of the superior vena cava SVC syndrome is most commonly due to extrinsic compression from mediastinal lymphadenopathy, often from malignancy.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: In the scenario of SVC syndrome, initial therapy includes all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Elevation of the head of the bed
answer_text: Administration of furosemide as needed to achieve diuresis Diuresis is not a standard initial treatment for SVC syndrome.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 58-year-old with metastatic breast cancer has acute paraplegia from spinal cord compression. First step?
answer_text: Administration of dexamethasone 10 mg IV Immediate IV steroids are the first step in managing spinal cord compression.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with breathlessness and haemoptysis. She is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lung. She has been a smoker for as long as she can remember. She has lived in central London for almost 30 years now and she worked in a shipbuilding yard for most of her working life. Both her father and mother died of lung cancer. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her cancer?
answer_text: Smoking Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is closely correlated with a history of tobacco smoking, the most common cause of lung cancer.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A middle-aged man is diagnosed with lung cancer. He worked in a shipbuilding yard for most of his life. He is distraught with the diagnosis as he says he has never smoked in his life. Which of the following types of lung cancer is he most likely to suffer from?
answer_text: Adenocarcinoma Adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer in lifelong nonsmokers, accounting for 40% of all lung cancers.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 53-year-old woman is diagnosed with lung cancer. Her main symptoms on presentation included breathlessness and haemoptysis. She complained of stretch marks on her abdomen and that her skin bruised easily. On examination you note purple abdominal striae. Which of the following types of lung cancer is she most likely to suffer from?
answer_text: Small cell Small cell carcinoma, due to its neuroendocrine nature, can produce ectopic hormones leading to Cushing syndrome features such as purple abdominal striae.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 63-year-old man is diagnosed with lung cancer. Which of the following extrapulmonary manifestations is he most likely to suffer from?
answer_text: Clubbing Clubbing is the most common extrapulmonary feature in lung cancer, particularly in nonsmall cell lung cancer.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 66-year-old woman with history of weight loss presents to the respiratory clinic with an 8-week history of nonproductive cough and chronic clearing of throat. She has a 52-pack year smoking history and quit 25 years ago. She was subsequently diagnosed with carcinoma of the lung. Which of the following is NOT a complication of carcinoma of the lung?
answer_text: Hypocalcaemia Squamous cell carcinomas are associated with hypercalcaemia, not hypocalcaemia. SCLC is linked to SIADH (hyponatraemia) and adenocarcinomas with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 65-year-old factory worker presents with a dry cough, right-sided chest pain and finger clubbing. He has lost 4 kg in weight in the last 2 weeks. He has a 30-year smoking history. On examination the right lung is dull to percussion with reduced chest expansion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) Small cell lung cancer, strongly associated with smoking and central lung lesions, is suggested by the presentation.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 50-year-old heavy smoker of 30 pack years presents to his GP with weight loss of 8 kg over 4 months and a chronic cough with two episodes of haemoptysis. He denies any history of fever. Chest radiograph shows a rounded lesion measuring 5 cm in diameter in the right upper lobe. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Bronchial carcinoma The presence of a large, rounded lesion in a heavy smoker is most consistent with bronchial carcinoma, likely squamous cell carcinoma.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 42-year-old male patient presented with a 5-month history of facial swelling and a tumoral mass in the right maxilla with infiltration into the skin. Recently, he had been suffering from difficulty in breathing and a dry cough. Face and sinus computerised tomography (CT) illustrated a right maxillary lesion. Maxilla surgery was performed without orbital removal and a grade III chondrosarcoma was diagnosed, with infiltration into bone, the anterior wall of the maxillary sinus and orbital floor. A subsequent chest x-ray was performed given his chest symptoms suggesting the appearance of lung metastases. What feature of lung metastases is characteristic for this tumour?
answer_text: Calcification Calcified lung mets suggest osteosarcoma/chondrosarcoma or papillary thyroid; cavitation common in squamous cell; adenocarcinoma may cause consolidation.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 66-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is referred by his GP to the Rapid Access Chest Clinic. He was recently treated with several courses of antibiotics and steroids for an exacerbation of COPD which failed to completely resolve. A chest x-ray was reported as follows: There is a suspicious 3cm mass in the right hilum. Background changes of COPD. Urgent referral to the chest clinic is advised. Report faxed to GP. Recent blood tests are also reviewed: Hb 14.2 g/dl; Platelets 323 * 10^9/l; WBC 9.1 * 10^9/l; Na+ 128 mmol/l; K+ 3.9 mmol/l; Urea 6.4 mmol/l; Creatinine 99 μmol/l. On examination there is no evidence of clubbing. Examination of chest demonstrates a fixed monophonic wheeze in the right lung. What is the most likely underlying cause?
answer_text: Small cell lung cancer Hyponatremia in lung cancer suggests SIADH → most associated with small-cell carcinoma.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 74-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of increased shortness of breath. He has smoked 40 cigarettes per day for the past 30 years. Medications include diclofenac and paracetamol for joint pain. He comes to the clinic with a chest X-ray from his GP which shows a spiculated left hilar mass. What would the classical respiratory findings over the abnormal area be?
answer_text: Pulmonary embolism In the postoperative setting, leg swelling and acute respiratory distress with supporting ECG changes strongly suggest a pulmonary embolism.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 74-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of increased shortness of breath. He has smoked 40 cigarettes per day for the past 30 years. Medications include diclofenac and paracetamol for joint pain. He comes to the clinic with a chest X-ray from his GP which shows a spiculated left hilar mass. What would the classical respiratory findings over the abnormal area be?
answer_text: Ethambutol Ethambutol toxicity can cause optic neuritis; patients should report visual changes.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 18-You are referred a 68-year-old man who smokes 40 cigarettes per day and has a proven diagnosis of bronchial carcinoma. You are considering radical radiotherapy in this man. Which of the following is the most significant contra indication to radical radiotherapy?
answer_text: C Malignant pleural effusion Malignant pleural effusion predicts poor outcome with radical radiotherapy.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 52-A 64-year-old mechanic and lifelong smoker noticed haemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows left upper-lobe collapse and predominantly left-sided hilar enlargement and mediastinal widening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: A Bronchial carcinoma Central endobronchial tumor → lobar collapse with ipsilateral hilar enlargement; proceed to bronchoscopy and/or CT. Respiratory Pharmacology

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A woman with history of bronchial carcinoma 2 months ago developed cough and dyspnea. Which of the following is the best treatment of choice for her persistent obstructive symptoms?
answer_text: Tiotropium Tiotropium, a long-acting anticholinergic, is often first-line for persistent COPD symptoms.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A 28 year old man of Chinese origin on treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis calls 2 weeks into therapy with painful eyes. What is the likely cause?
options: Short-acting beta-agonists (SABA) A. Drug resistance to ethambutol and pyrazinamide B. Ethambutol C. Immune reconstitution D. Intercurrent viral infection E. Non-tuberculous Mycobacterium
answer_text: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan or CT pulmonary angiogram A CT pulmonary angiogram (or V/Q scan) is used to confirm the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism when chest X-ray is unrevealing.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 24 year old man with cystic fibrosis inquires about ivacaftor. Ivacaftor corrects the function of which CFTR defect?
answer_text: G551D Ivacaftor is effective in patients with the G551D mutation.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 56 year old non-smoking man with metastatic adenocarcinoma (EGFR positive) of the left lung is evaluated. What is the treatment of choice?
answer_text: Erlotinib Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. er lotinib) are indicated in EGFR mutation-positive adenocarcinoma.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 24 year old CF patient fails to recover from an exacerbation. Sputum cultures now isolate Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which statement is true regarding P. aeruginosa in CF? E. Radiotherapy
answer_text: Montelukast LTRAs can precipitate eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg– Strauss).

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 61 year old woman on IV daptomycin for staphylococcal discitis, previously improving, spikes a fever after 2 weeks with rising WCC (including eosinophilia) and new bilateral upper zone consolidation on CXR. What should be the treatment?
answer_text: High-resolution CT scan of the chest High-resolution CT scanning is the investigation of choice to visualize bronchial dilatation characteristic of bronchiectasis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 70 year old woman with a 6-week history of cough, low-grade fever, and malaise, on nitrofurantoin for UTIs, has bi-basal infiltrates on CXR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Recurrent respiratory infections and hemoptysis Patients with bronchiectasis are prone to recurrent infections and may also develop significant hemoptysis.

heading: Formative MCQ’s
stem: A 58-year-old woman with a 28-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with progressive shortness of breath. Which pulmonary complication is most likely?
answer_text: All of the above Rheumatoid arthritis can cause pleural disease, ILD, nodules, and airway involvement.

heading: End Blocks 2025
stem: Dyspnea that associate with wheezing can be caused by the following EXCEPT;
answer_text: Pneumothorax. Pneumothorax typically does not cause wheezing.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 70-year-old postoperative male (72 hours after hip replacement) presents with left leg swelling, shortness of breath, hypotension, and an oxygen saturation of 78%. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a partial right bundle branch block. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
answer_text: If the Gram stain reveals numerous gram-positive diplococci, numerous white blood cells, and few epithelial cells, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most likely pathogen. CAP in >35 with rigors, pleuritic pain, lobar consolidation → pneumococcal pneumonia; diagnose via sputum GPC diplococci; empiric ceftriaxone or resp FQ (penicillin resistance common).

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: If the chest X-ray is normal, which investigation is most appropriate to support the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism?
options: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan or CT pulmonary angiogram
answer_text: Nausea Varenicline most common adverse effect = nausea; vivid dreams and insomnia occur but less frequent; constipation and DILE not typical.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: What is the immediate treatment for a hemodynamically unstable patient with suspected pulmonary embolism?
answer_text: Thrombolytic therapy In unstable patients with pulmonary embolism, prompt thrombolytic therapy is indicated.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: A 48-year-old man presents with an 8-month history of productive cough with yellowish sputum, occasional hemoptysis, exertional dyspnea, and finger clubbing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Bronchiectasis The chronic productive cough with clubbing and hemoptysis strongly suggests bronchiectasis.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which investigation is considered the gold standard for confirming a diagnosis of bronchiectasis?
options: High-resolution CT scan of the chest
answer_text: C Prednisolone Viral-triggered asthma exacerbation → give prednisolone.

heading: Log book MCQ
stem: Which two complications are most important to monitor for in patients with bronchiectasis?
answer_text: C Erythromycin Mycoplasma pneumonia → no cell wall → β-lactams ineffective.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 75 year old woman with a 10-year history of daily non-productive cough, back pain from vertebral fracture, a large hiatus hernia and kyphosis on CXR. What is the most likely cause of her cough?
answer_text: Gastro-oesophageal reflux The hiatus hernia and kyphosis point to reflux as the likely cause.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 42 year old non-smoker woman presents with a 4-month history of breathlessness occurring only in the daytime following an upper respiratory tract infection with nasal blockage. Her D-dimer is positive but CTPA is normal. Spirometry is normal. What should be the next investigation?
options: Dysfunctional breathing studies and a Nijmegen questionnaire
Lung volume and gas transfer studies
answer_text: Dysfunctional breathing studies and a Nijmegen questionnaire The presentation is typical of dysfunctional breathing post-infection.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 64 year old woman with COPD presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after a 3-week holiday. O2 saturations are 84% on room air; exam shows decreased air entry and mild bipedal oedema; D-dimer is elevated. What is the most likely cause of her chest pain?
answer_text: Pulmonary thromboembolism The acute onset in a high-risk patient points to pulmonary embolism.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 45 year old non-smoking man with longstanding finger clubbing (noted since his teens, similar to his father) presents with a sprained wrist. What is the next step the family physician should take?
options: Check bloods (including LFTs, thyroid function tests and ESR)
Sweat test to exclude cystic fibrosis
answer_text: Reassurance The longstanding familial clubbing without other symptoms requires no further investigation.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A patient with known bronchiectasis and a long-standing right apical cavity now coughs up 50 mL of fresh red blood. The CXR shows partial filling of the cavity. What is the likely cause of his haemoptysis?
answer_text: Klebsiella pneumoniae Cavitating upper-lobe pneumonia in elderly diabetic/alcoholic → think Klebsiella; Pseudomonas = HAP/CF; Mycoplasma/Legionella give atypical patterns.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 32 year old cystic fibrosis patient presents with massive haemoptysis (250 mL of fresh red blood) but is haemodynamically stable. What is the most useful investigation?
answer_text: Bronchial artery angiography Angiography is most useful to localise the bleeding site in CF patients.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 57 year old woman with a 3-year history of chronic productive cough (with green sputum) and frequent brief antibiotic responses is investigated. What is the best investigation?
answer_text: High-resolution CT chest HRCT is the investigation of choice to assess for bronchiectasis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: Acute coryza is most commonly caused by which of the following?
answer_text: Rhinovirus Rhinovirus is the most common cause of the common cold.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 45 year old man with a history of spontaneous VTE and family history presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, and a swollen right calf after ACL reconstruction abroad and a recent long- haul flight. What should the next test be?

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 28 year old woman recovering from ACL repair in an above-knee cast experiences near-syncope on standing, with BP 80/45 mmHg and sinus tachycardia. CXR is clear, D-dimer is elevated, and she subsequently suffers a cardiac arrest. What should the immediate management include?
answer_text: Thrombolysis In the setting of a massive pulmonary embolism with cardiac arrest, immediate thrombolysis is indicated.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 45 year old woman presents with a seasonal cough in May that resolves by autumn, with nasal discharge and watering eyes. Examination and spirometry are normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Allergic rhinitis The seasonal nasal symptoms point to allergic rhinitis.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding breathing during sleep?
options: Abnormal ventilatory drive is present in obstructive sleep apnoea
Forty per cent of middle-aged women snore
Palatoglossus and genioglossus contract actively during expiration
answer_text: Hypoventilation accompanies normal sleep During sleep, overall muscle tone decreases leading to slight hypoventilation.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 55 year old man with excessive daytime sleepiness, an Epworth score of 18, and a BMI of 36 undergoes a sleep study. What is the likely result?
answer_text: 20 apnoea/hypopneas per hour An AHI of 20 is diagnostic for moderate obstructive sleep apnoea.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: A 72 year old man with a history of ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, and childhood polio presents with increasing breathlessness and nocturnal symptoms. His CXR is under-inspired and a sleep study shows significant hypoventilation with decompensated type II respiratory failure on ABG. What is the likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Post-polio syndrome His history of polio and current hypoventilation suggest post-polio respiratory muscle weakness.

heading: Davidson Respiratory
stem: Which of these associations between pathophysiological features and conditions is correct?
options: Eventration of diaphragm and foramen of Bochdalek
answer_text: Thoracic kyphoscoliosis and tuberculosis Thoracic kyphoscoliosis is classically associated with tuberculous sequelae.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: At what lung volume does the outward recoil of the chest wall equal the inward elastic recoil of the lung?
answer_text: Functional residual capacity FRC is where outward chest wall recoil balances inward lung recoil.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 65-year-old man has a low-pitched wheeze over the mid-chest and a flow-volume curve showing fixed obstruction. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
answer_text: Subglottic stenosis A fixed obstruction on the flow-volume loop (box-shaped) is consistent with subglottic stenosis.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 22-year-old pregnant woman presents with acute dyspnea and a high A-a gradient on arterial blood gas with a normal chest x-ray. What is the next best step in diagnosis and management?
options: Initiate therapy with amoxicillin for acute bronchitis
Perform a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram
Reassure the patient that dyspnea is normal
Treat with clonazepam for a panic attack
answer_text: Perform a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram Suspected pulmonary embolism with an elevated A-a gradient should be confirmed by imaging (CTPA).

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Which of the following pulmonary function test results is consistent with Myasthenia gravis?
options: Increased TLC, decreased vital capacity, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio
Decreased TLC, decreased VC, decreased RV, increased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/ FVC ratio, decreased MIP
Normal TLC, normal RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, normal MIP
answer_text: Decreased TLC, increased RV, normal FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased MIP Myasthenia gravis causes a neuromuscular restrictive pattern with decreased maximal inspiratory pressure and air trapping.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 36-year-old woman in a house fire remains obtunded with seizures, hypotension, and a bitter almond odor. Which test will yield the diagnosis?
answer_text: Red blood cell cyanide concentration The bitter almond odor and clinical picture suggest cyanide poisoning.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 28-year-old has recurrent sinus and lung infections, suspect CF. Which finding best confirms the diagnosis?
options: DNA analysis showing one F508del allele
answer_text: Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L A sweat chloride value above 60 mmol/L is diagnostic for cystic fibrosis.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 42-year-old man with progressive dyspnea, weight loss, milky bronchoalveolar lavage fluid with PAS-positive debris. Diagnosis?
answer_text: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis PAS-positive, proteinaceous material in alveoli is characteristic of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: For the patient with pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, what is the most appropriate treatment?
answer_text: Whole-lung lavage Whole-lung lavage is the mainstay of treatment for pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 52-year-old with obesity hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian). Which statement is true?
options: Gene PHOX2b is associated with this condition.
CPAP alone is always adequate therapy.
Intubation is mandatory for acute hypercapnia.
Coexistent OSA occurs in only 25% of cases.
Weight loss will lead to improvements in PaCO2 over time.
answer_text: Weight loss will lead to improvements in PaCO2 over time Sustained weight reduction improves obesity hypoventilation syndrome.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 52-year-old man with loud snoring, high BMI, likely obstructive sleep apnea. Next step?
answer_text: Home sleep study A validated home sleep study is a cost-effective initial diagnostic tool for OSA.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 48-year-old with OSA refuses CPAP. Which advice about untreated OSA is correct?
options: No significant effect on mortality risk
Minimal risk of motor vehicle accidents
answer_text: All of the above is good advice to give to the patient Untreated OSA is associated with increased cardiovascular risk, depression, and accidents; thus, all are important.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Which patient is most likely to have the Cheyne-Stokes breathing pattern shown?
options: A 6-year-old with enlarged tonsils and adenoids
A 48-year-old obese man with loud snoring
A 52-year-old menopausal woman with frequent awakenings
A 68-year-old with atrial fibrillation, EF 15%, JVP elevation, edema
answer_text: A 68-year-old with atrial fibrillation and ischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 15% Cheyne-Stokes respiration is commonly seen in advanced heart failure.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 48-year-old man has obstructive sleep apnea with an AHI of 42/hr. What is the most appropriate initial therapy?
answer_text: CPAP CPAP is the first-line treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 25-year-old with cystic fibrosis is referred for lung transplantation. The main impediment to long-term survival post-transplant is:
answer_text: Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome Chronic rejection in the form of bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome is the main barrier to long-term survival.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 42-year-old with hemorrhagic shock has a lactate of 4.8 mmol/L. Which factor is least important in oxygen delivery?
answer_text: PaO2 Oxygen content is more dependent on hemoglobin and saturation than on PaO2.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 67-year-old woman intubated with pneumonia and COPD. All are measures to prevent ICU complications EXCEPT:
answer_text: Aggressive blood glucose control Overly tight glucose control has not improved outcomes and may cause harm.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: All of the following statements regarding shock pathophysiology are true EXCEPT:
options: Hypotension inhibits the vasomotor center, reducing adrenergic output.
Metabolic derangements raise extracellular osmolarity, pulling fluid from cells.
Mitochondrial dysfunction leads to lactate accumulation.
Proinflammatory mediators contribute to organ failure.
Severe stress increases cortisol, promoting gluconeogenesis and lipolysis.
answer_text: Hypotension inhibits the vasomotor center, reducing adrenergic output and increasing vagal activity. In shock, hypotension triggers sympathetic activation, not inhibition.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A patient with a C2-3 spinal transection is in shock. Which hemodynamic profile is expected?
options: Low CO, high SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SVO2
Low CO, high SVR, high RA pressure, high PCWP, low SVO2
High CO, low SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, high SVO2
Low CO, normal SVR, high RA pressure, low PCWP, low SVO2
Low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SVR, low SVO2, low CO
answer_text: Decreased RA pressure, decreased PCWP, decreased SVR, decreased SVO2, decreased CO Neurogenic shock from high spinal transection is characterized by vasodilation and low filling pressures.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: All of the following statements about the epidemiology of sepsis are true EXCEPT:
options: Gram-positive bacteria are the most commonly isolated causative organisms.
In septic shock, blood cultures are positive in 40%-70%.
Most sepsis occurs in patients with significant comorbidities.
Respiratory infections are the most common cause of sepsis.
Incidence of severe sepsis is ~3 per 1000 and rising.
answer_text: Gram-positive bacteria are the most commonly isolated causative organisms in sepsis syndromes. Gram-negative organisms are often predominant; statement A is inaccurate.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 62-year-old has pneumonia, hypotension responsive to fluids, pH 7.46, PaCO2 32, PaO2
answer_text: Sepsis The patient meets criteria for sepsis with organ dysfunction that is fluid responsive.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Which classification?

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 68-year-old asplenic man in septic shock, no clear source, local cephalosporin-resistant S. pneumoniae >1%. Which empiric regimen?
answer_text: Cefotaxime plus vancomycin Asplenic patients are at high risk for resistant S. pneumoniae; vancomycin is added.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: All of the following therapies have been found ineffective in improving sepsis mortality after initial promise EXCEPT:
options: ACTH stimulation tests for steroid therapy
answer_text: Erythrocyte transfusions to maintain a hemoglobin level >7 g/dL A restrictive transfusion strategy is recommended; other modalities have failed to show mortality benefit.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 62-year-old with acute anterior MI in cardiogenic shock continues to decline. Best initial treatment for hypotension?
answer_text: Placement of an intra-aortic balloon pump IABP improves coronary perfusion and reduces afterload in cardiogenic shock.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 72-year-old with known EF 20% and shock. All are indicated EXCEPT:
answer_text: Morphine 2 mg IV Morphine may worsen outcomes in cardiogenic shock.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 52-year-old with acute severe mitral regurgitation post-MI. What would a PA catheter show?
options: Low RA pressure, normal wedge, high CO
Normal RA pressure, low wedge, high SVR
Elevated wedge with prominent v waves
Equalization of pressures in all chambers
Low CO, low wedge, high RA pressure
answer_text: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure with prominent v waves Acute MR produces large v waves on the PA catheter tracing.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: All of the following statements about sudden cardiac death (SCD) are true EXCEPT:
options: An individual can be classified as SCD if death occurs within 30 days after resuscitation.
About two-thirds of SCD patients had prior cardiac events.
Asystole is commonly encountered in SCD ar rests.
Parental history of SCD increases risk in offspring.
Higher incidence in African Americans vs. white population.
answer_text: An individual can be classified as having sudden cardiac death following a resuscitated arrest if death occurs during the subsequent hospitalization or within 30 days. SCD is typically defined as death within 1 hour if unresuscitated.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Which state correctly identifies a patient in a coma?
answer_text: Metabolic encephalopathy Coma is defined as a state of deep unresponsiveness, distinct from other conditions.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 74-year-old with a large subdural hematoma and uncal herniation. The cause of coma is:
options: Compression of the midbrain against the opposite tentorial edge
Compression of the opposite cerebral peduncle
Cerebellar tonsils displaced into foramen magnum
answer_text: Compression of the midbrain against the opposite tentorial edge Uncal herniation compresses the midbrain, leading to coma.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 44-year-old found comatose, flushed, 5 mm pupils, muscle spasms, rapid breathing. Most likely cause of coma?
answer_text: Drug intoxication The clinical presentation suggests an overdose with anticholinergic features.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: Intraparenchymal ICP monitoring is preferred over ventriculostomy in which patient?
options: A 35-year-old with fulminant hepatic failure INR 3.5
A 68-year-old with a large hemorrhagic stroke and midline shift
answer_text: A 35-year-old with fulminant hepatic failure admitted with coagulopathy In coagulopathic patients, intraparenchymal monitors are safer than ventriculostomy.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 56-year-old with subarachnoid hemorrhage has ICP 45 mmHg. Next management?
answer_text: Drain ventriculostomy to attain an ICP <20–25 mmHg CSF drainage via ventriculostomy is indicated to reduce ICP in SAH.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 67-year-old with sepsis in ICU for 3 weeks, now cannot wean from ventilator, minimal muscle strength. Most likely cause?
answer_text: Critical illness polyneuropathy Critical illness polyneuropathy is common in septic ICU patients, impairing weaning.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 56-year-old with SAH improves, then day 7 abrupt decline with no new blood on CT. Most likely cause?
answer_text: Vasospasm Delayed cerebral vasospasm is a well-known complication 3–14 days post-SAH.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: What treatment do you recommend now for SAH-induced vasospasm (Question VI-93)?
options: IV norepinephrine and possible balloon angioplasty
answer_text: Intravenous norepinephrine and consultation for percutaneous transluminal angioplasty Induced hypertension with angioplasty is indicated for SAH-induced vasospasm.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: A 21-year-old with ALL, WBC 156k, induction chemo. Which is NOT a complication of tumor lysis syndrome?
answer_text: Hypercalcemia TLS typically features hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.

heading: Harrison Respiratory
stem: All of the following are important in preventing tumor lysis syndrome EXCEPT:
answer_text: Prophylactic hemodialysis prior to initiating chemotherapy Prophylactic dialysis is not standard for preventing TLS.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: An overweight middle-aged man presents to the general practitioner (GP) after his wife complains about his loud snoring. He tends to drink large amounts of alcohol in the evenings before going to bed. Which of the following features is he most likely to complain of?
answer_text: Daytime sleepiness Excessive daytime sleepiness is the hallmark of obstructive sleep apnoea, which in this case is due to alcohol-induced decreased muscle tone and obesity.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: You see a 55-year-old female for the first time. She has a 2-year history of chronic daily cough; thick, malodorous sputum and occasional haemoptysis. She has been treated with antibiotics for recurrent respiratory infections, but is frustrated with her continued symptoms. She has never smoked. Her forced expiratory volume in 1 second:forced vital capacity (FEV1:FVC) ratio is 60% and a CT scan shows bronchial wall thickening and luminal dilatation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis is characterized by chronic productive cough with thick, malodorous sputum, recurrent infections and CT findings of bronchial wall thickening and dilatation.

heading: Crash Respiratory
stem: A 67-year-old obese man presents with loud chronic snoring and gasping episodes during sleep. His wife has witnessed episodes where it appears as if he has stopped breathing. He reports unrefreshing sleep, multiple awakenings from sleep and morning headaches. He has excessive daytime sleepiness, which is interfering with his daily activities. He has been treated for hypertension, gastro-oesophageal reflux and type 2 diabetes. For adults with obstructive sleep apnoea, which one of the following is the most effective treatment?
options: Weight reduction to achieve a body mass index <30 kg/m2
answer_text: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) CPAP is the most effective treatment for obstructive sleep apnoea in adults.

heading: Harrison
stem: In which of the following patients who present to an emergency department reporting acute dyspnea would a positive D-dimer result prompt additional testing for a pulmonary embolus?
options: A 24-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant
A 48-year-old man with no past medical history who presents with calf pain following prolonged air travel; alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient is normal
A 56-year-old woman undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer
A 62-year-old man who underwent hip replacement surgery 4 weeks previously
A 72-year-old man who had an acute myocar dial infarction 2 weeks ago
answer_text: A 48-year-old man with no past medical history who presents with calf pain following prolonged air travel; alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient is normal In this scenario, the D-dimer is less likely to be elevated due to other causes, making a positive result more significant in prompting further testing.

heading: Harrison
stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with acute onset of shortness of breath. She recently had been to visit her parents out of state and rode in a car for about 9 hours each way. Two days ago, she developed mild calf pain and swelling, but she thought that this was not unusual after having been sitting with her legs dependent for the recent trip. On arrival to the emergency department, she is noted to be tachypneic. Her vital signs are: blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, heart rate 114 bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 92% on room air, and weight 89 kg. The lungs are clear bilaterally. There is pain in the right calf with dorsiflexion of the foot, and the right leg is more swollen when compared to the left. An arterial blood gas measurement shows a pH of 7.52, PCO2 of 25 mmHg, and PO2 of 68 mmHg. Kidney and liver function are normal. A helical CT scan confirms a pulmonary embolus. All of the following agents can be used alone as initial therapy in this patient EXCEPT:
options: Unfractionated heparin IV adjusted to maintain activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) two to three times the upper limit of normal
Warfarin 7.5 mg orally once daily to maintain international normalized ratio at 2–3
answer_text: Warfarin 7.5 mg orally once daily to maintain international normalized ratio at 2–3 Warfarin alone is not appropriate for initial treatment of pulmonary embolism due to its delayed onset and risk of transient hypercoagulability.

heading: Harrison
stem: Which of the following statements regarding pulmonary embolism is true?
options: Airway resistance usually decreases in the setting of an acute pulmonary embolism.
Almost all patients with pulmonary embolism have evidence of deep vein thrombosis at the time.
Alveolar hyperventilation is a typical physiologic abnormality in the presence of pulmonary embolism.
Hypotension in the setting of acute pulmonary embolism is often due to acute left ventricular systolic dysfunction.
The size of the arterial-alveolar gradient is invariably correlated with the size of the pulmonary embolism.
answer_text: Alveolar hyperventilation is a typical physiologic abnormality in the presence of pulmonary embolism. Pulmonary embolism typically results in hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis.

heading: Harrison
stem: A 57-year-old man with a history of hypertension is admitted to the hospital with pulmonary embolism after having sudden onset of chest discomfort. His blood pressure is 132/62 mmHg, heart rate is 85 bpm, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Echocardiography reveals normal right heart size and function, and cardiac troponin I is undetectable. Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound reveals an extensive deep vein thrombus from the right femoral popliteal vein. The patient is started on low-molecular-weight heparin and concomitant warfarin. On rounds the following day, he asks if insertion of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter would be appropriate. What is the most appropriate answer?
options: “No, you would not benefit from an IVC filter at this point.”
“No, there are currently no indications for IVC filter placement in the setting of deep vein thrombus or pulmonary embolism.”
“We will need to go back to review your images and see how large your pulmonary embolus clot burden is before deciding whether an IVC filter is appropriate for you or not.”
“Yes, given the presence of residual lower extremity thrombus, we will schedule you for IVC filter insertion.”
“Yes, given your age and gender, we will schedule you for an IVC filter insertion.”
answer_text: No, you would not benefit from an IVC filter at this point. IVC filters are reserved for patients with contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent embolism despite therapy.

heading: Harrison
stem: Mrs. Tupulo is a 45-year-old woman with a history of morbid obesity (weight 140 kg), hypertension, and diabetes who has been in the hospital for 4 days after open surgical gastric bypass. On postoperative day 4, she experiences sudden breathlessness, tachycardia, hypoxia, and an overwhelming sense of impending doom. Urgent chest CT angiography reveals a saddle pulmonary embolism. Her blood pressure is 70/45 mmHg, and urine output is poor. After administration of IV normal saline and dobutamine, her blood pressure modestly improves. What is the next most appropriate step?
answer_text: Surgical pulmonary embolectomy In a massive PE with contraindications to thrombolysis post major surgery, surgical embolectomy is the next appropriate intervention. Respiratory Pharmacology

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 30-year-old quadriplegic male presents to the emergency room with fever, dyspnea, and a cough. He has a chronic indwelling Foley catheter. Recurrent urinary tract infections have been a problem for a number of years. He has been on therapy to suppress the urinary tract infections. On examination, mild wheezing is audible over both lungs. A diffuse erythematous rash is noted. The chest x-ray shows a diffuse alveolar infiltrate. The CBC reveals a WBC of 13,500, with 50% segmented cells, 30% lymphocytes, and 20% eosinophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sepsis with ARDS secondary to urinary tract infection
A drug reaction to one of his medications
answer_text: A drug reaction to one of his medications Nitrofurantoin toxicity → acute eosinophilic pneumonitis → chronic fibrosis if unrecognized; stop drug, give steroids; eosinophilia and diffuse rash support.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 68-year-old woman with a prior diagnosis of asthma presents to your clinic for a routine clinic visit. She complains of occasional palpitations and tremor. Her dyspnea is well controlled. Her past medical history is remarkable for hospitalization for mild congestive heart failure 2 months ago; she notes occasional postprandial acid reflux. Her medications include lisinopril, digoxin, furosemide, an intermittent short-acting inhaled beta agonist, and theophylline. She uses an over-the-counter pill (whose name she cannot remember) for the reflux symptoms. On examination her heart rate is 112 beats per minute. S1 and S2 are normal; she has a mild tremor of the outstretched hands. What is the best next step in her management?
options: Chest x-ray to rule out congestive heart failure.
Discontinue beta agonist and substitute inhaled ipratropium.
answer_text: Theophylline level. Theophylline toxicity precipitated by CYP inhibition (e.g., cimetidine, macrolides, ciprofloxacin) or CHF/infection/age → tremor, palpitations; stop drug and check level; β-agonists preferred bronchodilators.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 23-year-old female is commenced on varenicline to help her stop smoking. Which one of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
answer_text: Nasal continuous positive airway pressure OSA with desaturations → CPAP first-line; grade by AHI; advise weight loss; surgery rarely first; oxygen alone inferior to CPAP.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 47-year-old man is reviewed in the smoking cessation clinic. Which one of the following conditions would contraindicate the prescription of bupropion?
answer_text: Epilepsy Bupropion lowers seizure threshold → contraindicated in epilepsy.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: An 18-year-old woman presents with an acute pulmonary embolism in the ninth week of pregnancy. No obvious factors contributed to the risk of pulmonary embolus. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient throughout her pregnancy?
answer_text: C Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin Postpartum PE/DVT risk → treat with daily LMWH; screen later for thrombophilia given age and no other risks.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 51-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis comes to the clinic with cough, wheeze and fever. Chest X-ray is clear and peak flow is reduced at 380 (510 expected). Labs show CRP 49 mg/l. Which single treatment is most appropriate now?
answer_text: Bronchiectasis Daily copious sputum → bronchiectasis; HRCT shows dilated bronchi with signet-ring; exclude TB, COPD bullae, abscess, cancer.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, headache and a non-productive cough. He has mildly raised liver enzymes, raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and anaemia and he is positive for cold agglutinins. What is the most appropriate treatment?
answer_text: Obtain carboxyhemoglobin level. Firefighter with headache/dizziness → suspect CO poisoning; draw carboxyhemoglobin before O₂, then give high-flow or hyperbaric O₂; CXR may be normal.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 46-A 46-year-old woman is admitted with acute dyspnoea. Investigation shows: Po₂ 7.4 kPa, Pco₂ 3.8 kPa, pH 7.45, peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) 250 L/min (~50% predicted), chest X-ray normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?
answer_text: E Nebulised salbutamol Severe acute asthma: give high-dose nebulized β₂-agonist first; severity markers include PEFR <50%, RR >25, incomplete sentences.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 40-year-old alcoholic develops cough and fever. Chest x-ray, shown below, shows an air-fluid level in the superior segment of the right lower lobe. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?
answer_text: Anaerobes RLL abscess with air–fluid level after aspiration risk and poor dentition → anaerobic necrotizing infection (superior segment RLL typical).

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 25-year-old male presents to the clinic for evaluation of infertility. He has a life-long history of a productive cough and recurrent pulmonary infections. On his review of symptoms he has indicated chronic problems with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and difficulty gaining weight. He also has diabetes mellitus. His chest x-ray suggests bronchiectasis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Cystic fibrosis Adult CF (≈7%) → bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, DM, male infertility; asthma/COPD less consistent at this age without A1AT deficiency.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 40-year-old man without a significant past medical history comes to the emergency room with a 3-day history of fever and shaking chills, and a 15-minute episode of rigor. He also reports a nonproductive cough, anorexia, and the development of right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Shortness of breath has been present for the past 12 hours. Chest x-ray reveals a consolidated right middle lobe infiltrate, and CBC shows an elevated neutrophil count with many band forms present. Which of the following statements regarding pneumonia in this patient is correct?
options: If the sputum Gram stain shows multiple squamous epithelial cells and the culture is reported as mixed flora, the patient probably has a viral infection.
If the Gram stain reveals numerous gram-positive diplococci, numerous white blood cells, and few epithelial cells, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most likely pathogen.
Although S pneumoniae is the agent most likely to be the cause of this patient’s pneumonia, this diagnosis would be unlikely if blood cultures prove negative.
The absence of rigors would rule out a diagnosis of pneumococcal pneumonia.
Penicillin is still the drug of choice in pneumococcal pneumonia.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: An obese 50-year-old woman complains of insomnia, daytime sleepiness, and fatigue. During a sleep study she is found to have recurrent episodes of arterial desaturationabout 30 events per hourwith evidence of obstructive apnea. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for this patient?

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old obese male complains of excessive daytime sleepiness. He has been in good health except for mild hypertension. He drinks alcohol in moderation. The patient’s wife states that he snores at night and awakens frequently. Examination of the oropharynx is normal. Which of the following studies is most appropriate?
options: Study of muscles of respiration during sleep
answer_text: Polysomnography Daytime somnolence + snoring → evaluate with polysomnography (distinguish obstructive vs central); oximetry alone can miss OSA.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 60-year-old male complains of shortness of breath 2 days after a cholecystectomy. He denies fever, chills, sputum production, and pleuritic chest pain. On physical examination, temperature is 37.2C (99F); pulse is 75; respiratory rate is 20; and blood pressure is 120/70. There are diminished breath sounds and dullness over the left base. Trachea is shifted to the left side. A chest x-ray shows a retrocardiac opacity that silhouettes the left diaphragm. Which of the following is the most likely anatomical problem in this patient?
options: Diminished lung volume in the left lower lobe, postoperative atelectasis
answer_text: Diminished lung volume in the left lower lobe, postoperative atelectasis Post-op basilar atelectasis → tracheal shift toward side, elevated density, hemidiaphragm loss; distinguish from pneumonia by lack of consolidation without volume loss.

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing chronic lung disease and episodes of acute bronchitis complains of increasing sputum production, which is now on a daily basis. Sputum is thick, and daily sputum production has dramatically increased over several months. There are flecks of blood in the sputum. The patient has lost 8 lb. Fever and chills are absent, and sputum cultures have not revealed specific pathogens. Chest x-ray and CT are shown on page 78. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s symptoms?

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: A 20-year-old fireman comes to the emergency room complaining of headache and dizziness after helping to put out a garage fire. He does not complain of shortness of breath, and the arterial blood gas shows a normal partial pressure of oxygen. Which of the following is the best first step in the management of this patient?

heading: Respiratory Pre-test MCQ’s
stem: An 18-year-old male presents to your office. His family has noted a blue discoloration of his nose, ears, and fingers. This finding has only been noticed for a few weeks. Which of the following is true?
options: Total hemoglobin is important in determining whether or not a patient will have cyanosis.
Central cyanosis with hypoxia suggests methemoglobinemia or sulfhemoglobinemia.
The presence of clubbing in a cyanotic patient confirms an acute cause of the cyanosis.
Large amounts of methemoglobin are required to produce cyanosis.
answer_text: Total hemoglobin is important in determining whether or not a patient will have cyanosis. Cyanosis workup: chronic vs new; peripheral vs central; central requires ≥4 g/dL deoxy-Hb—interpret with total Hb; check PaO₂/SaO₂; if normoxemic, test met-/sulf-Hb.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 77-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted to hospital with worsening shortness-of-breath. He started a course of amoxicillin given by his GP 5 days ago. On examination blood pressure is 88/60 mmHg with a respiratory rate of 36 / min. A chest x-ray reveals left lower lobe consolidation. Arterial blood gases on air are as follows: pH 7.37 | pCO2 5.5 kPa | pO2 9.1 kPa. What is the most suitable antibiotic therapy?
answer_text: Intravenous co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin CURB-65 = 3 → severe pneumonia → give IV combination antibiotics per BTS.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 22-year-old with known cystic fibrosis is being worked up for a potential lung transplant have suffered multiple chest infections and receiving a minimal response to treatments including chest physio, supplementation and a trial of lumacaftor/ivacaftor. Following assessment, the patient is deemed to meet the criteria for transplant and is placed on the national transplant list to await a potential donor. In this patient, chronic infection with what organism would be a contraindication to this treatment?
answer_text: Burkholderia cepacia CF with chronic Burkholderia cepacia infection → contraindication to lung transplant due to poor outcomes; Aspergillus colonization alone is not a strict contraindication.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 64-year-old woman with a background of asthma is referred to the respiratory clinic with worsening shortness of breath over the past few months. She was diagnosed with asthma when she was in her teens and currently takes an inhaled corticosteroid inhaler with an as required salbutamol inhaler which she rarely uses. She does not describe any wheeze or noctur nal symptoms and her inhaler technique in the clinic is excellent. She tells you that she is compliant with her medications. She has no other medical problems and is a non-smoker. On examination, the patient is sitting comfortably at rest and talking in full sentences. Her oxygen saturations are 96% on air and her body mass index is 30 kg/m^2. Chest examination is clear. As part of the work up the patient had a chest x-ray which shows a normal sized heart and clear lung fields. She has also had some lung function tests which show: FEV1 3.30L (96.1%); FVC 3.92L (88.6%); FEV1/FVC 0.84; TLCO 77.4%; KCO 101.9%. What is the likely cause of the patient’s shortness of breath?
answer_text: Obesity Normal CXR/spirometry, normal KCO with slightly low TLCO, controlled asthma → exertional dyspnea most likely from obesity after excluding other causes.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 76-year-old woman is currently being treated with antibiotics in hospital for a urinary tract infection. Over the last few days, she has developed a cough with productive sputum and is feeling very nauseous. She is also a known alcoholic with difficult social circumstances. A chest X-ray is carried out which shows bilateral cavitating opacities in the upper lobe. What is the most likely causative organism of this clinical picture?

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 55-year-old man attends his GP with 7 day history of general fever and malaise, and a 2 day history of non-productive cough. His eyes have also been sticky and sore for the last few days. He appears visibly unwell, with a fever of 38.2°C and a respiratory rate of 20 /min. There is also some mild splenomegaly. He has no history of recent foreign travel and denies any tuberculosis exposure or contact with anyone who has been ill. He is, however, the proud new owner of George, a red-crested Australian King Parrot, who he has had for a month. What is the most likely cause of this gentleman’s symptoms?
answer_text: Chlamydia psittaci infection Bird exposure + atypical pneumonia → Chlamydia psittaci; severity ranges from mild to multisystem.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 54-year-old man is admitted following presentation with a 10-day history of worsening shortness of breath, cough and fever. He has no past medical history of note. He lives alone and works at a bird sanctuary. He is commenced on treatment with IV co-amoxiclav, however, after 72 hours of treatment, there has been no clinical improvement. Blood culture results taken on admission are obtained and are as follows: Gram stain Negative; Culture positive for Chlamydia psittaci. What action will you take based on these results?
answer_text: Switch to doxycycline Psittacosis (C. psittaci) → treat with tetracyclines.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 29-year-old man is on a hiking expedition up Mount Everest. Upon reaching around 5000m, he starts to feel unwell, complaining to his team members of headache. He appears to have poor coordination and slurred speech. Given the likely occurrence, what is the most appropriate treatment?
answer_text: Descent and dexamethasone High-altitude cerebral edema → immediate descent + dexamethasone.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 34-year-old man is climbing Mount Kilimanjaro. For the past two days he has complained of nausea and a headache. The climbing team is now at an altitude of 4,500m when he develops shortness of breath and a pink frothy cough. Examination reveals bibasal crackles. What is the most appropriate treatment, other than descent?

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 28-year-old man develops nausea and a severe headache whilst trekking in Nepal. Within the next hour he becomes ataxic and confused. A diagnosis of high altitude cerebral oedema is suspected. Other than descent and oxygen, what is the most important treatment?
answer_text: Dexamethasone Acetazolamide is mainly for prevention of altitude illness, not acute treatment.

heading: Respiratory Passmedicine MCQ’s
stem: A 48-year-old male patient with a medical history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with painful swelling in the left submandibular and submental areas. There was tenderness on palpation over the swelling with discharging pus. A facial and oral incision and drainage (R&D) was performed under general anaesthesia. Post-operatively 72-hours later the patient developed a new oxygen requirement with oxygen saturations dropping to 89%. He had a regular heart rate of 75 beats per minute and remained apyrexial. An urgent portable chest radiograph was requested. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: Basal atelectasis Dyspnea and hypoxemia 72 h post-op without fever → suspect basal atelec tasis; CXR shows volume loss with mediastinal shift toward lesion; pneumonia or pneumothorax less likely here.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: A 59-year-old man with a recent CABG some 3 months earlier presents to the clinic for review. His main complaint is shortness of breath on exercise, and particularly on lying flat in bed. His operation is thought to have gone well and he has no residual angina. Medication includes ramipril 10 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg. On examination he looks well, his BP is 123/72 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular; his BMI is 31. His chest is clear on auscultation. Investigations: Haemoglobin 131 g/l, WCC 5.6 × 10^9/l, Platelets 178 × 10^9/l, Sodium 138 mmol/l, Potassium 4.8 mmol/l, Creatinine 110 μmol/l, Vital capacity 88% of predicted, falls to 55% of predicted on lying down. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his shortness of breath?
answer_text: A Diaphragmatic palsy Marked fall in VC supine → diaphragmatic palsy post-surgery.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 24-An anxious 22-year-old woman presented with mild shortness of breath on exertion and intermittent diplopia over the last few weeks. Chest X-ray, lung function tests and electrocardiography were all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer_text: B Myasthenia gravis Fluctuating fatigable weakness with ocular signs → myasthenia gravis; baseline cardiopulmonary tests may be normal.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 30-A 37-year-old man presents with increasing breathlessness and is diagnosed with unilateral emphysema after investigation. Which of the following conditions is most likely to predispose to the development of emphysema?
answer_text: C Childhood bronchiolitis MacLeod syndrome = unilateral hyperlucent lung from childhood bronchiolitis.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 43-In which of the following respiratory diseases is clubbing not a feature?
answer_text: C Chronic bronchitis Clubbing with malignancy, fibrosing alveolitis, asbestosis; not with chronic bronchitis.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 50-Which one of the following features is encountered least frequently in patients with sleep apnoea syndrome?
answer_text: B Female gender Typical phenotype: male, middle-aged, obese.

heading: Respiratory pastest MCQ’s
stem: 51-A 34-year-old woman, who is a non-smoker, is found to have normal lung volumes but a reduced Tico at 45% of predicted. The most likely cause for this picture is which one of the following?
answer_text: E Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation Normal volumes with isolated low TLCO → pulmonary vascular disease; TLCO rises in alveolar hemorrhage/polycythemia; emphysema shows hyperinflation.
